Timeouts are easy to implement and cheap, but choosing the time is hard: too short and you abort transactions that were just slow; too long and real deadlocks waste time. Many systems combine timeouts with detection.

Lock granularity: What exactly gets locked: a row, a page, a table, or the whole database? Fine granularity, such as rows, allows more concurrency but means many locks to manage. Coarse granularity, such as tables, means few locks but more waiting. Multiple granularity locking lets transactions lock at any level of a tree: database, then tables, then pages, then rows. To make this work, it adds intention locks: IS, intention shared, means 'I will take S locks somewhere below'; IX, intention exclusive, means 'I will take X locks somewhere below'; and SIX means shared on this whole node plus intention to write some parts below. Before locking a row in X, a transaction takes IX on the table. Another transaction that wants S on the whole table sees the IX and knows immediately, without checking every row, that it must wait.

Timestamp-ordering protocol: A completely different approach uses no locks. Each transaction Ti gets a timestamp TS(Ti) at start, and the protocol ensures the schedule is equivalent to the serial order of the timestamps. Each item Q keeps a read timestamp, the largest timestamp of any transaction that read Q, and a write timestamp, the largest timestamp of any transaction that wrote Q. If Ti wants to read Q but TS(Ti) is smaller than the write timestamp of Q, a younger transaction has already overwritten the value Ti should have seen, so Ti is rolled back and restarted with a new timestamp. If Ti wants to write Q but a younger transaction has already read or written Q, the write is rejected and Ti is rolled back. Otherwise, the operation runs and the timestamps are updated. There is no waiting, so there are no deadlocks, but there can be many restarts.

Thomas write rule: A small improvement: if Ti wants to write Q, and a younger transaction has already written Q but nobody younger has read it, then Ti's write is obsolete, since it would be overwritten anyway in timestamp order. Instead of rolling Ti back, the Thomas write rule simply ignores the obsolete write. This allows some schedules that are view serializable but not conflict serializable, the blind-write case from lesson 21.

Multiversion concurrency control: Many modern databases, including PostgreSQL, Oracle and MySQL's InnoDB engine, keep several versions of each row. When a transaction updates a row, it creates a new version instead of overwriting the old one. Each reading transaction sees a snapshot: the versions that were committed when it started, or when its statement started, depending on the isolation level. The big benefit is that readers never block writers and writers never block readers. Writers still conflict with other writers on the same row. Old versions are cleaned up later, when no transaction can need them; in PostgreSQL this cleanup is called vacuum.

SQL isolation levels: SQL lets you choose how much isolation you want, trading safety for speed, with SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL. READ UNCOMMITTED allows dirty reads, unrepeatable reads and phantoms. READ COMMITTED prevents dirty reads, but still allows unrepeatable reads and phantoms. REPEATABLE READ also prevents unrepeatable reads, but the standard still allows phantoms. SERIALIZABLE prevents all three and guarantees serializable execution. Defaults differ: PostgreSQL uses READ COMMITTED by default, and MySQL's InnoDB uses REPEATABLE READ. Real systems sometimes give more than the standard demands at a given level, so read your database's documentation.

Optimistic methods: Some systems use validation, also called optimistic concurrency control. Each transaction works on private copies without locks, in a read phase. At commit, a validation phase checks whether any conflict happened with transactions that committed meanwhile. If not, the write phase installs the changes; if so, the transaction is restarted. This works well when conflicts are rare, such as mostly-read workloads, and badly when many transactions fight over the same rows. Many web apps use a simple version of this idea with a version column: UPDATE ... SET qty = 4, version = 8 WHERE id = 10 AND version = 7; if zero rows change, someone else updated first.

Real-life example 1, bank transfers between the same accounts: Two transfers run at once: one from account A to B, another from B to A. Under strict 2PL, the first locks A and the second locks B, then each requests the other's account. That is a deadlock. The bank's DBMS detects the cycle in the wait-for graph within a second, aborts one transfer, and the app automatically retries it. A common trick to avoid such deadlocks entirely is to always lock accounts in a fixed order, such as by account number, so cycles cannot form.

Real-life example 2, flash sale on an e-commerce site: During a big sale, thousands of buyers read product pages while a few hundred buy. With MVCC, the readers browsing prices and pictures never wait for the buyers updating stock, because they read a snapshot. The buyers updating the same product's stock count do conflict with each other, so each update locks that row briefly and stock decreases correctly one at a time. Choosing READ COMMITTED for browsing and careful row locking, such as SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, for the purchase step keeps the site both fast and correct.

Common mistakes and exam favourites: Thinking 2PL prevents deadlocks; it does not. Mixing up wait-die and wound-wait; remember that in both, the older transaction never gets aborted for requesting, and in wound-wait the older one is the attacker. Forgetting that basic 2PL can cascade and only strict 2PL avoids it. Claiming SERIALIZABLE is the default everywhere; it usually is not. Typical exam questions: show that a schedule follows or breaks 2PL, find the lock point, draw a wait-for graph and find the deadlock, trace wait-die or wound-wait on given timestamps, apply timestamp-ordering rules to a schedule, and list which anomalies each isolation level allows.

Recap: Shared locks allow many readers; exclusive locks allow one writer. Two-phase locking, growing then shrinking, guarantees conflict serializability, and strict or rigorous 2PL also avoids cascading rollbacks. Deadlocks are handled by detection with wait-for graphs, prevention with wait-die or wound-wait, or timeouts. Intention locks make locking at several granularities efficient. Timestamp ordering and the Thomas write rule order transactions without locks, MVCC lets readers and writers avoid blocking each other, and SQL isolation levels let applications trade safety for speed. Next lesson covers what happens when the system crashes: recovery.
key_points: Shared (S) locks are compatible with each other; exclusive (X) locks are compatible with nothing.
Two-phase locking: a growing phase then a shrinking phase; it guarantees conflict serializability, ordered by lock points.
Strict 2PL holds X locks until commit or abort; rigorous 2PL holds all locks until the end; both avoid cascading rollbacks.
Deadlocks: detect cycles in a wait-for graph and abort a victim, or prevent with wait-die (older waits, younger dies) or wound-wait (older wounds younger, younger waits), or use timeouts.
Intention locks (IS, IX, SIX) make multiple-granularity locking efficient.
Timestamp ordering rolls back operations that arrive too late; the Thomas write rule ignores obsolete writes; MVCC keeps versions so readers and writers do not block each other.
Isolation levels: READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE, each preventing more anomalies.
lessons.tip: Learn wait-die and wound-wait with one sentence each: in wait-die, the old wait patiently and the young die; in wound-wait, the old push the young aside and the young wait. Then practise on a small table of timestamps until the answer is automatic.
lessons.task: T1 has timestamp 5, T2 has 10 and T3 has 15. T2 holds a lock that T1 requests, and T3 requests a lock held by T1. For both wait-die and wound-wait, write what happens to each request. Then write a schedule for two transactions that follows basic 2PL but not strict 2PL.

quiz.q: Which lock pair is compatible?
quiz.explain: Many readers can share an item; any exclusive lock must be alone.

quiz.q: What does two-phase locking guarantee?
quiz.explain: Every 2PL schedule is conflict serializable; it can still deadlock, and basic 2PL can still cascade.

quiz.q: In wait-die, an older transaction requests a lock held by a younger one. What happens?
quiz.explain: In wait-die, older transactions wait; younger requesters die.

quiz.q: How is a deadlock detected?
options: By finding a cycle in the wait-for graph
quiz.explain: A cycle in the wait-for graph means each transaction in it waits for the next, forever.

quiz.q: Which SQL isolation level prevents dirty reads but still allows unrepeatable reads?
quiz.explain: READ COMMITTED reads only committed data, but a value can change between two reads in the same transaction.

lessons.title: Recovery: Surviving Crashes Without Losing Data
lessons.content:
Load-shedding hits your area in the middle of the evening. Your laptop has a battery, but the bank's server room down the road might not be so lucky: the power drops, the UPS fails, and every computer goes dark in the middle of thousands of transactions. When the power comes back, some transfers were committed, some were halfway, and much of the recent work was only in memory, which is now empty. Yet when the bank's system restarts, every committed transfer is there and every unfinished one has vanished cleanly. The part of the DBMS that makes this happen is the recovery manager, and this lesson explains how it works.

The job of recovery: The recovery manager guarantees two ACID properties from lesson 20. Atomicity: transactions that did not commit must leave no trace. Durability: transactions that did commit must not lose any change. After any failure, it must bring the database back to a state that contains exactly the effects of committed transactions.

Types of failure: A transaction failure happens when one transaction cannot continue: a logical error such as a constraint violation or division by zero, or a system decision such as being chosen as a deadlock victim. A system crash is a power cut, an operating-system crash or a DBMS bug that wipes main memory but leaves disks intact; this is called the fail-stop assumption, because the disk contents are assumed not to be corrupted. A disk failure, such as a head crash, destroys data on disk, and recovering from it needs copies kept elsewhere.

Storage types: Volatile storage, main memory and caches, loses everything in a crash. Non-volatile storage, disks and SSDs, survives crashes but can still fail. Stable storage is an ideal: storage that never loses data. We approximate it by keeping multiple copies on separate devices, for example mirrored disks or copies in different buildings, and writing them carefully one after another so that at least one good copy always exists. The log must be kept on stable storage.

Why it is hard: buffers: As lesson 16 explained, the DBMS changes pages in its buffer pool in memory and writes them to disk later. So at the moment of a crash, a committed transaction's changes may still be only in memory, which threatens durability, and an uncommitted transaction's changes may already be on disk because the buffer manager wrote a page early to free space, which threatens atomicity. Recovery must fix both problems.

The log: The solution is the log, a sequential file of records describing every change. A typical update record is written <T1, A, 1000, 950>: transaction T1 changed item A, the old value was 1,000 and the new value is 950. Other records mark <T1 start>, <T1 commit> and <T1 abort>. The old value lets the system undo a change; the new value lets it redo a change. Because the log is written sequentially, appending to it is fast, much faster than writing the scattered data pages.

Write-ahead logging: The single most important rule in recovery is write-ahead logging, WAL. First, before a changed data page is written to disk, the log records describing changes on that page must already be on stable storage. Second, a transaction is committed only when its commit record, and all its earlier log records, are on stable storage. Rule one guarantees we can always undo anything that reached the disk. Rule two guarantees we can always redo any committed change, even if its data pages never reached the disk. The moment the commit record is safely in the log is the true moment of commit.

Deferred versus immediate modification: In deferred modification, a transaction does not change the database on disk until it commits; all its writes wait in the log or in private memory. Then recovery never needs undo, only redo. In immediate modification, changes may reach the database before commit, which is more flexible and what real systems do, so recovery needs both undo and redo. The rest of this lesson assumes immediate modification.

Undo and redo: undo(Ti) restores every item Ti wrote to its old value, working backwards through Ti's log records, and finally writes <Ti abort>. redo(Ti) sets every item Ti wrote to its new value, working forwards. Both must be idempotent: running them twice, for example if the system crashes again during recovery, gives the same result as running them once. Writing values, rather than applying 'subtract 50', makes this true.

Which transactions to undo and redo: After a crash, scan the log. A transaction with <Ti start> and either <Ti commit> or <Ti abort> in the log must be redone, which repeats its changes, or for an aborted one repeats its undo actions. A transaction with <Ti start> but neither commit nor abort was in progress at the crash and must be undone. Redoing even committed transactions whose changes may already be on disk is harmless because redo is idempotent.

Checkpoints: Without help, recovery would have to scan the whole log since the database was created, and redo everything. A checkpoint limits this. Periodically, the system writes all log records in memory to stable storage, writes all modified buffer pages to disk, and then writes a log record <checkpoint L>, where L is the list of transactions active at that moment. After a crash, transactions that committed before the last checkpoint need no redo, because their pages were already flushed. Recovery only needs to start from the last checkpoint, plus older log records of transactions in L that must be undone.

Worked example: The log at the moment of the crash reads: 1 <T1 start>; 2 <T1, A, 1000, 950>; 3 <T2 start>; 4 <T1, B, 2000, 2050>; 5 <T1 commit>; 6 <checkpoint {T2}>; 7 <T2, C, 700, 600>; 8 <T3 start>; 9 <T3, A, 950, 900>; 10 <T3 commit>; 11 <T2, D, 500, 400>; then the crash. T1 committed before the checkpoint, so its changes, A = 950 and B = 2,050, are already on disk.

The redo phase: Start at the checkpoint with an undo list of {T2}, the active transactions it names. Scan forward, repeating every update: set C = 600, see <T3 start> and add T3 to the undo list, set A = 900, see <T3 commit> and remove T3 from the list, set D = 400. This is called repeating history: it brings the database to its exact state at the crash. At the end of the scan, the undo list is {T2}.

The undo phase: Now scan backward from the end, undoing every update of transactions in the undo list. Record 11 belongs to T2: restore D = 500 and log the restore. Record 9 belongs to T3, which committed, so skip it. Record 7 belongs to T2: restore C = 700. Continue back to <T2 start>, then write <T2 abort>; the undo list is empty, so stop. Final state: A = 900, B = 2,050, C = 700, D = 500. T1's and T3's committed changes all survived; T2's unfinished changes all vanished. That is atomicity and durability, delivered.

Compensation and ARIES: The restore steps written during undo are called compensation log records or redo-only records; if the system crashes again during recovery, they are redone, not undone, so work is never undone twice. The industrial-strength algorithm, ARIES, developed at IBM in the early 1990s, refines these ideas with three phases, analysis, redo and undo, using log sequence numbers stored on every page so it can skip redo for changes already on disk. It also uses fuzzy checkpoints, which do not stop all activity, and many modern databases follow its design.

Shadow paging: An older alternative avoids a log for undo. The database keeps a page table pointing to pages on disk. A transaction copies each page before changing it and updates a new, shadow page table. At commit, one atomic write switches the root pointer from the old page table to the new one. A crash before the switch leaves the old, consistent database untouched. Shadow paging is simple, but it scatters data across the disk and makes concurrency hard, so large databases rarely use it. The same copy-on-write idea lives on in some file systems and in SQLite's rollback journal, which saves the original pages before they are changed.

Disk failure and backups: Logs protect against crashes, but if the disk itself dies, the data and perhaps the log are gone. Protection comes from regular backups, also called dumps or archives, copied to separate storage, together with archived logs. To recover, restore the latest backup, then redo the archived log from the backup time forward. This is how a bank can recover even if a whole data centre is lost: backups and log copies are shipped to a second site, often in another city. RAID disks, which store data redundantly across several disks, reduce how often this is needed but are not a replacement for backups.

Real-life example 1, mobile banking during load-shedding: A customer transfers money and sees 'Success' a split second before the bank's server room loses power. Was the transfer saved? Yes: the success message was sent only after the commit record reached stable storage, thanks to write-ahead logging. On restart, the redo phase reapplies the transfer from the log, even though the account pages in memory were lost. Another customer's transfer that had debited but not yet credited when the power failed is undone, and that customer simply sees the transfer did not happen.

Real-life example 2, a university server's disk dies: The disk holding the result database fails during exam season. The administrators install a new disk, restore last night's backup, and replay the archived log up to the moment of failure. Every mark entered today is back. If they had kept backups but no archived log, today's entries would be lost, and teachers would have to type them again, which shows why logs must be archived along with backups.

Common mistakes and exam favourites: Saying the commit happens when the data pages are written; it happens when the commit record is on stable storage. Forgetting that undo goes backward and redo goes forward. Redoing only committed transactions and forgetting the 'repeat history' approach that redoes everything after the checkpoint and then undoes the incomplete ones. Confusing a checkpoint with a backup. Typical exam questions: state the WAL rules, explain deferred versus immediate modification, and, most often, given a log with a checkpoint and a crash point, list which transactions are redone and undone and give the final values.

Recap: Failures can hit a single transaction, wipe memory, or destroy disks. The log records old and new values of every change; write-ahead logging forces log records to stable storage before data pages and before commit. Recovery redoes history from the last checkpoint and then undoes the transactions that never finished, using idempotent operations and compensation records. ARIES is the real-world refinement. Shadow paging is a log-free alternative, and backups with archived logs protect against disk loss. Next lesson leaves the single server behind: NoSQL and distributed databases.
key_points: Recovery guarantees atomicity and durability after transaction failures, system crashes and disk failures.
An update log record holds the transaction, item, old value and new value: <T1, A, 1000, 950>.
Write-ahead logging: log records reach stable storage before the data page they describe, and the commit record reaches stable storage before commit is reported.
Immediate modification needs both undo (old values, backward) and redo (new values, forward); deferred modification needs only redo.
Checkpoints flush log and dirty pages and record active transactions, so recovery starts from the last checkpoint.
Recovery repeats history in a forward redo pass, then undoes incomplete transactions in a backward pass, ending each with an abort record.
Backups plus archived logs protect against disk failure; shadow paging is a copy-on-write alternative to logging.
lessons.tip: Practise recovery questions with a table of four columns: log record number, record, action in redo pass, action in undo pass. Filling the table row by row turns a confusing log into a mechanical exercise, and examiners can follow your reasoning easily.
lessons.task: A log reads: <T1 start>; <T1, X, 10, 20>; <T2 start>; <T2, Y, 5, 15>; <checkpoint {T1, T2}>; <T1 commit>; <T3 start>; <T3, X, 20, 30>; <T2, Z, 1, 2>; crash. List the undo list after the redo pass, the actions in the undo pass, and the final values of X, Y and Z.

quiz.q: Under write-ahead logging, what must happen before a modified data page is written to disk?
options: The log records for changes on that page must be on stable storage
quiz.explain: WAL requires log records describing a page's changes to reach stable storage before the page itself, so the change can always be undone.

quiz.q: After a crash, which transactions must be undone?
options: Those with a start record but no commit or abort record
All transactions since the database was created
Only those listed in the last backup
quiz.explain: Transactions without commit or abort were in progress at the crash, so atomicity requires undoing them.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a checkpoint?
options: To limit how much of the log recovery must process
quiz.explain: By flushing dirty pages and recording active transactions, a checkpoint lets recovery start near the end of the log.

quiz.q: In the worked example, T2 wrote C from 700 to 600 and D from 500 to 400 but never committed. What are C and D after recovery?
quiz.explain: T2 is undone in the backward pass, restoring the old values 700 and 500.

quiz.q: Why must undo and redo operations be idempotent?
options: So that a crash during recovery and a repeated recovery give the same correct result
So that they need no log
So that checkpoints can be skipped
quiz.explain: Recovery itself might be interrupted; applying the same undo or redo twice must not change the result.

lessons.title: NoSQL and Distributed Databases: Beyond One Server
lessons.content:
Imagine a single shop in Dhaka that suddenly gets customers from every district, then from other countries. One shopkeeper, one counter and one register cannot keep up, no matter how fast they work. The solution is many branches, each with its own staff and records, that somehow stay in agreement. Big apps face the same problem with data. A relational database on one server works beautifully up to a point, but a social network with hundreds of millions of users, or a ride app tracking drivers every few seconds, needs data spread over many machines. This lesson covers how data is distributed, the trade-offs that come with it, and the NoSQL databases built for this world.

Scaling up versus scaling out: There are two ways to handle more load. Scaling up, or vertical scaling, means buying a bigger server: more CPU, memory and faster disks. It is simple, but there is a ceiling and the price rises steeply. Scaling out, or horizontal scaling, means adding more ordinary machines and splitting the work. It can grow much further and survive the loss of a machine, but it makes everything else harder: queries, transactions and consistency now involve the network.

Replication: Replication keeps copies of the same data on several machines. Benefits: if one machine dies, another has the data, giving high availability; and reads can be spread across copies, giving more read capacity. In a leader-follower setup, also called primary-replica, all writes go to the leader, which sends changes to the followers; reads can go anywhere. Synchronous replication waits for followers to confirm each write, which is safe but slower; asynchronous replication does not wait, which is fast, but a follower may briefly show old data, and recent writes can be lost if the leader dies before sending them.

Sharding: Sharding, also called horizontal partitioning, splits the rows of a table across machines, each holding a part called a shard. Students with ids 1 to 1,000,000 on server 1, 1,000,001 to 2,000,000 on server 2, and so on, is range sharding. Hashing the id to pick a server is hash sharding, which spreads load evenly but makes range queries visit every shard. Choosing the shard key is crucial: queries that include the key go to one shard and are fast; queries that do not must ask every shard. Real systems combine both ideas: each shard is replicated.

Adding machines and rebalancing: When a sharded system grows, data must move to the new machines. With naive hashing, such as id mod 4, adding a fifth server changes the target of most keys, so almost all data would move. Consistent hashing fixes this: servers and keys are placed on the same circle of hash values, and each key belongs to the next server clockwise. Adding a server takes over only the keys between it and its neighbour, a small fraction of the total. Many distributed key-value and column-family stores, including Cassandra, use this idea.

Distributed queries: A join between tables stored on different machines must ship data over the network, which is often slower than reading disks. So distributed optimizers count network transfer as a major cost. A classic trick is the semi-join: instead of sending a whole table to the other site, send only the distinct join-key values, let the other site keep only the rows that will match, and send those back. Placing tables that are often joined on the same shard key, so matching rows live on the same machine, avoids the problem altogether.

Distributed transactions and two-phase commit: If a transaction changes rows on two different servers, both must commit or both must abort. The classic protocol is two-phase commit, 2PC. A coordinator first sends 'prepare' to every participant; each one makes its changes durable in its log and votes yes, or votes no if it cannot. In phase two, if all voted yes, the coordinator sends 'commit'; if any voted no, it sends 'abort'. It is safe, but it has a famous weakness: if the coordinator crashes after participants voted yes, they are stuck, holding locks, unable to decide alone. That is why 2PC is called a blocking protocol, and why many large systems try to avoid distributed transactions.

The CAP theorem: In a distributed system, network links between machines can fail, splitting the machines into groups that cannot talk, called a network partition. The CAP theorem, proposed by Eric Brewer around 2000 and proved by Gilbert and Lynch in 2002, says that during a partition, a system must choose between consistency, meaning every read sees the latest write, and availability, meaning every request to a working machine gets a response. P, partition tolerance, is not really optional, because networks do fail. So the real choice is: during a partition, refuse some requests to stay consistent, or answer them and risk stale data.

CP and AP choices: A bank's balance system typically chooses consistency: it is better to show 'Service temporarily unavailable' than to let two branches each approve a withdrawal of the same money. A social network's like counter typically chooses availability: showing 1,203 likes instead of 1,205 for a few seconds harms nobody, while refusing to load the page annoys millions. When there is no partition, a system can offer both, but there is still a trade-off between consistency and latency, because waiting for other machines to agree takes time.

BASE and eventual consistency: In contrast to ACID, many distributed NoSQL systems describe themselves as BASE: Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent. Eventual consistency means that if no new updates happen, all replicas will eventually hold the same value, but in the meantime different replicas may answer differently. Some systems let you tune this per request using quorums: with N copies, a write waits for W of them and a read asks R of them; if R + W is greater than N, every read overlaps with every write and sees the latest value.

Weaker guarantees users still expect: Even an eventually consistent system should give some common-sense promises. Read-your-writes consistency means that after you post a comment, you yourself will see it, even if friends see it a moment later; systems often achieve this by sending your reads to the leader for a short time after you write. Monotonic reads mean you never see data go back in time, for example a like count dropping from 1,205 to 1,203 on refresh. These smaller guarantees make an eventually consistent app feel normal to its users.

What NoSQL means: NoSQL is a loose name, often read as 'not only SQL', for databases that do not use the relational table model as their main structure. They grew popular in the late 2000s, when web companies needed huge scale, flexible data shapes and high availability. There are four main families: key-value, document, column-family and graph stores. Many now support some SQL-like querying and some transactions, so the line between SQL and NoSQL is blurrier than it once was.

Key-value stores: The simplest model: a giant dictionary from keys to values. You can put a value under a key, get it back, and delete it, very fast, often from memory. The database does not look inside the value. Redis is a popular example, widely used for caching, session storage, counters and leaderboards. Use it when you always look things up by a known key, such as a session id or a user's shopping cart.

Document stores: A document store keeps self-describing documents, usually JSON-like, each with its own fields and possibly nested lists. A student document might hold name, department and a list of enrollments inside it, so one read fetches everything for a profile page, with no joins. Different documents in the same collection can have different fields. MongoDB is a well-known example. Document stores suit data that is naturally read as a whole unit, like a product with variable attributes; they are weaker when data is heavily shared and related across documents.

Column-family stores: Also called wide-column stores, they organize data into rows identified by a key, with many columns grouped into families, and each row can have different columns. They are designed for huge write volumes spread across many machines. Apache Cassandra and HBase are examples, used for things like sensor readings, message histories and activity logs. Data is usually modelled around the queries you will run, often duplicating it in several tables, each shaped for one query.

Graph databases: A graph database stores nodes, such as people, places or products, and edges, such as 'friend of', 'lives in' or 'bought', with properties on both. Queries follow edges: friends of friends who like cricket, or the shortest path between two stations. In a relational database, such multi-hop queries need many self-joins; in a graph database, following edges is the basic operation. Neo4j is a well-known example, used for social networks, recommendation and fraud detection.

SQL versus NoSQL, how to choose: Choose a relational database when data is structured and related, when you need joins, constraints and strong ACID transactions, such as for banking, inventory, accounts and student records. This is the right default for most applications. Choose a NoSQL store when a specific need dominates: massive scale with simple access patterns, very flexible or nested data, extremely low latency lookups, or graph-shaped questions. Many real systems use both: a relational database as the source of truth, plus Redis for caching and a search engine for full-text search. This is sometimes called polyglot persistence.

Real-life example 1, a ride-sharing app: Driver locations change every few seconds for thousands of drivers. Storing them in a key-value or in-memory store keyed by driver id gives fast updates and lookups. Trips and payments, which involve money and must be exact, go into a relational database with full ACID transactions. The map of nearby drivers can tolerate being a second out of date; the fare charged to a rider cannot. Choosing different stores for different consistency needs is exactly the CAP trade-off in practice.

Real-life example 2, a national e-commerce site during a sale: Product catalogue pages, with many different attributes for phones, clothes and groceries, fit a document model and are cached heavily. Orders and stock levels need consistency, so they live in a relational database, sharded by order id or region, with replicas for reads. If one data centre loses its network link, the site might keep showing products from a replica, choosing availability, but refuse to confirm orders until it can be sure stock is correct, choosing consistency for the part that handles money.

Common mistakes and exam favourites: Saying NoSQL is always faster or always better at scale; it is better for specific access patterns and often gives up joins and strong consistency. Reading CAP as 'pick any two of three'; partitions are not optional, so the choice is consistency or availability during a partition. Confusing replication, which copies the same data, with sharding, which splits different data. Forgetting that 2PC can block if the coordinator fails. Typical exam questions: compare SQL and NoSQL, describe the four NoSQL families with examples, explain CAP and BASE, explain 2PC, and contrast replication with sharding.

Recap: Scaling out spreads data over many machines through replication, which copies data for availability and read capacity, and sharding, which splits data for write capacity and size. Distributed transactions use two-phase commit, which is safe but can block. The CAP theorem says that during a network partition, a system must choose consistency or availability. BASE systems accept eventual consistency, which quorums can tune. NoSQL stores come in four families: key-value, document, column-family and graph, each fitting particular access patterns, while relational databases remain the right default for structured, related data. Next lesson closes the course with security, data warehouses and a full recap.
key_points: Scaling up buys a bigger server; scaling out adds more machines and makes queries and transactions distributed.
Replication copies the same data to several machines for availability and read capacity; sharding splits different rows across machines.
Two-phase commit: prepare and vote, then commit or abort; it is blocking if the coordinator fails.
CAP: during a network partition, a system must choose consistency or availability.
BASE systems are eventually consistent; with quorums, R + W > N ensures reads see the latest write.
NoSQL families: key-value (Redis), document (MongoDB), column-family (Cassandra, HBase), graph (Neo4j).
Relational databases remain the default for structured, related data needing ACID; many systems combine several stores.
lessons.tip: For each NoSQL family, remember one example product and one typical use: Redis for caching sessions, MongoDB for product catalogues, Cassandra for sensor or message logs, Neo4j for friend recommendations. Exam answers with concrete examples score better than definitions alone.
lessons.task: Design the data storage for a food delivery app in your city. Decide which data goes into a relational database, which into a key-value store, and which could use a document store, and explain each choice. Then describe what the app should do with restaurant menus and with payments if one data centre loses network contact.

quiz.q: What is the difference between replication and sharding?
options: Replication splits data; sharding copies it
Replication copies the same data to several machines; sharding splits different data across machines
Replication is only for NoSQL; sharding is only for SQL
quiz.explain: Replicas hold the same data for availability; shards hold different parts of the data for scale.

quiz.q: According to the CAP theorem, what must a distributed system choose during a network partition?
quiz.explain: Partitions cannot be ruled out, so during one the system either refuses some requests to stay consistent or answers them and risks stale data.

quiz.q: Which is the main weakness of two-phase commit?
options: It cannot handle more than two servers
Participants can be blocked if the coordinator fails after they vote yes
quiz.explain: Prepared participants cannot decide alone, so they wait, holding locks, until the coordinator recovers.

quiz.q: Which kind of database fits 'find friends of friends who like cricket' most naturally?
quiz.explain: Graph databases store relationships as edges and make following several hops the basic operation.

quiz.q: With N = 3 replicas, which quorum setting guarantees that every read sees the latest write?
quiz.explain: R + W = 4 is greater than N = 3, so every read set overlaps every write set.

lessons.title: Security, Data Warehouses and Course Wrap-up
lessons.content:
A bank vault is not protected by one lock. There is a guard at the door who checks who you are, a list of who may open which locker, cameras recording every visit, and thick walls so that even a stolen key is not enough. Databases need the same layers, because they hold the most valuable data a company has: money, health records, exam results, national ID numbers. This final lesson covers database security, then looks at a different use of data, analysis in data warehouses, and ends with a recap of the whole course so you can see how all 25 lessons fit together.

Security goals: Database security protects three things, often called CIA. Confidentiality: only authorized people can read data, so your medical history is not visible to random staff. Integrity: only authorized people can change data, and only in allowed ways, so nobody can quietly raise their own exam marks. Availability: authorized people can use the data when they need it, so attacks or failures do not lock out a hospital at night. Each security feature serves one or more of these goals.

Authentication: Authentication answers 'who are you?' Users log in with a username and password, and increasingly with a second factor, like a code sent to a phone, or with certificates for programs. A database should never store passwords as plain text; it should store a salted hash, produced by a slow password-hashing function such as bcrypt or Argon2, so that a stolen table does not reveal the passwords. Applications should connect with their own database accounts, never with the all-powerful administrator account.

Authorization and privileges: Authorization answers 'what may you do?' SQL uses GRANT and REVOKE, as you saw in lesson 12: GRANT SELECT ON student TO advisor; GRANT SELECT, UPDATE (grade) ON enroll TO teacher; REVOKE UPDATE ON enroll FROM teacher. Privileges can be on whole tables, on specific columns, or on views, which lets you show only certain rows and columns. The principle of least privilege says each user and program should get only the privileges it truly needs, so a mistake or a stolen password causes limited damage.

Roles: Granting privileges to hundreds of people one by one is error-prone. A role is a named bundle of privileges: CREATE ROLE teacher; GRANT SELECT, UPDATE (grade) ON enroll TO teacher; then GRANT teacher TO rahim, karim. When a new teacher joins, one GRANT gives them everything; when someone leaves, one REVOKE removes it. This is role-based access control, and it is how most organizations manage database permissions. Privileges can also be passed on WITH GRANT OPTION, but that should be used carefully, because revoking later can cascade.

SQL injection: The most famous database attack. Suppose a login page builds a query by gluing user input into a string: 'SELECT * FROM student WHERE name = '' + input + '''. If the user types ' OR '1'='1, the query becomes WHERE name = '' OR '1'='1', which is true for every row. In our test database, this glued-together query returned all 5 students instead of none. Worse inputs can drop tables or read password columns. Injection has caused many real data breaches, and it still appears regularly in security reports.

Preventing injection: The fix is prepared statements, also called parameterized queries: SELECT * FROM student WHERE name = ? with the input passed separately as a parameter. The database treats the parameter purely as a value, never as SQL code, so ' OR '1'='1 is just a strange name that matches nobody. In our test, the parameterized version returned 0 rows for the same input. Extra layers help too: validate input, use least-privilege accounts so even a successful injection cannot drop tables, and never show raw database error messages to users.

Encryption: Encryption protects data if someone gets the bytes without permission. Encryption in transit, with TLS, protects data travelling between the application and the database, so nobody on the network can read it. Encryption at rest protects data files and backups on disk, so a stolen disk or backup tape is useless without the key. Very sensitive columns, such as national ID numbers, can be encrypted individually. The keys must be stored separately from the data, or the protection is meaningless.

Auditing and other protections: Auditing records who did what and when: logins, failed logins, changes to grades or balances. Triggers from lesson 12 can write simple audit logs, and most database systems have built-in audit features. Logs help discover attacks and settle disputes. Backups, from lesson 23, protect availability against ransomware that encrypts data and demands payment. Statistical databases that publish only totals must also be careful, because combining many aggregate queries can sometimes reveal an individual's data.

Views as a security tool: Views from lesson 11 are one of the simplest security tools. Instead of giving an advisor access to the whole student table, you can create a view that shows only the name, department and CGPA of students in the advisor's department, and grant SELECT on that view only. The advisor never sees phone numbers or addresses, and never sees students from other departments. Some systems go further with row-level security, where the database itself automatically adds a filter to every query based on who is logged in.

OLTP versus OLAP: So far, most of this course has been about online transaction processing, OLTP: many small, fast transactions that read and write a few rows, like transfers, enrollments and orders. Online analytical processing, OLAP, is different: few but huge queries that read millions of rows to answer questions like 'total sales by district per month for the last three years'. Running such queries on the busy OLTP database would slow down customers. So organizations copy data into a separate system built for analysis.

Data warehouses: A data warehouse is a large database that collects historical data from many operational systems, cleaned and organized for analysis. It is subject-oriented, organized around topics like sales or students; integrated, combining data from different sources into one consistent format; time-variant, keeping history for years; and non-volatile, mostly loaded and read, rarely updated. Decision makers use it to see trends and plan.

ETL: Data reaches the warehouse through ETL: Extract, Transform, Load. Extract pulls data from sources, such as the sales database, the HR system and spreadsheets. Transform cleans and reshapes it: fixing spellings like 'Chittagong' versus 'Chattogram', converting currencies and dates, removing duplicates, and computing summary values. Load writes it into the warehouse, usually in scheduled batches, such as every night. Data cleaning in the transform step often takes most of the effort in a warehouse project.

Star schema: Warehouses usually use a star schema. In the centre is a fact table holding measurements of events, such as each sale: quantity, amount, plus foreign keys. Around it are dimension tables that describe the context: product, store, customer and date, with attributes such as category, district and month. Queries join the fact table with a few dimensions and group by dimension attributes. A snowflake schema normalizes the dimensions further, splitting district into a separate region table, for example; it saves space but needs more joins. Warehouses deliberately accept some redundancy in dimensions for simpler, faster queries, unlike the normalization rules of lessons 14 and 15.

OLAP operations: Analysts think of warehouse data as a cube with dimensions like product, place and time. Roll-up summarizes to a coarser level, from daily to monthly sales. Drill-down goes to finer detail, from district totals to individual stores. Slice fixes one dimension, such as only the year 2025; dice picks a sub-cube with several conditions. Pivot rotates the view, swapping rows and columns. SQL supports this with GROUP BY plus extensions like ROLLUP and CUBE in many systems, and warehouses use column storage and bitmap indexes, from lesson 17, to make it fast. Data mining then searches warehouse data for patterns, such as products often bought together.

Real-life example 1, a university portal: Students log in with authentication; advisors have a role that can read their advisees' records through a view; teachers can update only the grade column of enroll, for their own courses. All queries use parameters, so a student typing a quote into the search box cannot inject SQL. Grade changes are audited by a trigger, so if a grade changes after publication, the log shows who did it and when. Each of these is a small step, and together they make the system trustworthy.

Real-life example 2, a retail chain's warehouse: Every night, ETL extracts the day's sales from hundreds of outlet systems, cleans product names and district spellings, and loads them into a star schema with sales facts and product, outlet and date dimensions. The next morning, managers roll up sales by division, drill down into the outlets with falling sales, and slice by the Eid season to plan stock for next year. Meanwhile, the stores' OLTP systems keep processing customers at full speed, untouched by these heavy queries.

The whole course in one map: Lessons 1 and 2 explained why DBMSs exist and how they are built in layers. Lessons 3 to 6 covered modelling: ER diagrams, mapping to tables, the relational model and relational algebra. Lessons 7 to 12 taught SQL, from creating tables to joins, subqueries, views, triggers, privileges and programs. Lessons 13 to 15 covered design theory: functional dependencies and normal forms up to BCNF and 4NF. Lessons 16 to 19 opened the engine: storage, indexes, query processing and optimization. Lessons 20 to 23 covered transactions, serializability, concurrency control and recovery. Lesson 24 went beyond one server, and this lesson added security and analytics.

How it fits together: When you click 'Pay' in an app, every part of this course works at once. Authentication and privileges check who you are and what you may do. A prepared SQL statement, written against a well-normalized schema designed from an ER model, is parsed, optimized using statistics and run with indexes over pages in the buffer pool. It runs inside a transaction protected by locks or versions, logged ahead so a crash cannot lose it, perhaps replicated to another city. That night, ETL copies it into a warehouse where managers analyse it. Seeing this full chain is the real goal of a DBMS course.

Common mistakes and exam favourites: Building SQL by string concatenation with user input. Giving applications the administrator account. Confusing authentication, who you are, with authorization, what you may do. Running heavy analytics on the live OLTP database. Assuming warehouses must be fully normalized like OLTP schemas. Typical exam questions: explain SQL injection with an example and its prevention; write GRANT, REVOKE and role statements; compare OLTP and OLAP; draw a star schema for a given business; explain ETL; and define roll-up, drill-down, slice and dice.

Recap: Database security protects confidentiality, integrity and availability through authentication, authorization with GRANT, REVOKE and roles, least privilege, prepared statements against SQL injection, encryption in transit and at rest, auditing and backups. Analysis runs separately in data warehouses, fed by ETL and organized as star or snowflake schemas, with OLAP operations like roll-up and drill-down. With this, you have seen a database from its design and SQL down to pages, indexes, plans, transactions, logs and distributed copies. Build a small project that uses them together, and the whole course will come to life.
key_points: Security goals are confidentiality, integrity and availability.
Authentication checks who you are; authorization, with GRANT, REVOKE and roles, controls what you may do; follow least privilege.
SQL injection happens when user input is glued into SQL text; prepared statements with parameters prevent it.
Encrypt data in transit with TLS and at rest on disks and backups; keep keys separate; audit sensitive actions.
OLTP runs many small transactions; OLAP runs few large analytical queries, usually on a separate data warehouse.
ETL extracts, transforms (cleans) and loads data into the warehouse; star schemas have a fact table surrounded by dimension tables.
OLAP operations: roll-up, drill-down, slice, dice and pivot.
lessons.tip: In every project from now on, make two habits automatic: always use parameterized queries, and always create a separate database user for your application with only the privileges it needs. These two habits alone prevent a large share of real database breaches.
lessons.task: Design a star schema for a mobile recharge business: a fact table for recharges and at least three dimension tables. Write one query that rolls up recharge amounts by division and month. Then write the GRANT statements for an analyst role that may only read the warehouse, and explain how you would keep the recharge app safe from SQL injection.

quiz.q: A login form builds SQL by joining strings, and a user types ' OR '1'='1. What is the attack, and what prevents it?
options: Denial of service; prevented by backups
SQL injection; prevented by prepared statements with parameters
Phantom read; prevented by SERIALIZABLE isolation
quiz.explain: The input changes the SQL logic; with parameters, the database treats it as a plain value.

quiz.q: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
options: Authentication checks who you are; authorization decides what you may do
Authentication encrypts data; authorization backs it up
Authorization checks passwords; authentication grants privileges
quiz.explain: Logging in proves identity; GRANT and roles then control the allowed actions.

quiz.q: What does a role provide in SQL security?
options: A named bundle of privileges that can be granted to many users at once
quiz.explain: Roles make managing permissions for many users simple and consistent.

quiz.q: Which statement best describes OLAP compared with OLTP?
options: Few large queries reading many rows for analysis
quiz.explain: OLAP queries scan and summarize large amounts of historical data, unlike short OLTP transactions.

quiz.q: In a star schema, what is in the central table?
options: Facts, such as sale amounts, with foreign keys to dimension tables
Only descriptive attributes like product names
quiz.explain: The fact table holds measurements of events and links to dimensions like product, store and date.

lessons.title: What a Computer Network Is: Hosts, Links, Packets and the Internet
lessons.content:
Imagine you send a voice message on WhatsApp from Dhaka to your cousin in Sylhet. You press the button, speak for five seconds, let go, and a moment later her phone buzzes. Between your phone and hers there were radio waves, a cell tower, kilometres of fiber cable, maybe a dozen big boxes called routers, a data center that might be in another country, and then the same path in reverse. Nobody planned that exact path for you. It just worked, in less than a second. This course is about how that magic actually works, piece by piece.

What a computer network is: A computer network is a set of devices that can send data to each other over some kind of connection. The devices that run our apps, like phones, laptops, smart TVs and servers, are called hosts or end systems. The connections between them are called communication links: copper cable, fiber optic cable, radio (Wi-Fi, 4G) or satellite. In between the hosts sit packet switches, mainly routers and link-layer switches, whose job is to pass data along towards its destination. That is the whole cast: hosts at the edge, links to carry bits, and switches in the middle.

The problem networks solve: Before networks, if a bank branch in Chattogram wanted to share records with the head office in Motijheel, someone carried paper, or later a floppy disk, by bus. Computers were islands. The first step was to connect two computers with one wire. But a wire between every pair of computers does not scale: with n computers you need n(n-1)/2 wires, so 1,000 computers would need 499,500 wires. The solution is sharing: a few links and switches carry traffic for many users at once. Data Communication taught you how bits travel on one link; this course is about how millions of links work together.

Packets, the key idea: Hosts do not send a big file in one piece. They cut the data into small chunks called packets, each with a header that says where it is going, like the address on an envelope. If you send a 3 MB photo, it may become about 2,000 packets of 1,500 bytes each. Each packet travels hop by hop through routers. A router receives a whole packet, looks at the destination address, and sends it out of the right link. This is called store-and-forward packet switching. Because packets from many users mix on the same links, the links stay busy and no single user hogs a reserved line.

A worked number: A packet of L bits pushed onto a link of rate R bits per second takes L/R seconds just to get onto the wire. For L = 12,000 bits (1,500 bytes) and R = 100 Mbps, that is 12,000 / 100,000,000 = 0.00012 s, or 0.12 ms. If the path has 3 links of the same rate and every router must receive the whole packet before forwarding, the packet needs 3 x 0.12 = 0.36 ms of pushing time, ignoring other delays. We will study all the delays carefully in the next lesson.

What a protocol is: When two people meet, there are rules: you say salam, the other replies, then you talk, and you say goodbye before leaving. If one person suddenly starts shouting numbers, the other is confused. Computers need the same kind of rules, only much stricter. A protocol defines the format of the messages, the order in which they are exchanged, and the actions taken when a message is sent, received, or lost. Examples you will meet: HTTP for the web, SMTP for email, DNS for names, TCP and UDP for delivery between programs, IP for moving packets across the Internet, Ethernet and Wi-Fi for single links.

Who writes the rules: Internet standards are developed by the IETF, the Internet Engineering Task Force. Its documents are called RFCs, Requests for Comments. For example, the original TCP is RFC 793 and the original IP is RFC 791. Link technologies like Ethernet (IEEE 802.3) and Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11) are standardized by the IEEE. Because these documents are public, a phone made in China, a router made in the USA and a server run in Bangladesh can all talk to each other. Standards are what make the Internet one network instead of many incompatible ones.

The nuts-and-bolts view: One way to describe the Internet is by its parts: billions of hosts, connected by links and packet switches, organized into networks owned by Internet Service Providers (ISPs), all running the TCP/IP protocols. In this view the Internet is a giant machine made of hardware and software. You can point at a router, a cable, a server rack. This is how a network engineer at an ISP thinks every day while fixing cables and configuring routers.

The services view: The other way to describe the Internet is by what it offers to applications. The Internet is an infrastructure that provides services to distributed applications, programs running on many hosts that exchange data. Facebook, bKash, YouTube, online exams and multiplayer games are all distributed applications. The Internet gives them a programming interface, called the socket interface, through which a program can say: please deliver these bytes to that program on that host. A developer does not care which cables are used, just like you do not care which road a courier van takes, as long as the parcel arrives.

Network of networks: No single company owns the Internet. Your home Wi-Fi is a small network. It connects to a local ISP, perhaps a broadband company in your area. That ISP connects to a bigger national ISP. National ISPs connect to international gateways and to global transit providers, called tier-1 ISPs, which connect to each other. So the Internet is literally a network of networks, glued together by business agreements. A smaller ISP pays a bigger one (its provider) for transit, while two similar ISPs may agree to exchange traffic for free, which is called peering.

Internet exchange points: If two ISPs in Dhaka want to exchange local traffic, sending it to Singapore and back would be slow and costly. So they meet at an Internet Exchange Point (IXP), a building with switches where many networks connect and peer. Bangladesh has BDIX, which lets local ISPs exchange traffic inside the country. That is why some local servers and cache servers feel very fast on a home connection: the traffic never leaves Bangladesh. Big content companies also run their own networks and place servers close to users, which we will see when we discuss CDNs.

How Bangladesh connects to the world: International traffic leaves Bangladesh mostly through submarine cables landing at Cox's Bazar and Kuakata (SEA-ME-WE 4 and SEA-ME-WE 5), plus terrestrial cables through neighbouring countries. Inside the country, fiber networks carry traffic between cities. When you open a website hosted in the USA, your packets travel this long chain: your device, your ISP, a national backbone, an international gateway, a submarine cable, foreign ISPs, and finally the server. Every hop runs the same basic protocols, which is why it works at all.

LAN, MAN and WAN in one line each: A LAN (local area network) covers a home, office or campus, typically with Ethernet and Wi-Fi. A MAN covers a city, such as a cable operator's network. A WAN covers countries or continents, such as an ISP backbone. You met these and the topologies (bus, star, ring, mesh) in Data Communication, so we only use them as names here.

Circuit switching versus packet switching in one breath: The old telephone network reserved a circuit, a fixed share of every link, for the whole call. Even when you are silent, the reserved capacity is wasted. The Internet uses packet switching, where links are shared on demand. Suppose a 1 Mbps link and users who need 100 kbps but are active only 10% of the time. Circuit switching can support only 10 users. With packet switching, 35 users can share it, and the chance that more than 10 are active at the same moment is less than 0.0004. That statistical sharing is why the Internet is cheap and efficient.

Real life example 1, ordering on Daraz: You tap Place Order. Your phone builds an HTTP request, the request rides inside a TCP segment, which rides inside an IP packet, which rides inside a Wi-Fi frame. The Wi-Fi router passes it to your ISP, which forwards it across several routers to Daraz's servers. The server replies with an order confirmation that comes back as packets, possibly along a different path. Every layer did one small job, and all of them together made a single tap work.

Real life example 2, a cricket live stream: During a Bangladesh vs India match, millions of people watch the same stream. If every viewer pulled the video from one server in another country, that server and the international cables would choke. Instead, streaming services keep copies on servers inside or near Bangladesh, often reachable over BDIX or inside the ISP itself. Your app picks a quality that fits your speed and keeps adjusting. Topics like CDNs, adaptive streaming and congestion control all show up in this one everyday scene.

The course map: We go top-down. First the application layer: HTTP, email, DNS, P2P, streaming and socket programming, because that is what you use every day. Then the transport layer: UDP, reliable data transfer, TCP and congestion control. Then the network layer: routers, IPv4, addressing and subnetting, DHCP, NAT, ICMP, IPv6 and routing algorithms like Dijkstra and Bellman-Ford, plus OSPF and BGP. Then the link layer: MAC addresses, ARP, Ethernet switches and VLANs. Finally wireless networks and network security, ending with a full walk-through of what happens when you open a web page.

How to study networks: Networks are best learned by watching real packets. On any computer you can run ping and traceroute (tracert on Windows) to see delays and the routers on a path. Later you may install Wireshark to look inside packets. You will also do many small calculations: delays, round trip times, subnet ranges, routing tables. Do them on paper with tiny numbers until the pattern is obvious.

Common mistakes: Thinking the Internet and the Web are the same. The Web is one application (HTTP and browsers) running on top of the Internet; email, WhatsApp and online games are other applications. Thinking a router and a switch are the same: a router forwards using IP addresses between networks, a switch forwards using MAC addresses inside one LAN. Thinking data travels as one big piece: it travels as packets. And thinking someone controls the whole Internet: it is many independent networks cooperating.

What exams ask: Define a network, host, link, router and protocol. Describe the Internet from the nuts-and-bolts and service views. Explain the ISP hierarchy, peering and IXPs. Compare circuit and packet switching with a numeric example. Compute L/R for a packet on a link. Short notes on RFC, IETF and network of networks often appear too.

Recap: A network is hosts plus links plus packet switches running protocols. Data moves as packets with headers, forwarded store-and-forward by routers. Protocols fix message format, order and actions. The Internet is a network of networks held together by ISPs, peering and IXPs like BDIX, and it offers a socket interface to applications. Next we measure how fast and how well this machine works: delay, loss and throughput.
key_points: A network has hosts (end systems), communication links and packet switches (routers and switches).
Data is split into packets with headers and forwarded hop by hop using store-and-forward.
A protocol defines message format, message order and the actions taken on send, receive or loss.
Internet standards are written by the IETF as RFCs; Ethernet and Wi-Fi are IEEE standards.
The Internet can be seen as nuts-and-bolts (hardware and software) or as a service to distributed applications.
The Internet is a network of networks: access ISPs, national ISPs, tier-1 ISPs, peering and IXPs such as BDIX.
Packet switching shares links statistically and supports more users than circuit switching for bursty traffic.
The course goes top-down: application, transport, network, link, wireless and security.
lessons.tip: Keep a small notebook page called 'my path to the Internet' and fill it in as the course goes: your device, your Wi-Fi, your ISP, the cables, the protocols. Every new lesson adds one line to it.
lessons.task: Open a terminal or command prompt and run 'ping google.com' and then 'tracert google.com' (Windows) or 'traceroute google.com' (Mac/Linux). Count how many routers appear and note the time to the first and last hop.

quiz.q: What does a protocol define?
options: The format and order of messages and the actions taken
quiz.explain: A protocol fixes message format, the order of exchange and the actions on sending, receiving or loss.

quiz.q: How long does it take to push a 12,000-bit packet onto a 100 Mbps link?
What is BDIX?
options: An Internet Exchange Point where Bangladeshi networks exchange local traffic
quiz.explain: BDIX is an IXP where local ISPs peer so local traffic stays inside Bangladesh.

quiz.q: Which organization publishes Internet standards as RFCs?
quiz.explain: The IETF writes Internet standards, published as RFCs.

quiz.q: Why can packet switching support more users than circuit switching on the same link?
options: Users are not all active at the same time, so capacity is shared on demand
quiz.explain: Bursty users rarely transmit together, so statistical sharing serves many more of them.

lessons.title: Network Edge, Core and Performance: Delay, Loss and Throughput
lessons.content:
Think of a parcel going from a shop in Bogura to your home in Dhaka by courier. First a van picks it up from the shop. That first short trip is the edge. Then it goes onto a highway with trucks and sorting hubs. That is the core. Along the way it waits at hubs, gets loaded onto trucks, drives along roads, and sometimes, sadly, gets lost. The Internet works the same way, and in this lesson we learn to measure exactly how long a packet waits, travels and gets lost.

The network edge: The edge is where users live: phones, laptops, home routers, office PCs, and also the servers in data centers. Hosts are often split into clients, which ask for things, and servers, which answer. Your browser is a client; the Google server is a server. Most big servers today sit in huge data centers with hundreds of thousands of machines. Whatever their size, they are still end systems at the edge of the network.

Access networks, the first link: An access network connects a host to its first router, called the edge router. At home in Bangladesh you might use FTTH (fiber to the home), where a fiber reaches the building and is shared using a passive optical splitter. Older connections used DSL over the telephone wire or cable internet over the TV coaxial cable; those were covered in Data Communication, so we only name them. Many homes use local Ethernet broadband where a cable runs from a building switch to your flat. On the move, your phone uses 4G or 5G mobile access through a base station. Inside the home or office, Ethernet cables and Wi-Fi connect devices to the home router.

The network core: The core is the mesh of routers and high-capacity links that connect access networks. Its main tool is packet switching: messages are cut into packets, and each router stores a whole packet, then forwards it. Routers do two jobs. Forwarding is the local action of moving a packet from an input link to the correct output link, using a forwarding table. Routing is the network-wide process of deciding the paths and filling those tables. We will spend several lessons on each. For now, remember that a packet experiences delay at every router it crosses.

The four delays: At each hop a packet suffers four kinds of delay. Processing delay is the time to read the header, check for bit errors and decide the output link, usually microseconds. Queuing delay is the time spent waiting in the output buffer behind other packets; it can be zero or many milliseconds depending on traffic. Transmission delay is the time to push all the bits of the packet onto the link: L/R, where L is packet length in bits and R is link rate in bits per second. Propagation delay is the time for one bit to travel along the wire: d/s, where d is the length of the link and s is the propagation speed, about 2 x 10^8 m/s in copper or fiber. The total nodal delay is d_proc + d_queue + d_trans + d_prop.

Transmission versus propagation, the toll plaza story: Imagine ten cars driving together as a caravan on a highway. At a toll booth, each car takes 12 seconds to be served. Pushing all ten cars through the booth takes 120 seconds; that is like transmission delay, which depends on how many cars (bits) and how fast the booth works (link rate). Then the cars drive 100 km to the next booth at 100 km/h, taking one hour; that is propagation delay, which depends only on distance and speed. Students often mix these up. Transmission delay has nothing to do with distance; propagation delay has nothing to do with packet size.

Worked example 1: A 1,500-byte packet goes over a 10 Mbps link that is 2,000 km long. L = 1,500 x 8 = 12,000 bits. Transmission delay = 12,000 / 10,000,000 = 0.0012 s = 1.2 ms. Propagation delay = 2,000,000 m / (2 x 10^8 m/s) = 0.01 s = 10 ms. Here propagation dominates. Change the link to 100 m of cable inside a building: propagation becomes 0.5 microseconds, and transmission (still 1.2 ms) dominates. Which one matters depends on the situation, so always compute both.

Worked example 2, end-to-end: Suppose a path has N links, all with rate R, and no queuing. Sending one packet of L bits takes N x L/R of transmission time, plus propagation on each link. Sending P packets back to back through N links takes (N + P - 1) x L/R, because once the pipeline is full, one packet leaves the last link every L/R seconds. For N = 3, P = 4, L/R = 1 ms: (3 + 4 - 1) x 1 = 6 ms. Draw a little timeline with the three links to convince yourself.

Queuing delay and traffic intensity: Let a be the average arrival rate of packets per second at a router output, each of L bits, and R the output link rate. Traffic intensity is La/R. If La/R is greater than 1, bits arrive faster than they can leave, and the queue grows without limit; the golden rule is to design so that La/R stays below 1. When La/R is close to 0, queuing delay is tiny. As La/R approaches 1, average queuing delay shoots up very fast, not slowly. This is why a road that is 90% full feels fine but 98% full is a traffic jam. Example: L = 1,000 bits, a = 900 packets/s, R = 1 Mbps gives La/R = 900,000 / 1,000,000 = 0.9, which is already risky.

Packet loss: Router buffers are finite. When a packet arrives and the buffer is full, the router drops it. That packet is lost. The sender may retransmit it later (TCP does), or the application may simply live with the gap (a video call might show a small glitch). Loss rises sharply as traffic intensity nears 1. So the performance of a network is not only how fast, but also how often packets disappear.

Throughput: Throughput is the rate at which the receiver actually gets bits, in bits per second. Instantaneous throughput is the rate at one moment; average throughput is total bits divided by total time. If a 32 Mbit file takes 4 seconds, average throughput is 8 Mbps. Throughput is different from delay: a pipe can be wide (high throughput) but long (high delay), like a satellite link.

The bottleneck link: For a path of links with rates R1, R2, ..., the end-to-end throughput is roughly the minimum of them, min(R1, R2, ...). If a server has a 100 Mbps link, the core has 10 Gbps links, and your home connection is 20 Mbps, your download cannot exceed 20 Mbps. Worked: a 40 MB file is 320 Mbit; at 20 Mbps it takes 16 seconds at best. If ten users share one 50 Mbps core link equally, each gets 5 Mbps from that link, and if 5 Mbps is below their access rates, the shared core link becomes the bottleneck instead.

Round trip time: RTT is the time for a small packet to go from client to server and back. ping measures it. RTT includes propagation both ways, plus transmission, processing and queuing at each hop. From Dhaka, a server inside Bangladesh may show an RTT of a few milliseconds, a server in Singapore a few tens of milliseconds, and a server in the USA often over 200 ms. Many later formulas, such as HTTP response time and TCP throughput, are written in RTTs.

Traceroute, seeing the delays: traceroute sends packets with a small time-to-live value: first 1, then 2, then 3. Each router reduces the value by one, and when it hits zero, the router drops the packet and sends back an error message. So the first router reveals itself, then the second, and so on. traceroute sends three probes for each hop and prints three times. You often see times jump when a packet crosses a submarine cable. Sometimes a later hop shows a smaller time than an earlier one, because each probe sees a different queue at that moment.

Putting the four together, a worked hop: A router needs 20 microseconds to process a packet, the packet waits behind 3 others of the same size, each 1,000 bytes, on a 10 Mbps output link 500 km long. Transmission of one packet = 8,000 / 10,000,000 = 0.8 ms. Queuing = 3 x 0.8 = 2.4 ms. Propagation = 500,000 / (2 x 10^8) = 2.5 ms. Total nodal delay = 0.02 + 2.4 + 0.8 + 2.5 = 5.72 ms. Notice how waiting in line cost almost as much as the travel itself.

Real life example 1, morning vs night speed: Many students in Dhaka notice that the same broadband feels fast at 7 am and slow at 10 pm. The access link rate did not change. What changed is traffic intensity: at night everyone is streaming, so routers at the ISP and on international links have longer queues, causing higher queuing delay and some loss. Speed tests at both times show lower throughput and higher ping at night. That is La/R creeping toward 1.

Real life example 2, video call to abroad: A student in Rajshahi calls a relative in London on Messenger. Even with a good connection, voice has a slight lag. Most of it is propagation and processing over about 8,000 km plus routing detours: even at 2 x 10^8 m/s, 8,000 km takes 40 ms one way, and real paths are longer. No amount of bandwidth removes propagation delay, because it is set by distance and the speed of light in the medium.

Delay-bandwidth product in one line: The number of bits that fit in a link at once equals R x d_prop. For a 100 Mbps link with 10 ms propagation, that is 1,000,000 bits in flight. You saw this as the bandwidth-delay product in Data Communication; it will return when we discuss why TCP needs large windows.

Common mistakes: Using bytes where bits are needed; always multiply bytes by 8. Mixing up Mbps (megabits) and MBps (megabytes). Adding transmission delay only once for a multi-hop path, when store-and-forward means it is paid on every link. Thinking more bandwidth reduces propagation delay. Forgetting that traffic intensity above 1 means infinite queue in theory, not just big.

What exams ask: Define and compute the four delays. Compare transmission and propagation with the caravan analogy. Compute end-to-end delay for N links and P packets. Compute traffic intensity and comment on queuing. Find throughput and bottleneck for given link rates. Explain how traceroute works. List access network technologies.

Recap: The edge holds hosts and access networks such as FTTH, Ethernet, Wi-Fi and 4G/5G. The core is routers doing store-and-forward packet switching. Each hop adds processing, queuing, transmission (L/R) and propagation (d/s) delay. Queuing and loss depend on traffic intensity La/R. Throughput is limited by the bottleneck link. With these numbers in hand, we can now look at how the work is divided into layers.
key_points: The edge has hosts and access networks (FTTH, Ethernet, DSL, cable, Wi-Fi, 4G/5G); the core has routers.
Nodal delay = processing + queuing + transmission + propagation.
Transmission delay = L/R depends on packet size and link rate; propagation delay = d/s depends on distance.
N store-and-forward links and P packets take (N + P - 1) x L/R of transmission time.
Traffic intensity La/R must stay below 1; queuing delay grows sharply as it approaches 1.
Full buffers cause packet loss.
End-to-end throughput is about the minimum link rate on the path, the bottleneck.
traceroute uses increasing TTL values to reveal each router and its RTT.
lessons.tip: Write every delay problem as a small table: L, R, d, s, then L/R and d/s with units. Converting bytes to bits and km to m first prevents half of all mistakes.
lessons.task: Run a speed test on your phone or computer in the morning and again late at night. Note download speed and ping both times, and explain the difference using traffic intensity and queuing delay.

quiz.q: What is the transmission delay of a 1,500-byte packet on a 10 Mbps link?
Which delay depends on the physical length of the link?
quiz.explain: Propagation delay is d/s, distance divided by signal speed.

quiz.q: If traffic intensity La/R is greater than 1, what happens?
quiz.explain: Bits arrive faster than they can leave, so the queue keeps growing.

quiz.q: Links on a path are 100 Mbps, 1 Gbps and 20 Mbps. What is the end-to-end throughput about?
quiz.explain: Throughput is limited by the bottleneck, the slowest link.

quiz.q: How many ms to send 4 packets through 3 links if L/R = 1 ms and no other delays?

lessons.title: Layers and Encapsulation: How the Work of the Internet Is Divided
lessons.content:
Think about how you send Eid gifts to a relative in Khulna through a courier company. You pack the gift and write a note. The courier counter staff put it in their own bag with a tracking label. The bag goes into a sack for Khulna. The sack goes onto a truck. At the Khulna hub, the sack is opened, the bag is sorted, the label is read, and finally your relative opens the box and reads your note. Each person only does one job and only reads the wrapping meant for them. Networks are built exactly like this, and the idea is called layering.

Why layers at all: A network has to do a huge list of jobs: turn bits into signals, send frames on one link, find a path across the world, make delivery reliable, give data to the right program, and make the data meaningful to the app. If one giant program did all of that, changing anything, like moving from Ethernet to Wi-Fi, would mean rewriting everything. Layering splits the problem into a stack of layers. Each layer offers a service to the layer above, using only the service of the layer below. As long as the service stays the same, a layer's inside can be changed freely. Wi-Fi replaced cables in many homes, yet your browser did not change at all.

The five-layer Internet stack: The Internet uses five layers, from top to bottom. Application layer: where network applications and their protocols live, such as HTTP, SMTP, DNS. Transport layer: moves application messages between processes on two hosts, using TCP or UDP. Network layer: moves datagrams from source host to destination host across many routers, using IP and routing protocols. Link layer: moves frames across one single link, from one node to the next, such as Ethernet or Wi-Fi. Physical layer: moves the individual bits on the wire or through the air. A memory trick: All People Need Lots of Pizza, from application down to physical.
