Unique local addresses, fc00::/7, are for private use inside organisations, somewhat like IPv4 private ranges. Multicast addresses, ff00::/8, identify a group of interfaces. Anycast addresses are assigned to several interfaces, and a packet goes to the nearest one, which is how root DNS server instances can share an address. IPv6 has no broadcast; multicast to all nodes replaces it.

Automatic configuration: An IPv6 host can configure itself without a DHCP server using SLAAC, stateless address autoconfiguration. Routers periodically send router advertisements announcing the subnet's /64 prefix. The host combines that prefix with an interface identifier that it generates, often a random value for privacy, to form its global address, and checks that no one else uses it. DHCPv6 also exists for networks that want central control. In IPv6, the Neighbor Discovery Protocol, built on ICMPv6, replaces ARP for finding neighbours' link-layer addresses, and ICMPv6 also does the jobs of ICMP for IPv4.

The transition problem: There is no flag day. The Internet cannot switch off IPv4 and switch on IPv6 overnight, because billions of devices, routers, apps and websites would all need to change at once. So IPv4 and IPv6 must coexist for many years. Three main techniques help.

Dual stack: Hosts and routers run both IPv4 and IPv6 and have both kinds of addresses. When a dual-stack host looks up a name, DNS may return both an A record (IPv4) and an AAAA record (IPv6), and the host prefers IPv6 if it works, falling back to IPv4 quickly if not. This is the most common approach today on modern phones, operating systems and big websites.

Tunneling: When two IPv6 islands are connected only by IPv4 routers, the IPv6 node at the edge of the first island places the whole IPv6 datagram inside the data field of an IPv4 datagram, addressed to the IPv6 node at the edge of the other island. The IPv4 routers in between see only an ordinary IPv4 datagram (protocol number 41). The receiving node extracts the IPv6 datagram and forwards it on. The same idea, wrapping one protocol inside another, is used widely in networking, for example in VPNs.

Translation: Some networks, especially mobile ones, run IPv6 only inside and use NAT64 at the border to translate between IPv6 and IPv4 for reaching IPv4-only servers, together with DNS64, which synthesises IPv6 addresses for IPv4-only names. This lets operators avoid giving each phone an IPv4 address at all.

Adoption today: IPv6 adoption has grown steadily. Large content providers, many mobile networks and major cloud services support it, and Google's public statistics show a large and growing share of its users connecting over IPv6. Growth is uneven between countries and between mobile and fixed broadband. Meanwhile, CGNAT keeps IPv4 working, at the cost of complexity. Learning both versions is necessary for any network engineer today.

Real life example 1, your phone's two addresses: Open the Wi-Fi details or mobile network status on a modern Android phone. On many networks you will see an IPv4 address such as 10.x.x.x and one or more IPv6 addresses, including one starting with fe80, the link-local address, and possibly a global one starting with 2. When you open a big website that supports IPv6, your phone may already be using IPv6 without you noticing; dual stack makes the switch invisible.

Real life example 2, a smart city project: Imagine a city council in Bangladesh planning thousands of smart streetlights, water meters and traffic sensors. With IPv4, each would need a private address behind NAT, and reaching them from the control center would need complicated relays. With IPv6, each device can have its own global address from the council's prefix, and firewalls, not NAT, decide who may talk to whom. The sheer address space of IPv6 makes the Internet of Things much simpler to design.

Common mistakes: Using the double colon twice in one address. Dropping trailing zeros instead of leading zeros (0db8 becomes db8, but 2001 cannot become 21). Thinking IPv6 routers fragment. Saying IPv6 has a header checksum. Saying the IPv6 header is variable in length; the base header is always 40 bytes. Thinking IPv4 and IPv6 can talk directly without dual stack, tunneling or translation.

What exams ask: Why IPv6 was developed. Draw the IPv6 header and compare it with IPv4, explaining the removed fields. Compress and expand addresses. Explain address types, including link-local and the absence of broadcast. Explain SLAAC. Describe dual stack, tunneling and translation with diagrams.

Recap: IPv6 solves IPv4 exhaustion with 128-bit addresses written in hexadecimal groups, shortened by dropping leading zeros and using one double colon. Its fixed 40-byte header keeps version, traffic class, flow label, payload length, next header, hop limit and addresses, and drops router fragmentation, the checksum and in-header options. Hosts can configure themselves with SLAAC. IPv4 and IPv6 coexist through dual stack, tunneling and translation. Next we leave addressing and study how routers find good paths: routing algorithms.
key_points: IPv4's 32-bit space ran out; IANA's free pool was exhausted in 2011.
IPv6 addresses are 128 bits (about 3.4 x 10^38), written as eight hex groups separated by colons.
Shortening: drop leading zeros in a group; replace one run of zero groups with :: only once.
Typical LAN prefix is /64; the last 64 bits are the interface identifier.
Fixed 40-byte header: version, traffic class, flow label, payload length, next header, hop limit, source, destination.
Removed: router fragmentation (Packet Too Big instead), header checksum and in-header options (now extension headers).
Types: global unicast, link-local fe80::/10, unique local, multicast ff00::/8, anycast; no broadcast; SLAAC autoconfiguration.
Transition uses dual stack, tunneling (IPv6 inside IPv4) and translation such as NAT64.
lessons.tip: Practise compression with a three-step routine: first write all eight groups in full, then strip leading zeros group by group, then find the longest run of zero groups and replace it with ::. Doing it in order prevents the double-:: mistake.
lessons.task: Compress 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0001:0000:0000:0001 and expand 2001:db8:5::a:1. Then find the IPv6 addresses on your phone or laptop (Wi-Fi details or ipconfig) and identify which one is link-local.

quiz.q: How long is an IPv6 address?
quiz.explain: IPv6 addresses are 128 bits.

quiz.q: What is the correct compressed form of 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001?
quiz.explain: Drop leading zeros and replace the run of zero groups with one ::.

quiz.q: Which field was removed from the IPv6 base header?
quiz.explain: IPv6 has no header checksum; error checking is left to other layers.

quiz.q: What does an IPv6 router do with a packet too large for the next link?
options: Drops it and sends ICMPv6 Packet Too Big
quiz.explain: Only the source may fragment; routers report the problem instead.

quiz.q: In tunneling, how does an IPv6 datagram cross an IPv4-only region?
options: It is translated to IPv4 permanently
It is carried as data inside an IPv4 datagram
quiz.explain: The whole IPv6 datagram is encapsulated in an IPv4 datagram between tunnel endpoints.

lessons.title: Routing Algorithms: Dijkstra's Link-State and Bellman-Ford Distance-Vector
lessons.content:
Suppose you want to travel from Dhaka to Sylhet and you have two kinds of advice. In the first, you get a full road map of Bangladesh with every road and its travel time, and you calculate the best route yourself. In the second, you have no map; you only ask your neighbours in nearby towns, 'How long does it take you to reach Sylhet?', add the time to reach each neighbour, and pick the smallest. Both methods find good routes, but they behave very differently when a bridge suddenly closes. These are exactly the two classic families of routing algorithms: link-state and distance-vector.

The graph model: Routing is modelled as a graph G = (N, E). Nodes N are routers; edges E are links between them. Each edge has a cost c(x, y), which might reflect the link's length, its speed (for example, inversely proportional to bandwidth) or a value set by the administrator. If two routers are not directly connected, the cost is infinity. The cost of a path is the sum of its edge costs, and the goal of routing is to find, for each source and destination, a least-cost path. If all costs are equal, the least-cost path is simply the one with the fewest hops.

Centralised versus decentralised: A centralised, or global, algorithm computes paths using complete knowledge of the whole network: every link and its cost. These are link-state (LS) algorithms. A decentralised algorithm computes paths iteratively and distributedly: no node knows everything; each starts with only the costs of its own links and exchanges information with neighbours. The distance-vector (DV) algorithm is the main example. Algorithms can also be static (routes change slowly, often by hand) or dynamic (routes change automatically with topology or load).

Link-state, getting the map: In an LS algorithm, each router broadcasts link-state packets describing its directly connected links and their costs to all other routers in the network. After this flooding, every router has the same complete picture of the graph. Then each router independently runs Dijkstra's algorithm with itself as the source. OSPF, which we study in the next lesson, works this way.

Dijkstra's algorithm: Dijkstra computes the least-cost paths from one source node u to all others. It keeps three things: D(v), the cost of the best path found so far from u to v; p(v), the previous node on that path; and N', the set of nodes whose least-cost path is definitely known. Initialisation: N' = {u}; for each neighbour v of u, D(v) = c(u, v), others infinity. Loop: find the node w not in N' with the smallest D(w) and add it to N'. Then for each neighbour v of w not in N', update D(v) = min(D(v), D(w) + c(w, v)). Repeat until all nodes are in N'. After n - 1 iterations, every shortest path is known.

The example network: Six routers u, v, w, x, y, z with link costs: u-v 2, u-x 1, u-w 5, v-x 2, v-w 3, x-w 3, x-y 1, w-y 1, w-z 5, y-z 2. Draw it on paper before reading on: put u on the left, z on the right, v and w on top, x and y below.

Dijkstra worked, step by step: Step 0: N' = {u}. D(v) = 2 via u, D(w) = 5 via u, D(x) = 1 via u, D(y) = infinity, D(z) = infinity. Step 1: the smallest is x (1), add it. Update through x: D(v) = min(2, 1 + 2) = 2, unchanged; D(w) = min(5, 1 + 3) = 4 via x; D(y) = 1 + 1 = 2 via x. Step 2: smallest are v and y, both 2; break the tie by picking v. Through v: D(w) = min(4, 2 + 3) = 4, unchanged. Step 3: add y (2). Through y: D(w) = min(4, 2 + 1) = 3 via y; D(z) = 2 + 2 = 4 via y. Step 4: add w (3). Through w: D(z) = min(4, 3 + 5) = 4, unchanged. Step 5: add z (4). Done.

Reading the result: Final costs from u: v 2, x 1, y 2, w 3, z 4. Follow the predecessors backwards to get paths: z came from y, y from x, x from u, so the path to z is u-x-y-z with cost 1 + 1 + 2 = 4. The path to w is u-x-y-w with cost 3. The path to v is the direct link u-v. The forwarding table at u therefore says: for destination v, use link (u, v); for x, y, w and z, use link (u, x). Notice how the result is a shortest-path tree rooted at u.

Cost of Dijkstra: In the first iteration we search through n - 1 nodes for the minimum, then n - 2, and so on, giving n(n - 1)/2 comparisons, so O(n^2) with a simple implementation. With a heap, it can be done faster, roughly O(E log n). Each router runs it independently, which is fine for networks of hundreds or thousands of routers.

A danger, oscillation: If link costs depend on the traffic load, routes can oscillate. Suppose all routers see that path A is lightly loaded and switch to it at the same moment; now A is heavy and B light, so they all switch back, and so on. Solutions: do not use load-sensitive costs (most Internet routing does not), or ensure routers do not all compute at the same time, for example by randomising when each one sends its link-state advertisements.

Distance-vector, the idea: DV is distributed, iterative and asynchronous. Each node x keeps a distance vector Dx = [Dx(y) for all y], its estimate of the cost to every destination. It knows the cost to each directly attached neighbour, and it receives its neighbours' distance vectors. The heart of the algorithm is the Bellman-Ford equation: Dx(y) = min over neighbours v of { c(x, v) + Dv(y) }. In words: the best way from x to y is to go to some neighbour v and then take v's best way to y; choose the neighbour that minimises the total.

How DV runs: Each node starts with costs to its neighbours and infinity elsewhere, and sends its vector to its neighbours. When a node receives a new vector from a neighbour, or one of its own link costs changes, it recomputes its vector using Bellman-Ford. If its vector changed, it sends the new one to its neighbours. Nodes need no global map and do not need to work in lockstep. Over time, the estimates converge to the true least costs. Each node also records which neighbour gives the minimum, and that becomes the forwarding table entry. The old RIP protocol uses this approach.

DV worked example: Three nodes x, y, z with costs c(x, y) = 2, c(y, z) = 1, c(x, z) = 7. Initially x's vector is (to x, y, z) = (0, 2, 7), y's is (2, 0, 1), and z's is (7, 1, 0). After exchanging, x computes Dx(z) = min(c(x, y) + Dy(z), c(x, z) + Dz(z)) = min(2 + 1, 7 + 0) = 3. So x now knows a cost-3 route to z via y, better than the direct cost-7 link. Similarly, z computes Dz(x) = min(1 + 2, 7 + 0) = 3 via y. x and z send their new vectors; nobody's vector changes any more, and the algorithm has converged.

Good news travels fast: If the cost of link x-y drops, say from 4 to 1, the change spreads quickly: y updates its vector, tells x and z, they update, and in a couple of exchanges everyone is correct.

Bad news travels slowly, count to infinity: Take c(x, y) = 4, c(y, z) = 1, c(x, z) = 50. In steady state y reaches x directly at cost 4, and z reaches x via y at cost 5. Now the x-y link cost jumps to 60. y recomputes: directly 60, or via z, which claims 5, giving 1 + 5 = 6. So y wrongly chooses z, even though z's route goes through y itself. A routing loop forms: y sends to z, z sends to y. y tells z its cost is 6; z updates to 7; y updates to 8, and so on, rising by 2 each round. It takes 44 iterations before z finds that its direct link at cost 50 is better. If that link did not exist, they would count to infinity. This is the count-to-infinity problem.

Poisoned reverse: A fix for the simple two-node loop: if z routes to x through y, then z tells y that its distance to x is infinity, a lie on purpose. Now when the x-y cost becomes 60, y does not believe it can reach x via z, so it uses the direct route at 60 and the correct answer spreads quickly. Poisoned reverse does not, however, solve loops that involve three or more nodes. RIP also limits the maximum distance to 15 hops, treating 16 as infinity, so that counting stops quickly.

Comparing LS and DV: Messages: LS requires every node to know every link cost, so O(nE) messages are flooded whenever a link changes; DV exchanges messages only between neighbours. Speed of convergence: LS with Dijkstra converges quickly in O(n^2) computation; DV can converge slowly and suffer from routing loops and count-to-infinity. Robustness: in LS, each router computes its own table, so a malfunctioning router that advertises a wrong link cost affects only that link; in DV, a router advertising wrong costs to everything can spread its error to the whole network, since every node uses neighbours' calculations. In 1997 a router error in an ISP famously caused large parts of the Internet to route traffic to it, an example of how errors propagate. Both are used in practice.

Real life example 1, Google Maps rerouting: When you drive from Gulshan to Motijheel with navigation on, the app knows the whole road graph and current travel times, and computes a shortest path, much like Dijkstra on a link-state map. When a road becomes jammed, the edge cost rises and it recomputes. Because the app has the full map, it reacts quickly to bad news, just like LS routing.

Real life example 2, asking around in a village: Without a phone, a traveller in a village asks each neighbour how far it is to the upazila office and adds the distance to that neighbour, choosing the smallest total. If the bridge on the usual road collapses, neighbours keep repeating old answers that were based on that road for a while, and it takes several rounds of asking for everyone to correct their estimates. That slow spread of bad news is distance-vector's count-to-infinity in human form.

Common mistakes: In Dijkstra, adding a node to N' before it has the smallest D. Forgetting to record the predecessor, so paths cannot be reconstructed. Updating nodes already in N'. In DV, using the neighbour's vector without adding the link cost to that neighbour. Thinking poisoned reverse solves all loops. Confusing which algorithm needs the full map.

What exams ask: Run Dijkstra on a given graph and fill in the table of D and p values step by step; give the resulting shortest-path tree and forwarding table. Apply Bellman-Ford for a few nodes and show converged vectors. Explain count-to-infinity with a three-node example and how poisoned reverse helps. Compare LS and DV on message complexity, convergence and robustness.

Recap: Routing finds least-cost paths in a graph of routers. Link-state algorithms flood link costs so every router has the whole map, then run Dijkstra, which adds one node at a time with the smallest known cost. Distance-vector algorithms let each router use Bellman-Ford, Dx(y) = min over v of c(x, v) + Dv(y), with neighbours' vectors. DV is simple and local but can loop and count to infinity, partly fixed by poisoned reverse. Next we see how these ideas power the real Internet: OSPF inside networks and BGP between them.
key_points: Routing is modelled as a graph of routers with link costs; the goal is least-cost paths.
Link-state (global) algorithms flood all link costs so each router knows the full map; distance-vector (decentralised) uses only neighbours' information.
Dijkstra: repeatedly add the node with the smallest D to N' and update neighbours with D(w) + c(w, v); O(n^2).
Worked: from u, shortest costs v 2, x 1, y 2, w 3, z 4; path to z is u-x-y-z.
Bellman-Ford: Dx(y) = min over neighbours v of { c(x, v) + Dv(y) }.
DV is iterative, asynchronous and distributed; RIP uses it.
Good news travels fast; bad news causes routing loops and count-to-infinity; poisoned reverse fixes two-node loops only.
LS: more messages but fast convergence and robust; DV: fewer messages but slower and errors spread.
lessons.tip: For Dijkstra, draw one table with a row per step and a column per destination, writing each entry as cost,predecessor (for example 4,x). Circle the chosen node in each row. Examiners look for exactly this table.
lessons.task: Using the six-node graph in this lesson, run Dijkstra from node z instead of u. Fill in the step table, then write z's forwarding table showing the first link to use for each destination.

quiz.q: In Dijkstra's algorithm, which node is added to N' at each step?
options: The node with the smallest current D among those not in N'
The node with the most links
quiz.explain: The node with the smallest tentative cost is guaranteed to have its final shortest path.

quiz.q: c(x, y) = 2, c(x, z) = 7, Dy(z) = 1. What is Dx(z) by Bellman-Ford?
Which problem is typical of distance-vector routing?
options: Count-to-infinity after a link cost increase
quiz.explain: Bad news spreads slowly and can cause loops in DV.

quiz.q: In the lesson's graph, what is the least cost from u to z?
quiz.explain: u-x-y-z costs 1 + 1 + 2 = 4.

quiz.q: What does poisoned reverse do?
options: A node advertises infinite distance to the neighbour it routes through
quiz.explain: It prevents a neighbour from routing back through the node, breaking two-node loops.

lessons.title: Routing in the Internet: Autonomous Systems, OSPF, BGP and SDN
lessons.content:
Think about how a parcel travels from a shop in Rajshahi to a buyer in Singapore. Inside Bangladesh, the courier company decides its own routes between its hubs, choosing the fastest roads. But at the border, decisions change: which shipping line or airline to use depends on contracts, prices and agreements between companies, not just on distance. The Internet works exactly the same way. Inside one organisation's network, routing aims for the shortest paths. Between organisations, routing is about policy and business relationships. This lesson shows the two levels and the protocols that run them: OSPF inside and BGP between.

Why one algorithm is not enough: The previous lesson treated the network as one flat graph where every router runs the same algorithm. The real Internet has hundreds of millions of hosts and a very large number of routers. Flooding link-state information about every link in the world to every router, or running distance-vector across all of them, would be impossible to store and would never converge. There is also administrative autonomy: each ISP or company wants to run its own network its own way, hide its internal structure and choose its own routing.

Autonomous systems: The solution is to organise routers into autonomous systems, ASes. An AS is a group of routers under the same administrative control, such as one ISP, one large university or one big company. Each AS is identified by a globally unique AS number, ASN, assigned by the regional registries, APNIC in our region. Routers within an AS all run the same intra-AS routing protocol. Routers that connect to other ASes are called gateway routers, and they also run the inter-AS protocol, BGP. So routing has two levels: within an AS, and among ASes.

Intra-AS routing, RIP: The Routing Information Protocol is one of the earliest intra-AS protocols. It is a distance-vector protocol whose cost metric is simply the hop count, with a maximum of 15 hops; 16 means unreachable. Neighbours exchange their full vectors every 30 seconds in messages called RIP response messages, sent over UDP port 520. If a router hears nothing from a neighbour for 180 seconds, it considers that neighbour dead. Because of its small diameter limit and slow convergence, RIP is mainly found today in small networks and in textbooks, but it is a clear real example of distance-vector routing.

Intra-AS routing, OSPF: Open Shortest Path First is the widely used link-state protocol. Each router floods link-state advertisements to all other routers in the AS, whenever a link changes and periodically (at least every 30 minutes). OSPF messages are carried directly in IP datagrams with protocol number 89, not over TCP or UDP, so OSPF handles its own reliability. Every router builds the full topology map and runs Dijkstra to compute its shortest-path tree. Link weights are set by the network administrator: setting all to 1 gives minimum hop routing; setting them inversely proportional to link capacity steers traffic away from slow links.

OSPF's advanced features: Security: OSPF messages can be authenticated so that only trusted routers can inject routing information. Multiple equal-cost paths: when two paths have the same cost, OSPF can split traffic across both, which is called ECMP. Support for unicast and multicast routing. And hierarchy within a single AS, through areas.

OSPF areas: A large AS can be split into areas. Each area runs its own link-state flooding, so routers in an area know the detailed topology only of their own area. One special area, the backbone, area 0, connects all others. Area border routers sit in two areas and summarise routes between them. Traffic going from one area to another goes from the source area to the backbone and then to the destination area. This keeps flooding and Dijkstra calculations small even in large networks. A university campus could make each faculty an area connected through the backbone in the central data center.

Inter-AS routing, BGP: The Border Gateway Protocol, version 4, is the protocol that glues the whole Internet together. Every AS runs it. BGP lets each AS learn which destinations are reachable through neighbouring ASes, determine the best routes to those destinations, and advertise its own prefixes to the rest of the world, saying in effect, 'I am here, and these addresses are inside me.' In BGP, destinations are not individual hosts but CIDR prefixes, such as 138.16.68.0/22.

BGP sessions: BGP routers exchange information over semi-permanent TCP connections on port 179. A session between routers in two different ASes is called external BGP, eBGP. A session between routers in the same AS is internal BGP, iBGP, used to spread the routes learned from outside to all routers within the AS. Note that iBGP is not an intra-AS routing protocol; it carries BGP route information inside the AS, while OSPF or another IGP still computes paths inside.

BGP route attributes: When a router advertises a prefix over BGP, it includes attributes. A prefix plus its attributes is called a route. Two important attributes: AS-PATH, the list of ASes the advertisement has passed through. When an AS passes a route on, it adds its own ASN to the front. If a router sees its own ASN already in the AS-PATH, it rejects the route, which prevents loops. NEXT-HOP: the IP address of the router interface that begins the AS-PATH, the next router to send to. There are others, such as LOCAL-PREF and MED, used in policy.

How BGP picks a route: A router often learns several routes to the same prefix. BGP applies rules in order until one route remains. First, highest local preference, a value set by the AS's own policy. Second, among equal local preference, the shortest AS-PATH. Third, among those, the closest NEXT-HOP router according to intra-AS costs, which is hot potato routing. Fourth, if still tied, BGP identifiers are used to break the tie. Real routers have a few more steps, but these four capture the idea.

Hot potato routing: Hot potato means: get the packet out of my AS as quickly and cheaply as possible, regardless of how far it then travels outside. Like holding a hot potato, you pass it on fast. An AS with two gateways to other ASes, both leading to a destination, will send each packet to whichever gateway is closest inside its own network. This saves the AS's internal resources but may not give the shortest end-to-end path. It shows that BGP is selfish by design.

Policy, the real heart of BGP: Business relationships shape what gets advertised. A customer pays a provider for transit; a provider carries traffic for its customers. Two ASes of similar size may peer, exchanging traffic between their own customers for free, often at an Internet exchange point. A common rule: an AS will carry traffic to or from its customers, but will not provide free transit between two of its providers or peers. So if AS A peers with B and also with C, A will not advertise a route learned from B to C, because then C's traffic to B would cross A's network for free. BGP's policy controls, through which routes are advertised and local preference, implement these business decisions.

IXPs and peering: An Internet exchange point is a physical location where many ASes connect their routers, often with a shared switch, and set up BGP sessions to exchange traffic directly. This keeps local traffic local, reduces cost and lowers delay. BDIX, the Bangladesh Internet Exchange, which you met in lesson 1, plays this role for Bangladeshi ISPs, so traffic between two local ISPs does not need to go abroad and come back.

How Bangladesh reaches the world: ISPs in Bangladesh buy international bandwidth from International Internet Gateway operators. That bandwidth reaches the global Internet through submarine cables, such as the SEA-ME-WE 4 cable landing at Cox's Bazar and the SEA-ME-WE 5 cable landing at Kuakata, and through terrestrial cables across the border to India. Each of these networks is one or more ASes, and BGP sessions between them carry the routes to the rest of the world. When one cable is cut or under maintenance, BGP withdraws routes through it and traffic shifts to other paths, often with higher delay, which is why users notice slowdowns during cable repair periods.

Why separate intra and inter-AS routing: Policy: between ASes, policy dominates, and an administrator wants control over who carries its traffic; within an AS, there is one owner, so policy matters much less. Scale: the hierarchy keeps routing tables and update traffic manageable; inter-AS routing works with prefixes, not every link. Performance: within an AS, the goal is efficient paths; between ASes, policy often comes before performance.

Software-defined networking: In traditional routers, every router runs routing protocols and computes its own forwarding table: a per-router control plane. Software-defined networking separates them: a logically centralised remote controller computes forwarding tables and installs them into simple switches using a protocol such as OpenFlow. Each switch follows generalised match-plus-action rules that can match on fields from several layers, such as IP addresses and port numbers, and act by forwarding, dropping or modifying packets. Large data center operators and some wide area networks use SDN-style control because it makes network-wide policies easier to program and change. Google has described using SDN for its private wide area network.

Real life example 1, choosing between two upstreams: A Dhaka ISP buys transit from two upstream providers, X and Y. Both advertise a route to the prefix of a popular video platform. Through X the AS-PATH has 3 ASes; through Y it has 2. With equal local preference, BGP picks Y, the shorter AS-PATH. But X is cheaper per megabit, so the ISP's engineers set a higher local preference for routes from X. Now BGP prefers X regardless of AS-PATH length. This one knob, local preference, is how business decisions become routing decisions.

Real life example 2, a famous mistake: In October 2021, a configuration change caused Facebook's network to withdraw its BGP routes, along with routes to its own DNS servers. For several hours, routers around the world simply had no path to Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram, and the services disappeared from the Internet, including for users in Bangladesh. The servers themselves were running; the Internet just did not know how to reach them. It is a powerful reminder that BGP announcements are what make a network visible at all.

Common mistakes: Thinking BGP finds the shortest physical path; it follows policy first. Calling iBGP an intra-AS routing protocol. Forgetting that OSPF runs directly over IP while BGP uses TCP port 179 and RIP uses UDP port 520. Thinking AS-PATH is a list of routers; it is a list of ASes. Mixing up hot potato routing, which minimises cost inside one's own AS, with end-to-end shortest paths.

What exams ask: Explain why routing is split into intra-AS and inter-AS. Describe OSPF and its features, including areas. Describe BGP: eBGP and iBGP, the AS-PATH and NEXT-HOP attributes, route selection rules and hot potato routing. Explain with a diagram why an AS does not advertise routes between peers. Explain the SDN idea of a separated control plane.

Recap: The Internet is a network of autonomous systems. Inside an AS, an intra-AS protocol such as OSPF (link-state, Dijkstra, areas) or RIP (distance-vector, hop count) finds efficient paths. Between ASes, BGP over TCP port 179 advertises prefixes with attributes like AS-PATH and NEXT-HOP, and chooses routes by local preference, shortest AS-PATH, hot potato and tie-breakers, all shaped by business policy. IXPs like BDIX keep local traffic local, and SDN centralises the control plane. Next we go down to the link layer and see how frames travel on a single LAN.
key_points: The Internet is divided into autonomous systems (ASes), each with a unique ASN and its own routing policy.
Intra-AS protocols: RIP (distance-vector, hop count, max 15, UDP 520) and OSPF (link-state, Dijkstra, IP protocol 89).
OSPF features: authentication, equal-cost multipath, and hierarchical areas joined by backbone area 0.
BGP is the inter-AS protocol; it runs over TCP port 179 as eBGP between ASes and iBGP inside an AS.
BGP routes are prefixes with attributes; AS-PATH prevents loops and NEXT-HOP names the next router.
Selection order: highest local preference, shortest AS-PATH, closest NEXT-HOP (hot potato), then tie-breakers.
Policy rules: carry traffic for customers, do not give free transit between peers or providers.
SDN separates control from forwarding: a remote controller installs match-plus-action rules, for example with OpenFlow.
lessons.tip: Remember the BGP selection rules as 'Local, Length, Leave fast, Last tie-break': local preference, AS-PATH length, hot potato exit, then identifiers. It is the most frequently asked BGP question.
lessons.task: Look up the ASN of a Bangladeshi ISP you know using a public BGP looking glass or ASN lookup website. Note which prefixes it announces and which upstream ASes it connects to, and sketch the AS graph on paper.

quiz.q: Which protocol is used for routing between autonomous systems?
quiz.explain: BGP is the inter-AS routing protocol of the Internet.

quiz.q: What transport does BGP use?
quiz.explain: BGP sessions run over TCP port 179.

quiz.q: Why does a BGP router reject a route whose AS-PATH contains its own ASN?
options: Because the route is too long
quiz.explain: Seeing its own ASN means the route would loop back through itself.

quiz.q: In BGP route selection, what is checked first among these?
quiz.explain: Local preference, set by policy, comes first.

quiz.q: What is the role of area 0 in OSPF?
options: It is the backbone connecting all other areas
It is used only for RIP
quiz.explain: Inter-area traffic passes through the backbone area 0.

lessons.title: The Link Layer and LANs: MAC Addresses, ARP, Ethernet, Switches and VLANs
lessons.content:
Picture a long journey from Rangpur to Barishal: a bus to Dhaka, a launch from Sadarghat, and then a rickshaw to the final address. The overall plan, which cities to pass through, is like the network layer. But each leg of the trip has its own vehicle, driver and rules: the bus driver only cares about getting you from the Rangpur counter to the Dhaka counter. The link layer is that single leg: it moves a frame across one link, from one node to the next. This lesson studies how that works on the most common wired technology, Ethernet, and on the local area networks built from it.

Link layer services, a quick recap: The Data Communication course covered framing, error detection with parity, checksums and CRC, and medium access protocols such as ALOHA and CSMA/CD, so we only recap them here. Framing: encapsulating a network-layer datagram in a frame with a header and trailer. Link access: a MAC protocol decides who may transmit on a shared medium. Reliable delivery: some links, especially wireless ones, retransmit lost frames; wired Ethernet usually does not. Error detection, and sometimes correction, in hardware. The link layer is implemented mostly in the network adapter, also called the network interface card, with a chip that does framing, CRC and medium access, while a small part runs in software on the host.

MAC addresses: Every network adapter has a link-layer address, called a MAC address, which is 6 bytes, 48 bits, long. It is written in hexadecimal pairs, such as 1A-2F-BB-76-09-AD. The IEEE manages the address space: it sells a block, the first 24 bits, to each manufacturer, and the manufacturer assigns the remaining 24 bits uniquely, so no two adapters should share an address. A MAC address is flat: it says nothing about location, like a national ID number that stays the same when you move. An IP address is hierarchical, like a postal address that changes when you move to a new city. The special address FF-FF-FF-FF-FF-FF is the link-layer broadcast address. Modern phones often use randomised MAC addresses on Wi-Fi for privacy.

Why we need both kinds of address: Hosts use IP addresses to say where a datagram should end up, possibly on the other side of the world. Adapters use MAC addresses to deliver a frame on the local link. Keeping them separate means adapters can work with any network-layer protocol, and a host can move without changing its hardware address. It also means an adapter can quickly ignore frames not meant for it, without waking up the CPU.

ARP, the problem: Suppose host A, 222.222.222.220, wants to send a datagram to host B, 222.222.222.222, on the same subnet. A knows B's IP address, but to build the frame it needs B's MAC address. The Address Resolution Protocol answers the question: what MAC address belongs to this IP address on my subnet? Each host and router keeps an ARP table of mappings from IP to MAC address, each with a time-to-live, typically around 20 minutes, after which it is removed.

ARP worked: A looks in its ARP table and finds no entry for 222.222.222.222. It builds an ARP query packet containing its own IP and MAC addresses and the target IP 222.222.222.222, and sends it in a frame to the broadcast MAC address FF-FF-FF-FF-FF-FF. Every adapter on the subnet receives it and passes it to ARP; each checks whether the target IP is its own. Only B matches, and B sends back an ARP response in a unicast frame directly to A, containing B's MAC address, say 49-BD-D2-C7-56-2A. A stores the mapping in its table and now sends the original datagram in a frame addressed to 49-BD-D2-C7-56-2A. ARP is plug-and-play: tables build themselves.

Sending to another subnet: Now suppose A wants to send to a host on a different subnet, through router R. A does not ARP for the far host's MAC address; that host is not on A's link. Instead, A sends the frame to the MAC address of R's interface on A's subnet, the default gateway, which it finds by ARP for the gateway's IP. The datagram inside still has the final destination IP. R receives the frame, extracts the datagram, looks up its forwarding table, and builds a new frame on the outgoing link, using ARP on that subnet to find the next node's MAC address. So at each hop, the IP addresses in the datagram stay the same, while the MAC addresses in the frame change.

The Ethernet frame: Ethernet dominates wired LANs: it was the first widely deployed high-speed LAN technology, it is cheap and simple, and it has kept up with speed, from 10 Mbps to 100 Mbps, 1 Gbps, 10 Gbps and beyond. The frame has these fields. Preamble, 8 bytes: seven bytes of 10101010 followed by 10101011, which wake up the receiver and synchronise its clock; the final 11 says the real frame is starting. Destination MAC address, 6 bytes. Source MAC address, 6 bytes. Type, 2 bytes, telling which network-layer protocol is inside, such as IPv4 (0x0800), IPv6 or ARP, so the receiver can demultiplex. Data, 46 to 1,500 bytes: the datagram; 1,500 is the Ethernet MTU, and shorter data is padded to 46. CRC, 4 bytes, to detect errors.

Ethernet's service: Ethernet is connectionless: there is no handshake before sending. It is unreliable: if a frame fails the CRC check, the receiver silently drops it, with no ACK or NAK. Any recovery is left to higher layers, such as TCP. This keeps Ethernet simple and cheap, and on modern wired links bit errors are very rare.

From buses and hubs to switches: Early Ethernet used a shared coaxial bus, and later a star with a hub at the center. A hub is a physical-layer device: whatever bits arrive on one port, it copies out on all other ports. So all hosts share one collision domain and must use CSMA/CD. Today's Ethernet uses a switch at the center. A switch is a link-layer device that stores frames and forwards each one only toward its destination. Each port is its own collision domain, links are full duplex, and so collisions do not occur and CSMA/CD is not needed in practice.

Switch forwarding and filtering: A switch keeps a switch table, with entries of MAC address, interface and time. When a frame arrives on interface x, the switch looks up the destination MAC. If there is no entry, it floods the frame: forwards it on all interfaces except x. If the entry says the destination is on interface x itself, it filters: discards the frame, because the destination is on the same segment it came from. If the entry says interface y, it forwards the frame only on y. Filtering and forwarding are what make switches much more efficient than hubs.

Self-learning, worked: Switch tables build themselves. Consider a switch with interfaces 1, 2 and 3, and an empty table. Host A on interface 1 sends a frame to host C. The switch records 'A is on 1', and since C is unknown, floods to 2 and 3. C, on interface 3, replies to A. The switch records 'C is on 3', looks up A, finds interface 1, and forwards only on 1. Now host B on interface 2 sends to A: the switch learns 'B is on 2' and forwards only on 1. After a few frames, the switch knows everyone without any configuration. Entries age out after a period, often a few minutes, so moved hosts are relearned. Switches are plug-and-play and transparent: hosts do not even know they exist.

Switches versus routers: Both are store-and-forward packet switches, but a router works at layer 3 with IP addresses and a switch at layer 2 with MAC addresses. Switches are plug-and-play and fast, but in large networks their flooding and ARP broadcasts become heavy, and the active topology must be a tree (the spanning tree protocol prevents loops). Routers need IP configuration but keep broadcast traffic within each subnet, can use redundant paths and give firewall-like protection. Small networks use switches; large ones mix both, with routers between subnets.

VLANs: Imagine a university building where the CSE department, the accounts office and the library share the same switches. Without anything else, all of them form one broadcast domain: every ARP and DHCP broadcast reaches everyone, and an accounts computer is on the same LAN as student lab PCs, which is a security concern. A virtual LAN solves this: the switch's ports are grouped by the administrator, and each group behaves as a separate LAN. Traffic between VLANs must pass through a router. People can even be moved from one department to another by reconfiguring ports, without moving cables.

VLAN trunking: When VLANs span several switches, a special trunk port connects the switches and carries frames of all VLANs. To show which VLAN a frame belongs to, the IEEE 802.1Q standard adds a 4-byte tag to the Ethernet frame, including a 12-bit VLAN identifier, which allows up to 4,096 VLAN values. The tag is added by the sending switch and removed by the receiving switch, so hosts never see it.

A day in the life of a web request: Bring everything together. A student plugs a laptop into the CSE lab's Ethernet and opens www.google.com. Step 1, DHCP: the laptop has no IP, so it sends a DHCP Discover in a UDP segment, in an IP datagram to 255.255.255.255, in an Ethernet frame to FF-FF-FF-FF-FF-FF. The switch floods it; the DHCP server, perhaps in the lab router, answers. The laptop now has its IP address, mask, gateway and DNS server. Step 2, ARP: to send anything off the subnet, the laptop needs the gateway's MAC address, so it broadcasts an ARP query and gets the reply. Step 3, DNS: the laptop sends a DNS query for www.google.com in a UDP datagram, in a frame to the gateway's MAC address. Routers forward it, using forwarding tables built by OSPF and BGP, to the DNS server, which replies with Google's IP address.

The day in the life, continued: Step 4, TCP: the laptop opens a TCP socket to Google's IP on port 443 and performs the three-way handshake: SYN, SYNACK, ACK, each in datagrams routed across ASes. Step 5, TLS and HTTP: after the TLS handshake, the browser sends an HTTP GET request; Google's server replies with the page in a series of segments, with TCP flow and congestion control managing the rate. Each segment arrives in a frame from the gateway, the switch forwards it to the laptop's port, and the browser finally renders the page. Every layer in this course did its job in the space of a fraction of a second.

Real life example 1, a cybercafé in Bogura: A small cybercafé has 20 PCs connected with cables to a 24-port switch, which connects to a router from the ISP. When the owner first turns everything on, the switch's table is empty and it floods frames, but within seconds it has learned every PC's MAC address. If a customer runs a big download, only that PC's port and the uplink are busy; the other ports are not disturbed. Had the owner used an old hub, every PC's traffic would be repeated to all 20 ports and collisions would slow everyone down.

Real life example 2, an office VLAN design: A Dhaka garments company has one building with three floors of offices, plus a CCTV system. Its network engineer creates VLAN 10 for management, VLAN 20 for production staff, VLAN 30 for guest Wi-Fi and VLAN 40 for CCTV cameras, all over the same switches with 802.1Q trunks between floors. A guest on the Wi-Fi cannot see the accounts server, and the CCTV traffic is isolated. The router between VLANs allows only the specific traffic that policy permits.

Common mistakes: Thinking the MAC address changes when you move to another network; it is fixed by the adapter, apart from privacy randomisation. Saying ARP works across routers; it only resolves addresses on the same subnet. Forgetting that the destination MAC changes at every hop while the IP address does not. Thinking switches have IP addresses for forwarding; they forward by MAC. Confusing the preamble, which is not usually counted in the frame size, with the header.

What exams ask: Compare MAC and IP addresses. Explain ARP with a diagram, both within a subnet and when sending through a router. Draw the Ethernet frame and explain each field. Trace a switch's self-learning table across a sequence of frames. Compare hubs, switches and routers. Explain VLANs and 802.1Q tagging. Describe the day in the life of a web page request.

Recap: The link layer moves frames over one link. Adapters have flat 48-bit MAC addresses; ARP maps IP to MAC on the same subnet using a broadcast query and a unicast reply. The Ethernet frame carries preamble, addresses, type, 46 to 1,500 bytes of data and a CRC, with connectionless, unreliable service. Switches self-learn which MAC is on which port and forward, filter or flood accordingly; VLANs split one switch infrastructure into several logical LANs. Next we cut the cable and look at wireless and mobile networks.
key_points: The link layer moves a frame over a single link, implemented mostly in the network adapter.
MAC addresses are flat 48-bit addresses assigned by manufacturers; FF-FF-FF-FF-FF-FF is broadcast.
ARP finds the MAC for an IP on the same subnet: broadcast query, unicast reply, cached with a TTL.
To reach another subnet, the frame goes to the gateway router's MAC; IPs stay the same at each hop while MACs change.
Ethernet frame: preamble 8, destination 6, source 6, type 2, data 46 to 1,500, CRC 4 bytes; service is connectionless and unreliable.
Switches self-learn MAC-to-port mappings and forward, filter or flood; each port is its own collision domain.
VLANs split a switched LAN into separate broadcast domains; 802.1Q adds a 4-byte tag with a 12-bit VLAN ID on trunks.
A web request uses DHCP, ARP, DNS, TCP, TLS and HTTP, crossing every layer in this course.
lessons.tip: When tracing a packet across routers, draw two rows for each hop: one for the IP source and destination, one for the MAC source and destination. You will see at once that the IP row stays the same and the MAC row changes at every link.
lessons.task: Run 'arp -a' in a terminal on your laptop to see your ARP table, and find the entry for your default gateway. Then disconnect and reconnect to Wi-Fi, ping the gateway, and run 'arp -a' again to see the entry reappear.

quiz.q: How long is an Ethernet MAC address?
quiz.explain: MAC addresses are 6 bytes, 48 bits.

quiz.q: How is an ARP query sent?
options: To the broadcast MAC address FF-FF-FF-FF-FF-FF
quiz.explain: The sender does not know the target MAC, so it broadcasts the query.

quiz.q: As a datagram crosses several routers, what changes at each hop?
options: The source and destination MAC addresses
quiz.explain: Each link gets a new frame with new MAC addresses; the IP addresses stay the same.

quiz.q: A switch receives a frame for an unknown destination MAC. What does it do?
options: Floods it on all interfaces except the incoming one
Sends it back to the sender
quiz.explain: Unknown destinations are flooded until the switch learns where they are.

quiz.q: What is the maximum data field size of a standard Ethernet frame?
quiz.explain: The Ethernet MTU is 1,500 bytes; the minimum is 46.

lessons.title: Wireless and Mobile Networks: Wi-Fi, CSMA/CA, Cellular and Handover
lessons.content:
Imagine a crowded classroom where everyone talks at once. Voices fade with distance, the noise from the fan and the road outside drowns some words, echoes bounce off the walls, and two students at opposite corners cannot hear each other at all, even though the teacher in the middle hears both. That is the wireless world. A cable is a private, quiet corridor; the air is a shared, noisy hall. This lesson explains how Wi-Fi and cellular networks cope with that hall, and how your phone keeps its connection while you move.

The elements of a wireless network: Wireless hosts are the end devices, such as laptops, phones and IoT sensors. A base station connects wireless hosts to the wired network: in Wi-Fi it is called an access point, AP; in cellular networks it is a cell tower, called eNodeB in 4G and gNB in 5G. Hosts associated with a base station use it to relay all their traffic, which is called infrastructure mode. In ad hoc mode, there is no base station, and hosts talk directly to each other. Note the two separate ideas: wireless is about the link; mobility is about changing your point of attachment while staying connected.

What makes wireless links hard: First, decreasing signal strength: radio signals weaken as they travel and as they pass through walls, called path loss. Second, interference from other sources: other Wi-Fi networks, microwave ovens and Bluetooth devices share the 2.4 GHz band. Third, multipath propagation: signals reflect off buildings and the ground and arrive at slightly different times, blurring the received signal. The result is that bit error rates are much higher than on cables, so wireless links use stronger error detection, link-level ACKs and retransmissions.

SNR and adaptation: The signal-to-noise ratio, SNR, measures how much stronger the received signal is than the background noise, usually in decibels. For a given modulation, higher SNR gives a lower bit error rate. Faster modulations pack more bits per symbol, but need higher SNR. So wireless devices adapt: close to the access point, with strong SNR, they use a fast modulation; when you walk farther away and SNR falls, they switch to a slower but more robust one. That is why the speed shown on your laptop's Wi-Fi drops as you move to another room.

The hidden terminal problem: Suppose hosts A and C are on opposite sides of an access point B, or separated by a wall. Both can reach B, but A and C cannot hear each other. If both send to B at the same time, their signals collide at B, yet neither A nor C detects the collision, because each only hears itself. Fading over distance causes the same effect: A and C may be just far enough apart that their signals are too weak for each other. This makes collision detection, as in wired Ethernet, impossible, and calls for a different MAC design.

Wi-Fi, the 802.11 family: Wi-Fi is the IEEE 802.11 family of standards, operating in unlicensed bands around 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz, and in newer versions also 6 GHz. The generations have marketing names: Wi-Fi 4 is 802.11n, Wi-Fi 5 is 802.11ac, Wi-Fi 6 is 802.11ax, and Wi-Fi 7 is 802.11be. Each generation added techniques such as multiple antennas (MIMO), wider channels and more efficient modulation, raising peak speeds from hundreds of megabits per second to several gigabits. All of them use the same basic MAC protocol, CSMA/CA, and the same frame structure.

The 802.11 architecture: The basic building block is the basic service set, BSS: one access point and the wireless hosts associated with it. The administrator gives the AP a service set identifier, SSID, the network name you see in your Wi-Fi list, and chooses a channel. Several APs, connected by a wired switch, can form one larger network with the same SSID, such as across a university campus. The 2.4 GHz band is divided into overlapping channels; in most countries channels 1, 6 and 11 do not overlap, so neighbouring APs should use different ones among these.

Joining a network, scanning and association: An AP periodically sends beacon frames containing its SSID and MAC address. A host can do passive scanning, listening to beacons on each channel, or active scanning, broadcasting probe request frames and receiving probe responses. Your phone then shows the list of networks. When you choose one, the host sends an association request, the AP replies with an association response, and authentication follows, for example with a WPA2 or WPA3 password. Only after that does the host run DHCP to get an IP address in the AP's subnet.

CSMA/CA, collision avoidance: Because collisions cannot be detected reliably, 802.11 tries to avoid them and uses ACKs to confirm success. The sender rules: if the channel is sensed idle for a short period called DIFS, transmit the whole frame. If the channel is busy, choose a random backoff value and count down only while the channel is idle; when the counter reaches zero, transmit. If no ACK arrives, double the backoff range and try again. The receiver rule: if a frame arrives correctly, wait a very short period, SIFS, and send an ACK. Since SIFS is shorter than DIFS, the ACK gets priority. Note that, unlike Ethernet, the sender transmits the entire frame, even if a collision occurs; there is no aborting.

Why the random countdown helps: In wired CSMA/CD, a station that senses the channel busy transmits as soon as it becomes idle. In wireless, if two stations both waited for the same busy period to end and then sent immediately, they would surely collide, and with no collision detection, both full frames would be wasted. Counting down random backoff values only while the channel is idle means that one station will usually reach zero first; the other hears it start and freezes its counter. That is the 'collision avoidance' idea.

RTS and CTS: To further reduce collisions of long data frames, especially with hidden terminals, 802.11 has an optional reservation scheme. The sender first sends a short request to send, RTS, frame to the AP, stating how long it needs the channel. The AP replies with a clear to send, CTS, frame, which every host in range of the AP hears, including hidden ones. The CTS gives permission to the sender and tells all others to stay silent for the stated duration. Collisions can still happen, but only between short RTS frames, which costs little. Because it adds overhead, RTS/CTS is usually used only for long frames.

The 802.11 frame: The 802.11 data frame has four address fields, unlike Ethernet's two. Address 1 is the MAC address of the wireless receiver; address 2 is the MAC address of the wireless transmitter; address 3 is the MAC address of the router interface that the AP is connected to; and address 4 is used only in ad hoc and mesh setups. Address 3 is needed because the AP is a link-layer device: when a frame from the router must reach a host, the AP converts an Ethernet frame into an 802.11 frame and back, and the addresses let it do that. The frame also has a duration field for reservations, sequence numbers to detect duplicate retransmissions, and a CRC.

Moving within the same subnet: If you walk from one AP to another AP in the same subnet, for example from one corridor to another on campus with the same SSID, your IP address can stay the same. Your laptop disassociates from the old AP and associates with the new one. The switch connecting the APs, through self-learning, soon notices frames from your MAC address on the new port and updates its table, so traffic to you follows you. A TCP connection, such as a video call, may continue without interruption.

Cellular networks, 4G and 5G: Cellular networks cover large areas with many cells, each served by a base station. In 4G LTE, the base station is the eNodeB; the core network includes elements such as the mobility management entity, which tracks and authenticates users, the home subscriber server, which stores subscriber information, and gateways that forward data to and from the Internet. Your SIM card identifies you to your home network. 5G introduces a new radio and core: it adds higher frequency bands, including millimetre-wave bands for very high speeds over short distances, and aims at three uses: enhanced mobile broadband, ultra-reliable low-latency communication for things like industrial control, and massive machine-type communication for IoT sensors.

Handover in cellular: When you travel on a bus from Dhaka to Gazipur while on a call, you move from cell to cell. Your phone regularly measures the signal strength of nearby base stations and reports them. When a neighbouring cell becomes stronger, the current base station decides to hand you over: it asks the target base station to prepare resources, tells your phone to switch, and the network redirects your data path to the new base station. Done well, you do not notice anything. Your IP address and calls continue because the core network, not the base station, anchors your connection.

Mobility across networks: When a device moves to a completely different network, keeping the same address is harder. The general approach uses a home network, where the device permanently belongs, and a visited network, where it currently is. In indirect routing, traffic goes to the home network first and is then tunnelled to the visited network; in direct routing, the correspondent learns the device's current location and sends there directly. Mobile IP standardised the indirect approach, and cellular networks use similar home and visited roles for roaming, for example when a Bangladeshi SIM is used abroad and data still flows through the home operator.

Real life example 1, a crowded hall's Wi-Fi: During a programming contest at a Dhaka university, 300 laptops connect to Wi-Fi in one hall. With one access point, CSMA/CA backoffs and collisions make everything slow. The organisers install three APs on non-overlapping channels 1, 6 and 11 at 2.4 GHz and several more on 5 GHz channels, all with the same SSID, and limit each AP's power so neighbouring cells overlap less. Contention per AP drops, and the network becomes usable. The lesson: in wireless, more APs on separate channels beat one powerful AP.

Real life example 2, mobile data on a train: On the train from Dhaka to Chattogram, your mobile data speed rises and falls. Near towns, the train passes close to towers, SNR is high and the modulation is fast. In open countryside, towers are far apart, SNR drops, the phone uses slower modulation, and handovers happen more often at high speed, sometimes with brief pauses. Each handover is the base stations and core network cooperating to keep your session alive.

Common mistakes: Confusing wireless with mobility. Saying 802.11 uses collision detection; it uses collision avoidance and ACKs. Forgetting that 802.11 sends a link-layer ACK for each frame while Ethernet does not. Thinking RTS/CTS is always used. Saying an 802.11 frame has only two addresses. Thinking handover changes your IP address within the same cellular network.

What exams ask: List the characteristics of wireless links and explain the hidden terminal problem. Explain the 802.11 architecture, beacons, scanning and association. Describe CSMA/CA step by step and explain why it differs from CSMA/CD. Explain RTS/CTS with a timeline. Explain the four address fields. Describe handover and the home and visited network idea.

Recap: Wireless links suffer from path loss, interference and multipath, so they adapt modulation to SNR and use ACKs. Hidden terminals make collision detection impossible, so 802.11 uses CSMA/CA with DIFS, random backoff, SIFS and ACKs, and optional RTS/CTS reservations. An AP and its hosts form a BSS named by an SSID, joined through beacons and association. Cellular 4G and 5G networks use base stations and a core network that tracks users and performs handovers. Next, in the final lesson, we look at how all this communication is kept secure.
key_points: Wireless links suffer from path loss, interference and multipath, giving higher bit error rates than cables.
Devices adapt modulation to SNR: fast when the signal is strong, slower and robust when it is weak.
Hidden terminals and fading make collision detection impossible in wireless.
802.11 (Wi-Fi 4, 5, 6, 7 = n, ac, ax, be) uses 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz; an AP and its hosts form a BSS with an SSID.
Hosts find APs through beacons (passive) or probes (active), then associate, authenticate and run DHCP.
CSMA/CA: wait DIFS, random backoff counted down while idle, send whole frame; receiver ACKs after SIFS.
Optional RTS/CTS reserves the channel and silences hidden terminals; 802.11 frames have four address fields.
Cellular networks hand over users between base stations; mobility across networks uses home and visited networks.
lessons.tip: To remember why CSMA/CA needs ACKs, ask: can the sender hear a collision at the receiver? In wireless, no. So the only way to know a frame arrived is for the receiver to say so.
lessons.task: Install a Wi-Fi analyser app on your phone and look at nearby networks: note each one's channel, band and signal strength. Check whether neighbouring 2.4 GHz networks use the non-overlapping channels 1, 6 and 11, and suggest a better channel for your own router.

quiz.q: Why does 802.11 not use collision detection?
options: Collisions cannot be reliably detected, for example because of hidden terminals
quiz.explain: A sender cannot hear a collision at the receiver, especially with hidden terminals and fading.

quiz.q: In CSMA/CA, how long does a receiver wait before sending an ACK?
quiz.explain: SIFS is shorter than DIFS, giving ACKs priority.

quiz.q: Which frame does an AP send periodically to announce its SSID?
quiz.explain: Beacon frames carry the SSID and the AP's MAC address.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of the CTS frame?
options: To grant the channel to one sender and silence all others, including hidden terminals
quiz.explain: Every station near the AP hears the CTS and stays quiet.

quiz.q: Which Wi-Fi generation is 802.11ax?
quiz.explain: 802.11ax is marketed as Wi-Fi 6.

lessons.title: Network Security and Course Wrap-up: Cryptography, TLS, Firewalls, VPNs and Attacks
lessons.content:
Think about sending money with a mobile financial service. You want three things. Nobody else should be able to read your PIN as it travels: secrecy. Nobody should be able to change '500 taka' into '5,000 taka' on the way: integrity. And you must be sure that the app is really talking to your provider's server, not to a fake one built by a fraudster, while the server must be sure it is really you: authentication. Every one of these goals must be achieved over an Internet where, as we have seen all course long, packets pass through many routers and links owned by strangers. This final lesson explains how.

The security goals: Network security is usually described through four properties. Confidentiality: only the sender and the intended receiver should understand the message, so it must be encrypted. Message integrity: the receiver must be able to detect whether the message was altered in transit, by accident or on purpose. End-point authentication: each side must be able to confirm the identity of the other. Operational security: organisations must protect their networks from attack, using firewalls, intrusion detection systems and good practice. The classic cast is Alice and Bob, who want to communicate securely, and Trudy, the intruder, who may eavesdrop, insert, delete or modify messages, impersonate someone, or hijack a connection.

The language of cryptography: The original message is plaintext. An encryption algorithm turns it into ciphertext, using a key. Decryption, with the right key, turns ciphertext back into plaintext. A basic principle: the algorithms are public and standardised; the secrecy lies only in the keys. Attacks include ciphertext-only attacks, where Trudy has only intercepted ciphertext, known-plaintext attacks, and chosen-plaintext attacks. A good cipher remains secure against all of these as long as the key stays secret.

Symmetric key cryptography: In symmetric key systems, Alice and Bob share the same secret key, used both to encrypt and to decrypt. A simple historical example is the Caesar cipher, shifting each letter by k places; it is trivial to break, because there are only 25 possible keys. Modern symmetric ciphers are block ciphers, processing blocks of bits. DES, the old standard, used a 56-bit key and can now be broken by brute force. Today's standard is AES, the Advanced Encryption Standard, with 128-bit blocks and keys of 128, 192 or 256 bits, which is considered secure. Symmetric ciphers are fast, so they encrypt the bulk of data. Their big problem: how do Alice and Bob agree on the shared key in the first place, if they have never met?

Public key cryptography: Public key systems solve the key distribution problem. Each person has a pair of keys: a public key, which anyone may know, and a private key, known only to the owner. A message encrypted with Bob's public key can be decrypted only with Bob's private key. So anyone can send Bob a secret message without any prior shared secret. The best-known algorithm is RSA, whose security rests on the difficulty of factoring the product of two very large primes. Elliptic curve cryptography offers similar security with shorter keys. Public key operations are much slower than symmetric ones, so in practice they are used to exchange or agree on a symmetric session key, which then encrypts the actual data.

Diffie-Hellman key agreement: Another way to get a shared key is the Diffie-Hellman key exchange: Alice and Bob each choose a secret number, exchange values computed from them over the open network, and both arrive at the same shared secret, which an eavesdropper cannot compute from the exchanged values in practice. Modern TLS uses ephemeral Diffie-Hellman, with fresh secrets for each session, which provides forward secrecy: even if a server's long-term private key is stolen later, past recorded sessions cannot be decrypted.

Hash functions and integrity: A cryptographic hash function H takes a message of any length and produces a fixed-length digest, such as 256 bits for SHA-256. It must be computationally infeasible to find two different messages with the same hash, or to find a message matching a given hash. A one-bit change in the message gives a completely different hash. MD5 and SHA-1 are now considered broken for security purposes; SHA-256 and the SHA-3 family are used instead. A hash alone does not prove who sent a message, because Trudy can change the message and compute a new hash. So Alice and Bob use a message authentication code, MAC: they share an authentication key s and send H(m + s) along with m; Trudy, without s, cannot produce a valid MAC. HMAC is the standard construction. (Do not confuse this MAC with the link-layer MAC address.)

Digital signatures: A digital signature lets someone prove that they created a document, in a way anyone can verify and the signer cannot later deny. Bob computes the hash of the message and encrypts the hash with his private key; that is the signature. Anyone can decrypt the signature with Bob's public key and compare it with their own hash of the message. If they match, the message came from Bob and was not changed. Signing the hash, rather than the whole message, keeps it fast.

Certificates: Public key cryptography has one more problem: how do you know that a public key really belongs to Bob, and not to Trudy pretending to be Bob? A certification authority, CA, verifies an identity and issues a certificate binding the public key to that identity, signed with the CA's own private key. Browsers and operating systems ship with a list of trusted CA public keys, so they can verify certificates. When you open your bank's website, the server presents its certificate, your browser checks the CA's signature and that the name matches the site, and only then trusts the server's public key. A browser warning about an invalid certificate is a serious red flag.

TLS, putting it together: Transport Layer Security, the successor of SSL, secures HTTPS and many other applications. It runs on top of TCP and gives applications a secure socket. In TLS 1.3, the handshake normally takes one round trip: the client sends a hello with its supported cipher suites and its Diffie-Hellman key share; the server replies with its own key share, its certificate and a signature proving it holds the matching private key, plus a message confirming the handshake. Both sides now compute the same session keys. From then on, application data is sent in records encrypted with a fast symmetric cipher such as AES, each with integrity protection, and sequence numbers that stop Trudy from reordering or replaying records. TLS 1.3 removed older, weaker options.

Security at other layers: Security can be added at several layers. At the application layer, secure email can use encryption and signatures. At the transport layer, TLS is by far the most common. At the network layer, IPsec encrypts and authenticates IP datagrams between two hosts or networks; in tunnel mode it encrypts entire datagrams, which is used in many VPNs. At the link layer, Wi-Fi uses WPA2 and WPA3 to encrypt frames between your device and the access point, but this only protects the wireless hop, not the rest of the path.

VPNs: An organisation with offices in Dhaka and Chattogram wants them to communicate as if on one private network, without leasing expensive private lines. A virtual private network uses the public Internet but encrypts traffic between sites: a gateway at each office wraps outgoing datagrams in encrypted IPsec datagrams addressed to the other office's gateway, and the other gateway unwraps them. Remote employees run VPN software to join the same protected network from home. Like IPv6 tunneling, a VPN is encapsulation, with encryption added.

Firewalls: A firewall isolates an organisation's internal network from the Internet, allowing some packets through and blocking others. Traditional packet filters inspect each datagram on its own, using header fields: source and destination IP address, protocol, TCP or UDP ports, and TCP flags. For example: allow outgoing web traffic to port 443, block all incoming TCP SYN segments except to the public web server, block incoming ICMP echo requests. Stateful filters track TCP connections and only allow incoming packets that belong to connections started from inside, much like NAT's table. Application gateways inspect application data, for example allowing only authorised users to use a particular service. Intrusion detection and prevention systems go further, examining packet contents for signatures of known attacks.

Common attacks: Malware, including viruses, worms and ransomware, can spread through email attachments, downloads and unpatched services. Denial of service floods a target with traffic or requests so legitimate users cannot be served; distributed denial of service, DDoS, uses thousands of compromised machines, a botnet, at once. IP spoofing means forging the source address of packets, used in reflection attacks; ingress filtering by ISPs helps prevent it. Packet sniffing on shared or unencrypted networks lets attackers read traffic, which is why HTTPS everywhere matters. Phishing tricks users into giving passwords or OTPs on fake websites or by phone; it attacks people, not protocols, and is among the most common frauds in Bangladesh, often targeting mobile financial service users.

Real life example 1, mobile banking safety: When you use a bank's app, TLS protects the connection, the server's certificate proves it is the real bank, and your PIN and OTP authenticate you. But none of this helps if you read your OTP aloud to a caller pretending to be from the bank. Banks and mobile financial services in Bangladesh repeatedly warn customers never to share a PIN or OTP with anyone. Strong cryptography protects the channel; only the user can protect their secrets.

Real life example 2, a small office firewall: A software company in Dhaka hosts its own staging server in its office. Its engineer configures the firewall to allow incoming HTTPS only to the staging server's address, allow SSH only from the VPN, and block everything else from outside. Staff laptops can browse freely, because the stateful firewall allows replies to connections they start. When a botnet later scans the office's public IP for open ports, almost nothing responds.

Course wrap-up: Look back at the whole stack. The application layer gave us HTTP, DNS, email, video streaming and sockets. The transport layer gave us UDP's simplicity and TCP's reliable, flow-controlled, congestion-controlled byte stream. The network layer gave us IPv4 and IPv6 addressing, subnetting, DHCP, NAT, ICMP, routing algorithms, OSPF and BGP. The link layer gave us MAC addresses, ARP, Ethernet, switches, VLANs and Wi-Fi. Today we added security across every layer. When you next open a website, you can follow every step, from the DHCP lease to the TLS record.

What to study next: For hands-on skills, practise with Wireshark to read real packets, and with a network simulator such as Cisco Packet Tracer or GNS3 to configure routers, VLANs, OSPF and firewalls. Write socket programs, perhaps a small chat server. Read about cloud networking and data center networks. If security interests you, study cryptography more deeply and look into ethical hacking courses and certifications. For research, explore SDN, 5G and network performance. Networking skills are needed in ISPs, telecom operators, banks, software companies and cloud providers, in Bangladesh and abroad.

Common mistakes: Thinking encryption alone ensures integrity and authentication. Confusing a hash with encryption; a hash cannot be reversed. Signing with the public key; signatures use the private key, verification uses the public key. Thinking HTTPS hides which site you visit from your ISP; the destination IP and often the server name are still visible. Thinking a firewall stops phishing.

What exams ask: State and explain the security goals. Compare symmetric and public key cryptography and explain why both are used together. Explain hash functions, MACs and digital signatures, and the role of certificates and CAs. Outline the TLS handshake. Explain packet filters and stateful firewalls with example rules. Describe VPNs and IPsec briefly. Explain DDoS, spoofing and phishing.

Recap: Security needs confidentiality, integrity, authentication and operational protection. Symmetric ciphers like AES encrypt bulk data; public key systems like RSA and Diffie-Hellman exchange keys; hashes, MACs and digital signatures protect integrity and prove origin; certificates from CAs bind keys to identities. TLS combines all of these to secure TCP connections, IPsec and VPNs secure the network layer, and firewalls control what enters a network. With this, the Computer Networks course is complete: you now understand how the Internet works from your browser down to the radio waves and back.
key_points: Security goals: confidentiality, message integrity, end-point authentication and operational security.
Symmetric ciphers (AES) use one shared key and are fast; DES's 56-bit key is too short today.
Public key cryptography (RSA, elliptic curves) uses a public/private key pair and solves key distribution; Diffie-Hellman agrees on a shared key.
Hashes (SHA-256) give fixed-length digests; a MAC adds a shared secret; a digital signature encrypts the hash with the private key.
Certificates signed by CAs bind public keys to identities, letting browsers trust servers.
TLS 1.3 uses a one-round-trip handshake with key exchange and certificates, then AES-encrypted, integrity-protected records.
IPsec and VPNs secure the network layer; firewalls filter packets by headers, by connection state or by application.
Common attacks: malware, DDoS with botnets, IP spoofing, sniffing and phishing, which targets people rather than protocols.
lessons.tip: Remember the key rule with one sentence: encrypt with the receiver's public key for secrecy, sign with your own private key for authenticity. Most public key exam questions test exactly this.
lessons.task: Open any HTTPS website, click the lock icon in the address bar and view the certificate. Note who issued it, the validity dates and the name it was issued to. Then write down which of the four security goals the certificate helps to achieve.

quiz.q: Which security goal is achieved by encrypting a message?
quiz.explain: Encryption prevents others from understanding the message.

quiz.q: To create a digital signature, what does the signer encrypt, and with which key?
options: The hash of the message, with the signer's private key
The whole message, with the receiver's public key
The hash, with the signer's public key
quiz.explain: Anyone can verify with the signer's public key.

quiz.q: Why is public key cryptography usually combined with symmetric encryption?
options: Public key operations are slow, so they are used to set up a fast symmetric session key
quiz.explain: Public key methods handle key exchange; AES encrypts the bulk data.

quiz.q: What does a certification authority do?
options: Signs certificates binding public keys to identities
quiz.explain: Browsers trust CA signatures to verify that a key belongs to a site.

quiz.q: A stateful firewall allows an incoming TCP packet when:
options: It belongs to a connection started from inside
quiz.explain: Stateful filters track connections and accept matching replies.

lessons.title: What Is Software Engineering?
lessons.content:
Imagine two people who both want a house. The first one buys some bricks, cement and tin, and starts building with his cousin on a Friday. No drawing, no plan, no budget. It works for a small shed. But if he tries to build a ten-storey building in Dhaka this way, the walls will crack, the stairs will end in the wrong place and the money will finish halfway. The second person hires an engineer. There is a plan, a drawing, a soil test, a budget, a schedule, inspections at each floor and a team where everyone knows their job. Software engineering is the second way of building, but for software.

What it is: Software engineering is the disciplined, systematic way of building, testing, delivering and maintaining software, so that it works correctly, is finished on time and within budget, and can be changed safely later. The IEEE defines it as the application of a systematic, disciplined, quantifiable approach to the development, operation and maintenance of software.
