A well-calibrated forecaster is one for whom, over many days with a 70% forecast, it rains on about 70% of them. You use this number with your own utilities: a 30% chance of rain may be enough to carry an umbrella to class, but not enough to cancel a cricket match planned for weeks.

Common mistakes and exam questions: The most common mistake is confusing P(a | b) with P(b | a): the probability of a positive test given disease (90%) is not the probability of disease given a positive test (about 15%). Others: forgetting to normalise, assuming independence without justification, and treating probabilities above 1 or summing distributions that do not add to 1 as acceptable. Typical questions: compute marginal and conditional probabilities from a joint table; apply Bayes' rule to a medical test; explain why logic fails for uncertain domains; define independence and conditional independence; and classify a message with naive Bayes.

Recap: Agents face uncertainty because of laziness, theoretical ignorance and practical ignorance, so they use probability as a degree of belief and choose actions by expected utility. Probabilities obey the Kolmogorov axioms; conditional probability is P(a | b) = P(a and b) / P(b). The full joint distribution answers any question by enumeration and normalisation, but grows as 2^n. Independence and especially conditional independence shrink it. Bayes' rule turns causal knowledge into diagnosis, and the disease-test example shows why priors matter. Naive Bayes applies these ideas to spam filtering. Next lesson, Bayesian networks put conditional independence into a graph.
key_points: Agents use probability because of laziness, theoretical ignorance and practical ignorance.
A probability is a degree of belief given the agent's knowledge; rational agents maximise expected utility.
Conditional probability: P(a | b) = P(a and b) / P(b); product rule: P(a and b) = P(a | b) P(b).
The full joint distribution answers any query by summing entries, but has 2^n entries for n Boolean variables.
Bayes' rule: P(b | a) = P(a | b) P(b) / P(a), turning causal knowledge into diagnostic knowledge.
In the test example (1% prior, 90% sensitivity, 5% false positives), a positive result gives only about 15% chance of disease.
Conditional independence makes naive Bayes possible: P(Cause) times the product of P(Effect | Cause).
lessons.tip: For any Bayes' rule question, first draw a table of 1,000 imaginary people: how many have the disease, how many of those test positive, how many healthy people test positive. Counting people is much harder to get wrong than juggling formulas, and it shows the base rate clearly.
lessons.task: Take the dental joint table from this lesson and compute by hand: P(Catch), P(Cavity | Catch), and P(Cavity | toothache and catch). Then check whether Toothache and Catch are conditionally independent given Cavity by comparing P(toothache and catch | cavity) with P(toothache | cavity) x P(catch | cavity).

quiz.q: Why does a logical rule like Toothache => Cavity fail?
options: Because logic cannot use the word Cavity
Because toothaches have other causes and we cannot list every exception
quiz.explain: Laziness, theoretical ignorance and practical ignorance make exact rules impractical.

quiz.q: Using the dental table, what is P(Cavity | Toothache)?
What is Bayes' rule?
options: P(b | a) = P(a | b) P(b) / P(a)
quiz.explain: It follows from writing the product rule in two ways.

quiz.q: A disease affects 1% of people; a test has 90% sensitivity and 5% false positives. After a positive test, the chance of disease is about:
quiz.explain: 0.009 / 0.0585 is about 0.154; most positives come from the many healthy people.

quiz.q: What does naive Bayes assume?
options: Effects are conditionally independent given the cause
The cause has only one effect
quiz.explain: This lets the joint be written as P(Cause) times the product of P(Effect | Cause).

lessons.title: Bayesian Networks
lessons.content:
Your neighbour Jamal calls: "Your house alarm is ringing!" Should you rush home from the office in Motijheel? Maybe there is a burglar. But the alarm also goes off sometimes when there is a small earthquake, and Jamal sometimes confuses your alarm with a phone ringtone. Another neighbour, Mitu, usually calls too when she hears it, but she plays loud music and often misses it. Today Mitu also called. How worried should you be? Reasoning like this, with several causes and several pieces of noisy evidence, is exactly what Bayesian networks were built for. This lesson shows how a graph plus small tables can represent a full probability model compactly, and how to answer questions with it.

From the full joint to a network: Last lesson we saw that the full joint distribution answers every question but needs 2^n numbers, and that conditional independence can shrink it. A Bayesian network (also called a belief network or Bayes net) is a way to write down exactly which conditional independences hold, as a graph, and then to specify the model with a small number of local probabilities. It was developed largely by Judea Pearl in the 1980s, and it changed AI by making probabilistic reasoning practical.

The structure: A Bayesian network is a directed acyclic graph (DAG). Each node is a random variable. A directed arrow from X to Y means X has a direct influence on Y; X is called a parent of Y. Usually arrows go from causes to effects. Each node has a conditional probability table (CPT) that gives P(node | parents) for every combination of parent values. A node with no parents simply has a prior probability. The graph must have no directed cycles, so no variable can, through a chain of arrows, influence itself.

The burglary network: The classic textbook example has five Boolean variables: Burglary (B), Earthquake (E), Alarm (A), JohnCalls (J) and MaryCalls (M), which we can read as Jamal and Mitu. Arrows: B to A, E to A, A to J, A to M. The neighbours do not hear the burglar or feel the earthquake directly; they only react to the alarm. The CPTs, with the textbook's numbers: P(B) = 0.001, P(E) = 0.002. P(A | B, E) = 0.95, P(A | B, not E) = 0.94, P(A | not B, E) = 0.29, P(A | not B, not E) = 0.001. P(J | A) = 0.90, P(J | not A) = 0.05. P(M | A) = 0.70, P(M | not A) = 0.01.

Counting the numbers: For a Boolean node with k Boolean parents, the CPT needs 2^k numbers (we only store P(true); P(false) is one minus that). The burglary network needs 1 + 1 + 4 + 2 + 2 = 10 numbers. The full joint for five Boolean variables needs 2^5 - 1 = 31 numbers. The saving grows dramatically: if each of n variables has at most k parents, the network needs at most n times 2^k numbers, which grows linearly with n, while the full joint grows as 2^n. With 30 variables and at most 5 parents each, that is 960 numbers instead of over a billion.

The meaning: the chain rule: A Bayesian network defines the full joint distribution as the product of the local CPT entries: P(x1, ..., xn) = product over i of P(xi | parents(Xi)). This comes from the general chain rule of probability, P(x1, ..., xn) = product of P(xi | x1, ..., xi-1), together with the network's assumption that each variable, given its parents, is conditionally independent of its other predecessors. So the graph is not just a picture; it is a precise statement about the joint distribution.

Computing one joint entry: What is the probability that the alarm rings, both neighbours call, but there is neither a burglary nor an earthquake? P(j, m, a, not b, not e) = P(j | a) P(m | a) P(a | not b, not e) P(not b) P(not e) = 0.90 x 0.70 x 0.001 x 0.999 x 0.998, which is about 0.00063. Every entry of the full joint can be computed this way by multiplying five numbers, so the network contains all the information of the table.

Conditional independence in the network: The network's structure tells us which independences hold. The key rule: each node is conditionally independent of its non-descendants, given its parents. So JohnCalls is independent of Burglary and Earthquake given Alarm: once you know the alarm rang, learning there was a burglary does not change the chance Jamal calls. An equivalent, sometimes more useful rule: a node is conditionally independent of all other nodes given its Markov blanket, which is its parents, its children and its children's other parents.

Three basic patterns: Most reasoning about independence comes down to three patterns. A chain, X to Y to Z (Burglary to Alarm to JohnCalls): X and Z are dependent, but independent given Y. A common cause, Y to X and Y to Z (Alarm to JohnCalls and Alarm to MaryCalls): X and Z are dependent (if Jamal calls, Mitu is more likely to call too), but independent given Y. A common effect, X to Y and Z to Y (Burglary to Alarm and Earthquake to Alarm): X and Z are independent, but become dependent when Y is observed. That last one is surprising and deserves a closer look.

Explaining away: Burglaries and earthquakes are independent: one does not make the other more likely. But suppose you know the alarm rang. Now if you hear on the radio that there was an earthquake, the earthquake explains the alarm, and a burglary becomes less likely. Two independent causes become dependent once their common effect is observed. This is called explaining away, and people do it naturally: if your friend is late and you learn there was a huge jam on the Mohakhali flyover, you stop worrying that they forgot the meeting. Bayesian networks capture this pattern correctly, while many simple rule systems do not.

Building a network: To construct a network, choose an ordering of the variables, preferably with causes before effects. Add the variables one by one; for each, choose as parents the smallest set of earlier variables that it directly depends on, and fill its CPT. Causal orderings produce compact networks with numbers experts can estimate (how often does an earthquake trigger the alarm?). A bad ordering, for example adding MaryCalls, JohnCalls, Alarm, Burglary, Earthquake in that order, produces more arrows and needs probabilities that are hard to judge, like P(Earthquake | Burglary, Alarm), even though it represents the same distribution.

Inference by enumeration: The main task is computing a posterior, P(Query | evidence). Example: given that both Jamal and Mitu called, what is the probability of a burglary? P(B | j, m) = alpha times the sum over e and a of P(B) P(e) P(a | B, e) P(j | a) P(m | a). We sum over the hidden variables Earthquake and Alarm. Carrying out the calculation with the CPTs above gives unnormalised values of about 0.000592 for burglary and 0.001492 for no burglary, so P(b | j, m) is about 0.000592 / 0.002084, roughly 0.284. Even with two calls, the chance of a burglary is only about 28%, because burglaries are rare and false alarms and false calls happen.

Making inference faster: Enumeration repeats the same sub-calculations many times. Variable elimination does the sums from the inside out and stores intermediate results, called factors, so nothing is computed twice; it also drops variables that are irrelevant to the query, such as nodes with no observed descendants. For networks shaped like trees (polytrees, with at most one undirected path between any two nodes), exact inference takes time linear in the size of the network. For general networks, exact inference is NP-hard in the worst case, so for big networks we turn to approximation.

Approximate inference by sampling: Sampling methods generate many random worlds from the network and count. In direct (prior) sampling, sample each variable in topological order from its CPT given the already sampled parents. To estimate P(b | j, m), rejection sampling throws away samples that disagree with the evidence and counts burglaries among the rest; it is simple but wasteful when evidence is rare. Likelihood weighting fixes the evidence variables and weights each sample by how likely the evidence was. Markov chain Monte Carlo methods, such as Gibbs sampling, wander through states by resampling one variable at a time given its Markov blanket. With enough samples, the estimates approach the true probabilities.

Beyond the basics: Real networks often have continuous variables, like temperature or blood pressure, handled with distributions such as the Gaussian. Dynamic Bayesian networks repeat a network over time slices to model processes that change, and hidden Markov models, used for many years in speech recognition, are a simple special case. Bayesian networks can also be learned from data: both the CPT numbers and, with more effort, the structure. And adding decision and utility nodes gives decision networks, which choose actions with the highest expected utility.

Real life example 1, medical diagnosis: A network for respiratory illness might have nodes for Smoking, Air pollution (high in Dhaka winters), Tuberculosis, Lung cancer, Bronchitis, Cough, Shortness of breath and X-ray result. Doctors and data supply the CPTs. Entering a patient's symptoms and test results gives posterior probabilities for each disease, and explaining away works naturally: a positive TB test makes lung cancer a less likely explanation for an abnormal X-ray. Systems of this type have been studied extensively in medical research, alongside careful evaluation before any clinical use.

Real life example 2, troubleshooting: Technical support systems have used Bayesian networks to diagnose faults: printer problems, car engine faults, or network outages. For an internet provider in Chattogram, nodes might be Router fault, Fibre cut, Area power cut, Customer's light on, Neighbours affected. Observing "neighbours also offline" explains away a router fault and points towards a fibre cut or power cut, so the technician checks the right thing first.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often think an arrow must mean strict cause; it means direct dependence, though causal arrows give the best networks. Others forget that CPTs need one row per combination of parent values, or think two causes are dependent before the effect is observed. In enumeration, they forget to sum over hidden variables or to normalise. Typical questions: draw a network for a story and write its CPT sizes; compute a joint entry with the chain rule; compute a posterior like P(B | j, m) by enumeration; identify conditional independences; explain explaining away; and describe rejection sampling.

Recap: A Bayesian network is a directed acyclic graph with a CPT at each node, representing the full joint as the product of P(xi | parents(Xi)). It needs far fewer numbers than the full joint. Each node is independent of its non-descendants given its parents; chains and common causes are blocked by observing the middle node, while common effects create dependence (explaining away). Exact inference by enumeration or variable elimination, and approximate inference by sampling, answer queries like P(Burglary | both neighbours call), which is about 0.28. Next lesson, we look at how machines learn such models, and much more, from data.
key_points: A Bayesian network is a directed acyclic graph with a conditional probability table at each node.
The joint distribution is the product of P(xi | parents(Xi)) over all nodes.
The burglary network needs 10 numbers, compared with 31 for the full joint.
Each node is conditionally independent of its non-descendants given its parents.
Explaining away: two independent causes become dependent when their common effect is observed.
P(Burglary | Jamal and Mitu both call) is about 0.28, computed by summing over Earthquake and Alarm and normalising.
Exact inference is NP-hard in general; sampling methods like rejection sampling and likelihood weighting give approximations.
lessons.tip: When computing a posterior by enumeration, write the product of CPT terms first, then list the hidden variables to sum over, then compute the unnormalised value for each query value, and only at the end normalise. Doing the steps in this fixed order prevents most errors.
lessons.task: Draw a Bayesian network for being late to class: nodes Rain, Traffic jam, Bus late, Overslept, Late to class. Decide the arrows, write the CPT sizes, and invent reasonable numbers. Then explain in words how learning "there was a big traffic jam" changes your belief that you overslept, given that you were late.

quiz.q: What does an arrow from X to Y in a Bayesian network mean?
options: X directly influences Y; X is a parent of Y
quiz.explain: Each node's CPT gives P(node | parents), and arrows usually go from causes to effects.

quiz.q: How many numbers does the burglary network need, compared with the full joint of 31?
How is P(j, m, a, not b, not e) computed in the burglary network?
options: P(j) + P(m) + P(a) + P(not b) + P(not e)
P(a | j, m) times P(not b)
P(j | a) P(m | a) P(a | not b, not e) P(not b) P(not e)
quiz.explain: The chain rule multiplies each node's CPT entry given its parents.

quiz.q: What is explaining away?
options: A node becomes independent of its children
Evidence is ignored when computing a posterior
Two independent causes become dependent once their common effect is observed
quiz.explain: Learning of an earthquake makes a burglary a less likely explanation for the alarm.

quiz.q: After both neighbours call, P(Burglary) is about:
quiz.explain: The prior is so low that, even with two calls, a burglary is only about 28% likely.

lessons.title: Introduction to Machine Learning and Neural Networks
lessons.content:
How did you learn to tell a ripe mango from an unripe one? Nobody gave you a rulebook with exact colours and firmness values. You saw many mangoes, tasted some, were corrected by your grandmother at the bazaar, and slowly your brain built its own sense of "ripe". The expert systems of lesson 20 needed humans to write every rule, which was slow and brittle. Machine learning (ML) takes the other path: the program improves its performance at a task by learning from data and experience. This lesson is an introduction only; you will study ML properly in its own course later. Here we see the main types of learning, a few classic methods, and the basic idea of neural networks.

What learning means for an agent: An agent is learning if it improves its performance on future tasks after making observations about the world. Learning is needed when the designer cannot anticipate every situation (a robot in a new building), when conditions change over time (spam keeps evolving), or when nobody knows how to write the program at all (how exactly do you recognise your friend's face?). In ML, we give the computer examples and a way to measure how well it is doing, and the algorithm adjusts a model, a function with adjustable parts called parameters, to do better.

Three main kinds of learning: In supervised learning, each training example comes with the correct answer, called the label: emails marked spam or not spam, house descriptions with their prices. The goal is a function that predicts labels for new examples. When the label is a category, it is classification; when it is a number, it is regression. In unsupervised learning, there are no labels; the algorithm finds structure on its own, for example grouping customers of a shop into clusters with similar buying habits. In reinforcement learning, the agent acts in an environment and receives rewards or punishments, like a dog being given treats, and learns which actions lead to more reward over time.

Supervised learning more precisely: We have a training set of N example pairs (x1, y1), ..., (xN, yN), where each y was produced by some unknown function f, so that y = f(x). The task is to find a hypothesis h, from a chosen hypothesis space (all straight lines, all decision trees of some size, all networks of a certain shape), that approximates f well. "Well" means not just on the training examples but on new examples it has never seen. This ability is called generalisation, and it is the whole point.

Decision trees: A decision tree makes a prediction by asking a sequence of questions. Example, a tree for "will the customer wait for a table at a restaurant in Dhanmondi?": first ask "How many people are inside?"; if none, predict no; if some, predict yes; if full, ask "What is the estimated wait?", and so on. Each internal node tests an attribute, each branch is a possible value, and each leaf gives a prediction. Trees are easy for people to read and explain, which is a big advantage in fields like banking or medicine.

Learning a decision tree: The standard algorithm builds the tree top-down, greedily. At each node, choose the attribute that best separates the examples into pure groups (all yes or all no), split the examples by that attribute's values, and repeat on each branch. "Best" is measured by information gain, based on entropy: entropy measures how mixed a set is, being 0 bits for a pure set and 1 bit for a 50/50 mix of two classes. The attribute that reduces entropy the most gives the most information. Stop when a group is pure or no attributes are left.

Training, validation and test sets: How do we know if a learned model is good? Never judge it only on the data it learned from; it may simply have memorised it. The standard practice is to split data into a training set (to learn the parameters), a validation set (to choose settings like tree depth, called hyperparameters), and a test set (used once at the end to estimate real performance). When data is limited, k-fold cross-validation splits the data into k parts, trains on k minus 1 parts and tests on the remaining one, rotating k times and averaging. Using test data during development is a serious mistake, because the reported accuracy then becomes too optimistic.

Overfitting and underfitting: A model overfits when it fits the training data very closely, including its noise and accidents, and then performs poorly on new data. Think of a student who memorises last year's answers word for word and fails when the questions are rephrased. A model underfits when it is too simple to capture the real pattern, like predicting every house price with a single average. A good model sits between: complex enough to capture the pattern, simple enough to generalise. Remedies for overfitting include more data, simpler models, pruning decision trees, and regularisation, which adds a penalty for complexity to the learning objective.

Linear models: Another simple and very useful hypothesis is a straight line or flat plane. Linear regression predicts a number as a weighted sum of inputs: for a flat in Mirpur, price might be estimated as w0 + w1 times area + w2 times number of rooms. Learning means finding weights that minimise the average squared error on the training data, which can be done exactly with a formula or step by step with gradient descent: repeatedly nudge each weight in the direction that reduces the error. For classification, a linear classifier draws a line (or plane) separating the classes, and logistic regression outputs a probability with a smooth S-shaped curve.

The artificial neuron: Neural networks are loosely inspired by brain cells. A single artificial neuron, or unit, takes inputs x1, ..., xn, multiplies each by a weight, adds a bias b, and applies an activation function g: output = g(w1 x1 + ... + wn xn + b). If g is a step function (output 1 if the sum is above 0, otherwise 0), the unit is a perceptron, a linear classifier introduced by Frank Rosenblatt in the late 1950s. Common modern activation functions are the sigmoid, which squashes any number to between 0 and 1, and the ReLU, which outputs max(0, sum).

The perceptron learning rule: The perceptron learns by correcting its mistakes. For each training example, compute the output y; if it is wrong, change each weight by (target minus y) times the input: wi = wi + (t - y) xi, and similarly b = b + (t - y). If the output is right, change nothing. If the data can be separated by a line, this rule is guaranteed to find such a line in a finite number of steps.

A perceptron worked example, learning OR: Inputs (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1) with targets 0, 1, 1, 1. Start with w1 = w2 = 0, b = 0, step output 1 if the sum is above 0. Pass 1: (0,0) gives 0, correct. (0,1) gives 0 but target 1, so update: w2 = 1, b = 1. (1,0): sum 0 + 1 = 1, output 1, correct. (1,1): correct. Pass 2: (0,0): sum = 1, output 1, wrong; b becomes 0. (0,1): sum 1, correct. (1,0): sum 0, output 0, wrong; w1 = 1, b = 1. (1,1): correct. Pass 3: (0,0): sum 1, wrong; b = 0. The rest are correct with w = (1, 1), b = 0. Pass 4: all four correct, so learning stops. The final perceptron computes OR exactly.

The limit of one perceptron: A single perceptron can only learn patterns separable by a straight line. Minsky and Papert famously pointed out in 1969 that it cannot learn XOR (output 1 when exactly one input is 1), because no single line separates (0,1) and (1,0) from (0,0) and (1,1). This contributed to a period of reduced interest in neural networks. The fix is to stack units into layers: a network with one hidden layer can compute XOR easily.

Multilayer networks and backpropagation: A feedforward neural network has an input layer, one or more hidden layers, and an output layer, with each unit feeding the next layer. With enough hidden units, such networks can approximate a very wide range of functions. Training uses gradient descent on a loss function that measures error. The challenge is knowing how much each hidden weight contributed to the error. Backpropagation solves this: compute the output error, then pass it backwards layer by layer using the chain rule of calculus, giving the gradient for every weight efficiently. The idea was popularised in the mid-1980s and remains the core of training today.

Deep learning: Deep learning means using neural networks with many layers. Since around 2012, deep networks have made dramatic progress, helped by three things: large datasets, fast parallel hardware such as GPUs, and better training techniques. Special architectures suit special data: convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for images, which reuse the same small filters across the image; recurrent networks for sequences; and transformers, introduced in 2017, which use a mechanism called attention and now underlie most large language models. Deep networks often need a lot of data and computation, and their reasoning is hard to inspect, which raises the explainability issues of the next lesson.

Real life example 1, Bangla handwritten digit recognition: Researchers in Bangladesh have built datasets of handwritten Bangla digits and characters, collected from many writers, and trained CNNs to recognise them. Such systems can help digitise forms, postal codes and old records. A model trained only on neat writing from university students may do worse on writing from older people or children; this is overfitting to the kind of data seen, and it shows why diverse training data matters.

Real life example 2, credit scoring for mobile loans: A digital lending service might predict whether a borrower will repay, using features like transaction history and repayment of earlier small loans. A decision tree or logistic regression can be explained to customers and regulators ("rejected because of three missed payments"), while a deep network might be slightly more accurate but harder to justify. The choice of model is therefore not only about accuracy, but also about fairness and explanation.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students confuse classification with regression, or supervised with unsupervised learning. Many judge a model by training accuracy, missing overfitting. In the perceptron rule, they forget to update the bias, or update when the output is already correct. Typical questions: define the three types of learning with examples; build a small decision tree or choose the root attribute by information gain; explain overfitting and how to detect it with a validation set; trace the perceptron learning rule on AND or OR; explain why one perceptron cannot learn XOR; and describe backpropagation in words.

Recap: Machine learning builds models from data instead of hand-written rules. Supervised learning uses labelled examples, unsupervised learning finds structure, and reinforcement learning learns from rewards. Decision trees split data by the most informative attribute; linear models use weighted sums. Good models generalise, which we check with separate validation and test sets, guarding against overfitting. A perceptron learns linearly separable patterns like OR by correcting mistakes, but not XOR; multilayer networks trained by backpropagation, and deep learning, go much further. The final lesson looks at language, vision and the ethics of AI.
key_points: Machine learning improves performance at a task by learning from data rather than hand-written rules.
Supervised learning uses labelled examples (classification or regression); unsupervised finds structure; reinforcement learns from rewards.
Generalisation to unseen data is the goal; use separate training, validation and test sets.
Overfitting means fitting noise in training data and doing poorly on new data; underfitting means the model is too simple.
Decision trees choose splits by information gain, based on entropy.
The perceptron rule updates wi = wi + (t - y) xi only on mistakes; it learns OR but cannot learn XOR.
Multilayer networks are trained by backpropagation and gradient descent; deep learning uses many layers.
lessons.tip: Whenever you see a model's accuracy, ask two questions: "Measured on which data?" and "Compared with what simple baseline?". A 95% accuracy is meaningless if 95% of the examples belong to one class and the model just always predicts it.
lessons.task: Trace the perceptron learning rule by hand for the AND function, starting with w1 = w2 = 0 and b = 0 and the same step function as in the lesson. Record the weights after every update and count how many passes it needs. Then try XOR for a few passes and describe what happens.

quiz.q: Grouping shop customers by buying habits without any labels is an example of:
quiz.explain: No labels are given; the algorithm finds clusters itself.

quiz.q: What is overfitting?
options: A model too simple to capture the pattern
A model that has not finished training
Fitting noise in the training data so that performance on new data is poor
quiz.explain: The model memorises accidents of the training set instead of the real pattern.

quiz.q: What is the perceptron learning rule for weight wi when the output is wrong?
quiz.explain: The weight moves in the direction that corrects the mistake; no change when correct.

quiz.q: Why can a single perceptron not learn XOR?
options: XOR's positive and negative examples cannot be separated by a straight line
quiz.explain: A single perceptron is a linear classifier; XOR needs a hidden layer.

quiz.q: What does backpropagation compute?
options: The gradient of the error with respect to every weight, layer by layer from the output back
quiz.explain: It applies the chain rule backwards so gradient descent can update hidden weights.

lessons.title: Language, Vision, AI Ethics and Course Wrap-Up
lessons.content:
Your aunt in Sylhet sends a voice message in Sylheti, your cousin replies in Banglish typed with English letters, and a shop sign in the photo they share mixes Bangla and English. A human reads all of this without effort. For a computer, every part is hard: understanding speech, handling a dialect, reading text written in two scripts, and recognising letters in a blurry photo. This final lesson gives an overview of two big application areas of AI, natural language processing and computer vision, then looks carefully at the ethical questions AI raises, and ends with a recap of the whole course.

Natural language processing: Natural language processing (NLP) is the part of AI that deals with human languages: understanding, generating and translating them. Common tasks include text classification (spam, sentiment, topic), information extraction (finding names, dates and places in news), machine translation, question answering, summarisation, speech recognition and speech synthesis. Language is hard for computers because it is ambiguous ("I saw the man with the telescope": who has the telescope?), depends on context and world knowledge, and keeps changing with new words and slang.

Classic approaches to language: Early NLP used hand-written grammars and rules, close to the logic-based methods of this course. Grammars describe how words combine into phrases and sentences, and parsing finds the structure of a sentence as a tree. From the 1990s, statistical methods became dominant: language models assign probabilities to word sequences, often using n-grams (the probability of a word given the previous one or two words), and naive Bayes and similar models classify text using word counts. These methods learn from large text collections instead of relying only on rules written by linguists.

Neural language models: Modern NLP mostly uses neural networks. Words are represented as vectors of numbers, called embeddings, learned so that words used in similar contexts get similar vectors. Transformer networks, introduced in 2017, process whole sequences using attention, which lets each word look at all other words to decide what matters. Large language models are transformers trained on enormous amounts of text to predict the next piece of text; after further training, they can answer questions, write and summarise. They are useful but have well-known limits: they can produce fluent but false statements, often called hallucinations; they reflect biases in their training data; and their abilities depend heavily on how much data exists for a language.

Challenges for Bangla: Bangla is one of the most spoken languages in the world, yet it has historically had far fewer digital resources (labelled datasets, tools, large clean text collections) than English, so it is often described as a low-resource language in NLP. Specific challenges include rich word forms (one root with many suffixes and inflections), compound characters (juktakkhor) and Unicode encoding issues, code-mixing with English and Banglish written in Latin letters, dialects such as Sylheti and Chittagonian, and fewer high-quality annotated datasets for tasks like named entity recognition. Researchers in Bangladesh and abroad have been building datasets and models for Bangla, and this is an area where local students can contribute a lot.

Speech and translation: Speech recognition turns audio into text, and speech synthesis turns text into natural-sounding audio; both are now mostly done with neural networks trained on many hours of recorded speech. Machine translation has moved from rule-based systems, through statistical systems that learned from aligned sentence pairs, to neural systems. Translation between Bangla and English has improved a lot, but it still struggles with idioms, dialect words, names and long sentences, so important documents, like legal papers or medical instructions, should still be checked by a fluent person.

Computer vision: Computer vision is the part of AI that extracts information from images and video. Core tasks include image classification (what is in this picture?), object detection (where are the objects, with boxes around them?), segmentation (which pixels belong to which object?), face recognition, optical character recognition (reading printed or handwritten text), and tracking objects through video. Vision is hard because the same object looks very different under different lighting, angles, distances and partial occlusion, while a photo is just a grid of numbers.

How vision systems work today: Classic vision used hand-designed features, such as edges and corners, with separate classifiers. Since around 2012, convolutional neural networks have become the standard approach: early layers learn simple patterns like edges, deeper layers combine them into textures, parts and whole objects. A widely cited turning point was the 2012 ImageNet competition, where a deep CNN greatly reduced the error rate compared with earlier methods. Today, transformer-based models are also used for vision, and some models handle both images and text together.

Vision applications around us: Phones unlock by recognising faces; apps translate signs by reading their text; cars in some countries use cameras to keep lanes and detect pedestrians; doctors use systems that help flag possible problems in X-rays and retinal scans; and farmers can photograph leaves to check for disease. In Bangladesh, possible uses include reading vehicle number plates in traffic systems, monitoring crops and rivers from satellite images, and digitising old Bangla documents. Each of these also raises the ethical questions we turn to now.

Limits of today's systems: It is important to be realistic. Current AI systems are powerful at specific tasks with plenty of data, but they can fail in surprising ways when inputs differ from their training data: a vision model may be fooled by small, carefully designed changes to an image (adversarial examples), and a language model may give different answers to the same question phrased slightly differently. They do not have the broad common sense, grounded understanding of the physical world or reliable reasoning that people often assume. Whether and when more general AI will be achieved is debated among experts, and confident predictions in either direction should be treated with care.

Why AI ethics matters: AI systems now influence who gets a loan, which job applicants are shortlisted, what news people see and how police allocate attention. Mistakes or unfairness can harm many people quickly, and harms are often hard to see from inside the system. Engineers who build AI therefore carry responsibility not only for accuracy, but also for fairness, privacy, transparency and safety. These questions are not only for philosophers; they shape design decisions every day.

Bias and fairness: A model learns from data, and data reflects the past, including past discrimination and uneven coverage. A widely reported example: some commercial face analysis systems were found to have much higher error rates on darker-skinned women than on lighter-skinned men, because training data and testing had not covered all groups well. A hiring model trained on past hiring decisions can learn to repeat past biases. Defining fairness is itself hard: equal accuracy across groups, equal approval rates and other definitions can conflict, so choices must be made openly. Good practice includes checking performance separately for different groups, such as rural and urban users, or speakers of different dialects.

Privacy and surveillance: AI works best with lots of data, and much of that data is about people: messages, locations, faces, purchases. Collecting and combining such data can reveal private facts, and face recognition makes large-scale surveillance technically easy. Responsible systems collect only the data they need, protect and anonymise it, ask for meaningful consent, and follow data protection laws where they exist. Techniques such as differential privacy and federated learning, which trains models without collecting raw data in one place, can help.

Explainability and accountability: When a deep network denies a loan, the person deserves a reason, and regulators need to check the system. Yet large networks are hard to interpret. Methods for explainable AI try to show which inputs mattered most for a decision, and in high-stakes areas simpler, interpretable models are sometimes preferred. Accountability asks who is responsible when an AI system causes harm: the developer, the company deploying it, or the user. Recall MYCIN from lesson 20: one reason it was not used routinely was exactly this question of responsibility, which remains important today.

Work, misinformation and safety: AI can automate some tasks, which may change or reduce some jobs while creating others; the effect on any particular country, including Bangladesh's large garment and service sectors, is debated and uncertain, so we should be cautious about confident predictions either way. Generative models can create realistic fake images, audio and text, which can be misused for scams and misinformation, especially around elections. Researchers also study AI safety: making sure systems reliably do what their designers intend, behave well in unexpected situations, and cannot easily be misused. These are active, open problems.

Guidelines and good practice: Many governments, companies and organisations have published principles for trustworthy AI, typically including fairness, transparency, privacy, safety, accountability and human oversight, and some regions have begun to pass laws regulating high-risk AI uses. For a student, practical habits matter most: know where your data came from, test on diverse users, document your model's limits, keep a human in the loop for important decisions, and ask "who could be harmed if this is wrong?" before deploying.

Real life example 1, a Bangla customer service chatbot: A telecom company wants a chatbot that answers customers in Bangla. The team must handle Banglish and dialect words, avoid confidently making up wrong information about tariffs, protect customer data in the logs, offer an easy way to reach a human, and test the bot with users from different districts and age groups, not only young city users. Each of these is both a technical and an ethical requirement.

Real life example 2, AI in exam proctoring: Some online exams use cameras and AI to flag suspicious behaviour. If the system was trained mostly on well-lit faces and quiet rooms, it may wrongly flag students in poorly lit homes or shared rooms, more often from poorer families. A fair deployment would test for such differences, let humans review every flag, explain the decision to students and allow appeals.

Course wrap-up, the big picture: We started with agents: an agent perceives and acts, and a rational agent does what is expected to maximise its performance measure (lessons 1 to 3). We learned to formulate problems and solve them by search: uninformed methods like BFS, UCS and IDS (lessons 4 to 7), and informed methods like greedy search and A* with admissible heuristics (8 and 9); local search for optimisation (10 and 11); adversarial search with minimax and alpha-beta for games (12 and 13); and constraint satisfaction with backtracking and arc consistency (14 and 15). We then represented knowledge in propositional and first-order logic and reasoned with resolution and chaining (16 to 19), organised it in ontologies and expert systems (20), and planned actions (21). Finally we handled uncertainty with probability, Bayes' rule and Bayesian networks (22 and 23), learned from data (24), and looked at language, vision and ethics today.

Where to go next: Machine learning, in its own course, deepens lesson 24. Courses on natural language processing, computer vision, robotics and reinforcement learning build on the search, logic and probability ideas here. Whatever you choose, the habits from this course remain useful: formulate the problem clearly, choose a representation, pick an algorithm whose guarantees you understand, test honestly, and think about the people your system affects.
key_points: NLP covers understanding, generating and translating human language; ambiguity and context make it hard.
Modern NLP uses embeddings and transformers; large language models can be fluent but may state false things.
Bangla faces low-resource challenges: rich word forms, compound characters, code-mixing and dialects.
Computer vision tasks include classification, detection, segmentation, OCR and face recognition, mostly using CNNs and transformers today.
Bias in data can make AI systems unfair; test performance separately for different groups.
Privacy, explainability, accountability, misinformation and safety are central ethical issues in AI.
The course covered agents, search, games, CSPs, logic, knowledge, planning, probability and learning.
lessons.tip: For any AI project, write a one-paragraph "limits" note before you finish: what data it was trained on, where it may fail, and who could be harmed if it is wrong. Examiners, employers and users all value an engineer who knows the limits of their own system.
lessons.task: Pick one AI system you use (a translator, a face unlock, a recommendation feed). Write down: what task it performs, which AI areas from this course it likely uses, one group of users it might work worse for, one privacy risk, and one change you would make to reduce harm.

quiz.q: Why is Bangla often called a low-resource language in NLP?
options: It has had far fewer digital datasets and tools than languages like English
quiz.explain: Despite many speakers, labelled data and tools have historically been limited.

quiz.q: What is a "hallucination" in a large language model?
options: A fluent but false statement produced by the model
A model that refuses to answer
A spelling mistake in the input
quiz.explain: The model can produce confident text that is not true.

quiz.q: Which task finds where objects are in an image by drawing boxes around them?
quiz.explain: Detection gives locations; classification only says what is present.

quiz.q: A face analysis system has much higher error rates for one group of people. This is mainly an issue of:
quiz.explain: Uneven training data and testing can make systems unfair to some groups.

quiz.q: Which practice best supports accountability for an AI system making important decisions?
options: Keeping a human in the loop, documenting limits and allowing appeals
Using only the largest available model
quiz.explain: People affected need explanations, review and a way to challenge decisions.

lessons.title: What Computer Graphics Is: Pixels, Raster and Vector Images
lessons.content:
Pick up your phone and look closely at the screen, really closely, maybe with a magnifying glass or the zoom of another phone's camera. The smooth photo of your family, the sharp letters of a WhatsApp message, the bright green field in a cricket game, all of it breaks down into a grid of tiny glowing squares. Every single one of those squares was told, by some program, exactly what colour to be, around 60 times every second. Computer graphics is the science of deciding those colours: how a computer turns ideas like a line, a circle, a 3D car or a sunset into millions of coloured dots, quickly and correctly.

What computer graphics is: Computer graphics is the part of computer science that deals with creating, storing, changing and displaying pictures using a computer. The input is usually a description: points, lines, shapes, 3D models, colours, lights and a camera. The output is an image on a screen, on paper or in a file. The opposite direction, taking a photo and understanding what is inside it, is called image processing or computer vision. Graphics goes from model to picture; vision goes from picture to model. This course is about the first direction.

Where graphics is used: Almost every screen you touch uses it. Games like PUBG Mobile or FIFA draw full 3D worlds in real time. Engineers use CAD (computer aided design) software to design buildings, bridges such as the Padma Bridge, and machine parts before anything is built. Google Maps and Barikoi draw roads and labels. Doctors look at 3D views of CT and MRI scans. Films and cartoons use graphics for effects and whole animated movies. Even the buttons, fonts and scroll animations of a simple app like bKash are drawn by graphics code. Data charts in a report, weather maps on TV and the Pathao rider moving on your map are graphics too.

A short history: In 1963 Ivan Sutherland built Sketchpad at MIT, a program where a user drew directly on a screen with a light pen and could move, copy and resize shapes. It is often called the start of interactive computer graphics. Early screens drew lines directly with an electron beam (vector displays). In the 1970s cheaper memory made raster displays with a frame buffer possible, and algorithms like Bresenham's line drawing, the z-buffer and Phong shading appeared. The 1980s and 1990s brought personal computers with graphical user interfaces, then 3D graphics cards. Today a phone contains a GPU, a graphics processing unit, that can shade billions of pixels per second.

The pixel: A raster screen is a rectangular grid of picture elements, called pixels. Each pixel shows one colour at a time. A pixel is addressed by two whole numbers, a column x and a row y. In many systems the origin (0,0) is at the top-left and y grows downwards, while in maths and in many graphics textbooks the origin is at the bottom-left and y grows upwards. Both are fine as long as you know which one you are using. A pixel is not a perfect little square of light in real hardware, but thinking of it as a small square cell is a good starting model.

Resolution: Resolution is the number of pixels across and down. Full HD is 1920 x 1080, which is 1920 times 1080 = 2,073,600 pixels, about 2 million. A 4K UHD screen is 3840 x 2160, which is exactly four times as many, about 8.3 million. More pixels can show finer detail, but they also need more memory and more work every frame. Pixel density, measured in pixels per inch (PPI), tells how tightly packed they are. A 6 inch phone with Full HD looks sharper than a 40 inch TV with the same resolution because its pixels are much smaller.

Raster images: A raster image, also called a bitmap, stores the colour of every pixel in a grid. A photo from your phone camera saved as JPEG or PNG is a raster image. Raster images are great for photos and complex scenes because any pattern of colours can be stored. Their weakness is scaling. If you zoom a small raster image a lot, each stored pixel becomes a big visible block, and edges look jagged or blurry. The image simply does not contain information finer than its pixels.

Vector images: A vector image stores shapes as mathematical descriptions instead of pixels. A circle is stored as centre (50, 50) and radius 20, with a red fill. A line is stored as its two end points and a thickness. When the image is shown, the program turns these descriptions into pixels at whatever size is needed. That is why logos, fonts and maps are usually vector: an SVG logo or a TrueType letter stays perfectly sharp whether printed on a visiting card or on a giant billboard at Kawran Bazar. The weakness is that a real photo with millions of different colours is very hard to describe as shapes.

Raster vs vector in one small example: Suppose you want a black circle of radius 100 on a 300 x 300 white canvas. As a raster PNG with 1 byte per pixel, you store 300 x 300 = 90,000 values (compression makes the file smaller, but the idea is a full grid). As a vector, you store roughly: circle, centre (150,150), radius 100, colour black, a few dozen bytes. If you now want the same picture at 3000 x 3000, the raster version must be redrawn or it will look blocky, while the vector version just gets drawn again at the larger size with smooth edges.

Rasterization, the central job: Since our screens are raster grids, every vector description must finally be converted into pixels. This conversion is called scan conversion or rasterization. Deciding which pixels best approximate a straight line from (2,3) to (10,8), which pixels lie on a circle, or which pixels are inside a triangle, are exactly the algorithms we study in the first part of this course: DDA, Bresenham, midpoint circle and ellipse, and polygon filling.

Object space and image space: Graphics people often say an algorithm works in object space or in image space. Object space means working with the geometric description itself, for example comparing two triangles in 3D to see which is in front. Image space means working pixel by pixel on the screen, for example storing a depth value for every pixel. We will meet this distinction again in hidden surface removal, where the z-buffer is an image space method and back-face culling works in object space.

Interactive and non-interactive graphics: In passive or non-interactive graphics the user only watches, like a printed chart or a pre-rendered movie. In interactive graphics the user changes the picture while it is shown: moving a game character, rotating a 3D model, zooming a map. Interactive graphics must be fast, usually 30 or 60 frames per second or more, so a lot of graphics research is about doing the same job with fewer calculations, which is why integer tricks like Bresenham's algorithm matter.

The basic pipeline in one paragraph: A typical 3D picture is made in steps. First we describe objects, usually as many small triangles. Then we place them in a world using transformations: move, rotate, scale. Then we choose a camera and project the 3D world onto a 2D image plane. We clip away parts outside the view. We decide which surfaces are hidden behind others. We compute colour using lights and materials. Finally we rasterize triangles into pixels and write them into a frame buffer that the display shows. Each of these steps is a lesson in this course.

The maths you need: You already know vectors, dot product, cross product and matrix multiplication from Linear Algebra, and you have seen 2D rotation and scaling matrices and homogeneous coordinates there. We will reuse them a lot, but always with graphics examples and small numbers. You also need simple coordinate geometry: the slope of a line, the equation of a circle, and similar triangles. No heavy calculus is required for this course.

Real life example 1, a Ludo game on your phone: When you roll the dice in a Ludo app, the board is probably stored as a raster image or drawn from vector shapes, the tokens are small images moved to new positions using translation, the dice spins using rotation, and everything is drawn into a frame buffer 60 times per second. If the tokens look slightly blurry when you zoom, that tells you they are raster images being scaled up.

Real life example 2, a shop banner at Dhaka New Market: A designer makes a banner in a tool like Illustrator or Inkscape using vector shapes and fonts, then sends it to a large-format printer. Because it is vector, the same file prints sharply at 1 metre or 10 metres wide. The printer itself is a raster device: it finally places tiny ink dots. So even here a vector description is rasterized at the last step.

The course map: We start with display hardware and the frame buffer. Then raster algorithms: lines with DDA and Bresenham, circles and ellipses with the midpoint method, polygon filling and antialiasing. Then 2D transformations with homogeneous matrices, windowing and viewports, and clipping with Cohen-Sutherland, Liang-Barsky and Sutherland-Hodgman. Then 3D: objects, transformations, projections and the viewing pipeline, followed by hidden surface removal. Then appearance: colour models, illumination, shading, curves and texture mapping. We finish with the modern GPU pipeline and shaders, animation basics and an introduction to ray tracing.

How to study this course: Draw. Keep graph paper and a pencil, and actually plot the pixels each algorithm picks. Run the decision parameters by hand in a small table; exams love these tables. When a formula appears, try it once with tiny numbers. If you can program, write each algorithm in a few lines of Python or C and print the pixel list; seeing your own code draw a circle is very satisfying.

Common mistakes: Thinking raster means bad quality and vector means good quality. Each is right for different jobs: photos are raster, logos are vector. Thinking a vector image is never turned into pixels. It always is, at display time. Mixing up computer graphics with image processing: graphics creates images from models, image processing changes or analyses existing images. And forgetting which way the y axis points on a given system, which flips pictures upside down.

What exams ask: Define computer graphics and list applications. Differentiate raster and vector graphics, or raster scan and random scan displays. Define pixel, resolution and aspect ratio, and compute pixel counts. Explain interactive versus passive graphics. Short notes on Sketchpad, rasterization or the graphics pipeline also appear.

Recap: Computer graphics turns descriptions of shapes, objects, lights and cameras into pictures. Screens are grids of pixels, described by resolution. Raster images store every pixel; vector images store shapes and are rasterized when shown. Rasterization, transformations, viewing, hidden surfaces and shading are the big steps of every rendering system, and this course walks through each of them. Next we look inside the display itself and the memory that holds the picture: the frame buffer.
key_points: Computer graphics creates and displays pictures from descriptions of shapes, objects, lights and cameras.
Image processing and computer vision go the other way: from images to information.
A raster screen is a grid of pixels; resolution is pixels across times pixels down (Full HD = 1920 x 1080, about 2.07 million).
Raster (bitmap) images store every pixel and are good for photos but get blocky when enlarged.
Vector images store shapes mathematically and stay sharp at any size, but are poor for photos.
Rasterization (scan conversion) turns shapes into pixels and is the core job of graphics.
Ivan Sutherland's Sketchpad (1963) is often called the start of interactive computer graphics.
The course follows the pipeline: raster algorithms, 2D transforms and clipping, 3D viewing, hidden surfaces, colour and shading, GPU and ray tracing.
lessons.tip: Buy a cheap graph-paper notebook just for this course. Every algorithm from lesson 3 onwards, plot its pixels by hand at least once; your eyes will catch mistakes your calculations miss.
lessons.task: Open any photo on your phone and zoom in as far as possible until you see blocks. Then open a PDF with text and zoom in the same way. Write two lines on why the photo gets blocky but the PDF letters stay sharp.

quiz.q: Which kind of image stores a circle as centre, radius and colour?
quiz.explain: Vector images store shapes as mathematical descriptions, not pixel grids.

quiz.q: How many pixels does a 1920 x 1080 screen have?
quiz.explain: 1920 x 1080 = 2,073,600 pixels, about 2 million.

quiz.q: What is rasterization (scan conversion)?
options: Converting a shape description into pixels
quiz.explain: Rasterization decides which pixels represent a line, circle or polygon.

quiz.q: Who built Sketchpad in 1963?
quiz.explain: Ivan Sutherland's Sketchpad at MIT is often called the start of interactive graphics.

quiz.q: Why is a logo usually stored as a vector image?
options: It stays sharp at any size
quiz.explain: Vector shapes are redrawn at any size, so edges remain sharp.

lessons.title: Display Hardware and the Frame Buffer
lessons.content:
Think of a big stadium card show, like the crowd pictures you see in opening ceremonies. Thousands of people each hold up a coloured card, and together they form a giant flag of Bangladesh. Each person is a pixel. But someone must have a master sheet that says which colour each seat should show, and the crowd must read it and hold up the right card, again and again. In a computer, that master sheet is a block of memory called the frame buffer, and the crowd is the display. This lesson is about how the picture in memory becomes light on the screen.

Why hardware matters for graphics: Every algorithm in this course ends by writing colours into memory. How much memory that takes, how fast it must be read, and why screens flicker or tear all depend on the display hardware. You do not need to be an electronics engineer, but you must know the vocabulary: raster scan, random scan, refresh rate, frame buffer, bit depth, lookup table, double buffering and aspect ratio. Exams ask these directly.

The CRT, the classic display: For decades screens were cathode ray tubes (CRTs). At the back sits an electron gun that shoots a narrow beam of electrons. Deflection coils or plates bend the beam left-right and up-down. Where the beam hits the front glass, a phosphor coating glows. In colour CRTs there are three guns and tiny red, green and blue phosphor dots for each spot. The glow fades quickly, in a fraction of a second; the time it keeps glowing is called persistence. So the picture must be redrawn many times per second, or it fades and flickers. Redrawing is called refreshing.

Refresh rate: The number of times per second the whole screen is redrawn is the refresh rate, measured in hertz. If it is too low, say below about 50 Hz, many people see flicker. Common values today are 60 Hz, and gaming monitors and many phones run at 90, 120 or 144 Hz. Do not confuse refresh rate with frame rate: refresh rate is how often the display shows a picture; frame rate is how often the program produces a new picture. A game running at 30 frames per second on a 60 Hz screen shows each frame twice.

Raster scan displays: In a raster scan system the beam sweeps the whole screen in a fixed pattern, row by row. It starts at the top-left, moves across the first row (a scan line), switching the beam stronger or weaker according to each pixel's value, then quickly jumps back to the left of the next row. That jump is the horizontal retrace. After the last row, the beam returns to the top-left; this is the vertical retrace. The picture comes from a frame buffer holding a value for every pixel. Television and almost all modern computer displays work in the raster way, which is why they can show photos and filled areas easily.

Interlacing: Older TVs used a trick to reduce flicker with limited bandwidth. Instead of drawing all lines in one pass, they drew the odd numbered lines in one pass (one field) and the even lines in the next pass. Two fields make one frame. The eye sees the screen refreshed twice as often, although each full frame still takes two passes. This is interlaced scanning, the i in 1080i; drawing all lines in order is progressive scanning, the p in 1080p.

Random scan (vector) displays: In a random scan display, also called vector or calligraphic display, the beam does not sweep every row. It moves directly from one point to another, drawing only the lines of the picture, like a pen plotter in light. The picture is stored as a list of line drawing commands called a display list or display file, and the system runs through this list 30 to 60 times per second. Lines look very smooth because there are no pixel steps. But filled areas and photos are almost impossible, and a very complex drawing with too many lines takes too long to refresh and begins to flicker. Early CAD systems and some radar screens used this approach.

Raster vs random scan in one table of words: Raster scan draws the whole screen every refresh, stores pixels in a frame buffer, handles filled areas, photos and colour well, but lines show jagged steps. Random scan draws only the lines, stores drawing commands, gives very smooth lines, and its refresh time depends on picture complexity. Exams often ask for exactly this comparison.

Flat panels: LCD, LED and OLED: Modern screens are flat panels. An LCD (liquid crystal display) has a light source behind it, the backlight, and in front of each subpixel a cell of liquid crystal between polarizing filters. A voltage changes how the crystals twist the light, so each cell lets more or less light through a red, green or blue filter. What shops call an LED TV is usually an LCD with an LED backlight. An OLED screen is different: each subpixel is an organic LED that makes its own light, so a black pixel is simply switched off, giving deep blacks and thin panels; many modern phones use OLED. Although none of these use an electron beam, they still update the image row by row from a frame buffer, so the raster ideas remain.

The frame buffer: The frame buffer, also called refresh buffer, is the memory that holds the colour value of every pixel. A part of the graphics hardware called the video controller (display controller) reads the frame buffer row by row, in step with the display's refresh, and sends the values to the screen. The program never draws on the glass directly; it only writes numbers into the frame buffer. Change the numbers and the next refresh shows the change.

Bit depth: How many bits are stored per pixel is the bit depth or colour depth. With 1 bit per pixel each pixel is either on or off, a black and white bitmap. With 8 bits there are 2^8 = 256 possible values. With 24 bits, 8 bits each for red, green and blue, there are 2^24 = 16,777,216 colours, called true colour. Often a fourth 8-bit channel called alpha is stored for transparency, making 32 bits per pixel.

Worked example, frame buffer size: How much memory does a 1920 x 1080 frame buffer need at 24 bits per pixel? Pixels = 1920 x 1080 = 2,073,600. Bytes per pixel = 24 / 8 = 3. Memory = 2,073,600 x 3 = 6,220,800 bytes. Dividing by 1,048,576 bytes per MiB gives about 5.93 MiB. At 60 refreshes per second the video controller must read 6,220,800 x 60 = 373,248,000 bytes per second, about 373 MB/s, just to show the picture. For a smaller example, 640 x 480 at 24 bits needs 640 x 480 x 3 = 921,600 bytes.

The colour lookup table: When memory was expensive, systems stored fewer bits per pixel and used a colour lookup table (CLUT), also called a palette. Each pixel stores an 8-bit index from 0 to 255. The table has 256 entries, and each entry holds a full 24-bit colour. To show a pixel, the controller reads its index, looks up the entry, and sends that colour. The image can use any 256 colours out of 16.7 million at once. A 640 x 480 image then needs 307,200 bytes plus a 768-byte table instead of 921,600 bytes. A neat trick: changing one table entry instantly changes every pixel using that index, which old games used for simple animation like flowing water. GIF images still use a palette of up to 256 colours.

Double buffering and tearing: If the program draws a new picture directly into the frame buffer that is being shown, the viewer may see half-drawn frames, and if the image changes while the controller is in the middle of the screen, the top part shows the old frame and the bottom part the new one, a visible horizontal break called tearing. The solution is double buffering: two buffers, a front buffer being displayed and a back buffer being drawn. When the new frame is complete, the two are swapped, ideally during the vertical retrace (vertical blank). Waiting for that moment is called vertical sync, or vsync. The cost is twice the memory.

Aspect ratio: Aspect ratio is the ratio of width to height. A 1920 x 1080 screen has 1920 / 1080 = 16 / 9, written 16:9; old monitors were 4:3, like 1024 x 768. There is also pixel aspect ratio: if pixels are not square, a mathematically perfect circle will look like an ellipse unless the program corrects for it. Most modern displays have square pixels, which makes our algorithms simpler.

Real life example 1, a phone screen: A phone with a 2400 x 1080 OLED panel at 32 bits per pixel needs 2400 x 1080 x 4 = 10,368,000 bytes, about 10 MB, per buffer. With double buffering that doubles. At 120 Hz the display pipeline reads the shown buffer 120 times a second. This is one reason a high refresh rate setting drains battery faster: more frames to produce and more data to move.

Real life example 2, a cricket match on an old TV: Grandfather's old CRT television in a village tea stall shows a Bangladesh match with a slight flicker and thin horizontal lines visible on fast moving players. That is interlacing at work: each field holds only half the lines, so fast motion between fields creates a comb-like edge. A modern LED TV showing the same match progressively looks steadier.

Common mistakes: Confusing refresh rate with frame rate. Thinking an LED TV is the same as an OLED TV. Forgetting to divide bits by 8 when computing bytes, or using 1,000,000 instead of 1,048,576 without saying which. Thinking random scan stores pixels; it stores line commands. And thinking a lookup table reduces the number of colours a screen can ever show; it limits how many can appear at once.

What exams ask: Compare raster and random scan displays. Explain the working of a CRT and the meaning of refresh, persistence and interlacing. Compute frame buffer size for a given resolution and bit depth. Explain the colour lookup table with an example. Explain double buffering and why it prevents flicker and tearing. Define aspect ratio.

Recap: Displays must be refreshed many times per second. Raster scan sweeps every row and shows the contents of a frame buffer; random scan draws only lines from a display list. Flat panels like LCD and OLED replaced CRTs but still update from a frame buffer. Memory = width x height x bits per pixel / 8. Lookup tables save memory, and double buffering hides drawing and prevents tearing. Next we start writing pixels into that frame buffer with our first algorithm: drawing a line.
key_points: A CRT shoots an electron beam at phosphor that glows briefly, so the picture must be refreshed many times per second.
Raster scan sweeps every row using horizontal and vertical retrace and shows a frame buffer; random scan draws only lines from a display list.
Interlacing draws odd lines then even lines (two fields per frame); progressive scanning draws all lines in order.
LCD panels filter a backlight; OLED subpixels emit their own light; both still refresh from a frame buffer.
Frame buffer memory = width x height x bits per pixel / 8; 1920 x 1080 x 24 bits = 6,220,800 bytes (about 5.93 MiB).
A colour lookup table stores small indices per pixel and a table of full colours, saving memory.
Double buffering draws into a back buffer and swaps during vertical blank to avoid flicker and tearing.
Aspect ratio is width to height, e.g. 16:9; non-square pixels distort circles.
lessons.tip: Memorise one worked frame buffer calculation with units written at every step (pixels, bits, bytes, MiB). Exams often give odd resolutions, and the units are where marks are lost.
lessons.task: Find your phone's screen resolution (Settings or a quick web search of the model). Compute its frame buffer size at 32 bits per pixel, then the bytes read per second at 60 Hz and at 120 Hz.

quiz.q: What does a random scan display store to make its picture?
options: A list of line drawing commands
quiz.explain: Random scan systems store a display list of line commands and trace them directly.

quiz.q: How many bytes does a 640 x 480 frame buffer need at 24 bits per pixel?
quiz.explain: 640 x 480 x 3 bytes = 921,600 bytes.

quiz.q: What problem does double buffering mainly solve?
options: Flicker and tearing from drawing into the visible buffer
quiz.explain: Drawing into a hidden back buffer and swapping at vertical blank hides partial frames.

quiz.q: In interlaced scanning, what is drawn in one field?
options: Either the odd lines or the even lines
Only the top half of the screen
quiz.explain: One field holds the odd lines, the next holds the even lines; two fields make a frame.

quiz.q: With an 8-bit colour lookup table, how many different colours can appear on screen at once?
quiz.explain: Each pixel stores an 8-bit index, so 256 table entries can be used at once.

lessons.title: Drawing Lines: Output Primitives and the DDA Algorithm
lessons.content:
Imagine you are tiling a floor with square tiles, and someone asks you to make a straight diagonal line of black tiles from one corner of the room to a spot on the far wall. You cannot cut tiles; each tile is either black or white. So you walk along the wall, one tile at a time, and at each step you ask: which tile is closest to the true line? The line you get is a staircase, but a good staircase looks straight from a distance. A computer screen is exactly that floor of tiles, and drawing a line on it is the first real problem of raster graphics.

Output primitives: The simplest building blocks a graphics system can draw are called output primitives: points, straight line segments, circles and other curves, filled polygons and text. Everything else, from a bar chart to a building plan, is made of these. A point is easy: set one pixel in the frame buffer, often written setPixel(x, y, colour). A line is the first primitive that needs an algorithm, because we must choose many pixels that together look like a straight segment between two end points.

Pixel coordinates: In this lesson pixels sit at integer coordinates (x, y). A line from (x0, y0) to (x1, y1) with integer end points passes between pixel centres most of the time, so at each step we must pick the nearest pixel. Our goal is three things: the line should look straight, it should look continuous with no gaps, and it should be drawn fast, because a game may draw millions of line pixels every second.

The line equation: From school geometry, a straight line can be written y = m x + b. The slope is m = dy / dx, where dx = x1 - x0 and dy = y1 - y0, and b is where the line crosses the y axis: b = y0 - m x0. For the line from (2,3) to (10,8): dx = 8, dy = 5, m = 5/8 = 0.625, and b = 3 - 0.625 x 2 = 1.75.

The naive method: Step x from x0 to x1 one pixel at a time, compute y = m x + b and round it. At x = 3, y = 0.625 x 3 + 1.75 = 3.625, rounded to 4. It works for gentle slopes, but every pixel needs a floating point multiplication and an addition, plus rounding. Worse, if the slope is steep, say m = 4, stepping x by 1 makes y jump by 4, leaving gaps in the line. We need something cheaper and gap-free.

The DDA idea: DDA stands for Digital Differential Analyzer. The key observation is that on a straight line, when x increases by 1, y always increases by exactly m. So instead of computing m x + b each time, we keep the previous y and add m. This turns a multiplication into an addition, an incremental method. In general, if x changes by delta x, y changes by m times delta x. DDA chooses the direction with more change and steps that one by exactly 1 per pixel.

Choosing the number of steps: Let steps = max(|dx|, |dy|). Then x increment = dx / steps and y increment = dy / steps. One of these increments is always +1 or -1, and the other has absolute value at most 1. That guarantees no gaps: in the direction of the larger change, we put exactly one pixel per column or per row.

The DDA algorithm in pseudo-code: dx = x1 - x0; dy = y1 - y0; steps = max(|dx|, |dy|); xinc = dx / steps; yinc = dy / steps; x = x0; y = y0; setPixel(round(x), round(y)); repeat steps times: x = x + xinc; y = y + yinc; setPixel(round(x), round(y)). That is all. Note that x and y are kept as real numbers; only the plotted pixel is rounded.

Worked example, (2,3) to (10,8): dx = 8, dy = 5, so steps = 8, xinc = 8/8 = 1, yinc = 5/8 = 0.625. Start at (2, 3) and plot (2, 3). Step 1: x = 3, y = 3.625, plot (3, 4). Step 2: x = 4, y = 4.25, plot (4, 4). Step 3: x = 5, y = 4.875, plot (5, 5). Step 4: x = 6, y = 5.5, plot (6, 6), rounding half up. Step 5: x = 7, y = 6.125, plot (7, 6). Step 6: x = 8, y = 6.75, plot (8, 7). Step 7: x = 9, y = 7.375, plot (9, 7). Step 8: x = 10, y = 8, plot (10, 8). The pixels are (2,3), (3,4), (4,4), (5,5), (6,6), (7,6), (8,7), (9,7), (10,8): nine pixels, one per column, ending exactly at the end point.

Worked example, a steep line (0,0) to (3,7): dx = 3, dy = 7, so steps = 7, xinc = 3/7, about 0.4286, yinc = 1. Now y moves by 1 each step and x creeps. The x values are 0.43, 0.86, 1.29, 1.71, 2.14, 2.57, 3.00, which round to 0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3. Pixels: (0,0), (0,1), (1,2), (1,3), (2,4), (2,5), (3,6), (3,7). One pixel per row, no gaps. If we had wrongly stepped x by 1, we would plot only 4 pixels for a line 7 rows tall, with big holes.

Negative slopes and direction: DDA handles all directions automatically because the increments carry the sign. For (0,0) to (5,-3): steps = 5, xinc = 1, yinc = -0.6. The y values are -0.6, -1.2, -1.8, -2.4, -3.0, which round to -1, -1, -2, -2, -3. Pixels: (0,0), (1,-1), (2,-1), (3,-2), (4,-2), (5,-3). If the line is given from right to left, dx is negative and xinc becomes -1; the same pixels are drawn in reverse order.

Why DDA is better than the naive method: It removes the multiplication per pixel, replacing it with additions. It automatically avoids gaps by stepping along the major axis. It is simple to write and easy to understand, which is why it appears in every syllabus and every exam.

The weaknesses of DDA: First, it still uses floating point numbers and a rounding operation for every pixel. On older hardware, and even now in tight loops, integer operations are cheaper. Second, because yinc is stored with limited precision, adding it hundreds of times accumulates round-off error. For a very long line the computed position can drift away from the true line, and the last pixel might not match the end point exactly. Third, rounding itself costs time. These weaknesses are what Bresenham's algorithm, the next lesson, removes by using only integers.

A note on rounding: Different books round 0.5 differently. Rounding half up gives 5.5 to 6, as we did. Some languages round half to even (Python's round gives 6 for 5.5 but 4 for 4.5). In exams, say which rule you use and stay consistent. A common safe formula is floor(v + 0.5).

Line attributes in brief: Real systems also let you set line width, line style (solid, dashed, dotted) and colour. A dashed line can be drawn by the same DDA loop, turning setPixel on for some steps and off for others, like a pattern 11110000 repeated. A thick line can be drawn by plotting a short vertical span at each column for gentle slopes, or a horizontal span for steep ones. These ideas reappear when we discuss attributes and antialiasing.

Counting the work: For our first example, DDA did 8 additions for x, 8 additions for y and 16 rounding operations, and no multiplications at all. The naive method did 8 multiplications, 8 additions and 8 roundings for y alone. On a modern computer both finish in a blink, but a 4K game screen may draw tens of millions of edge pixels per second, and in the 1960s and 1970s plotters and display processors had very weak arithmetic. Saving one multiplication per pixel was a big deal, and saving the floating point entirely, as Bresenham does, was even bigger.

Why diagonal lines look dimmer: A horizontal line of 10 pixels covers a length of 10 units. A 45 degree line from (0,0) to (10,10) also uses 11 pixels, one per column, but its true length is about 14.1 units, because the length is 10 times the square root of 2. The same number of pixels is spread over a longer distance, so the diagonal line looks a little thinner and dimmer than the horizontal one. High quality systems correct this by adjusting intensity with the slope or by using antialiasing, which we will meet in lesson 8.

Polylines: Most drawings are not single lines but chains of connected segments, called polylines: the outline of a country on a map, a graph of temperature over a week, the edge of a polygon. A polyline with points P0, P1, P2, P3 is drawn by running the line algorithm on P0P1, then P1P2, then P2P3. One small care is needed: the shared end point, like P1, would be plotted twice. For a solid colour that is harmless, but for transparent drawing or XOR drawing it makes a visible dot, so careful code skips the first pixel of every segment after the first.

Real life example 1, a cricket wagon wheel: TV graphics during a Bangladesh match show a wagon wheel, lines from the batter to where each shot went.
